Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids, then pg_terminate_backend), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

What is the difference between a shared and an exclusive lock?

A shared (read) lock lets others read the row but not change it, and many sessions can hold one at the same time. An exclusive (write) lock lets only its owner change the row. Every UPDATE and DELETE takes an exclusive lock until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Pessimistic or optimistic locking?

Pessimistic locking locks the row before you change it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Use it when clashes are common, such as the last seat on a bus. Optimistic locking takes no lock: each row has a version number, and the UPDATE works only WHERE row_version = the value you read. If 0 rows change, someone else was first, so read again and retry. Use it when clashes are rare.

Oracle Database 12c or newer (Oracle XE is free). Use SQL*Plus or SQL Developer. Step 1 creates the schema and Step 5 needs a DBA account. Oracle differs from the other three in several small ways, and the notes point them out.

Practise on a test server only. These commands create and delete things. Never run them on a live database, and never type a real password into this page.

Start here Install Oracle and log in

A database has two parts. The server is the program that stores the data and runs in the background. The client is the tool you type in (a command-line program or a window like Workbench). So you install the server and a client, start the server, and then log in with the client. In Oracle, a "database" is also called an instance, and users own schemas.

Step 1 Create the schema and tables

What it is: A database is a container for your data. A table stores the data in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet where every column has a fixed type.
Why use it: Every other step needs a place to keep the data.

01_create.sql

In Oracle a schema is a user, so "create the database" means creating the user company_db as a DBA. Connect to a pluggable database such as XEPDB1 (Oracle XE) first. In a container database, Oracle may require common user names to start with C##; a pluggable database does not.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. Oracle uses VARCHAR2 and NUMBER. Identity columns need Oracle 12c or newer.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create the schema user

As DBA, create the user company_db identified by "Str0ng_Pass1" with QUOTA UNLIMITED ON users. Grant it CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE TRIGGER.

Connect

Write CONNECT company_db/Str0ng_Pass1@localhost/XEPDB1.

departments table

Create departments with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY and department_name VARCHAR2(50) NOT NULL.

employees table

Create employees with id (same style), name VARCHAR2(100), department_id NUMBER REFERENCES departments(id) and salary NUMBER(10,2).

Step 2 Insert and query data

What it is: INSERT adds rows. SELECT reads them. WHERE keeps only the rows you want, and ORDER BY sorts them.
Why use it: This is the daily work: putting data in and getting answers out.

02_insert_query.sql

Oracle does not accept a list of rows in one VALUES, so use one INSERT per row. Oracle does not save changes until you COMMIT.

  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • COMMIT – saves your inserts for good. Without it, other sessions cannot see the new rows.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Insert

Insert 'IT' and then 'Human Resources' into departments (department_name) with two statements. Insert 'John', 1, 800000 into employees (name, department_id, salary). Finish with COMMIT;.

Select

Write SELECT * FROM employees;, then select name, salary where salary > 500000 ordered by salary DESC.

Step 3 JOIN

What it is: A JOIN combines rows from two tables using a matching column, for example employees.department_id = departments.id. A plain (inner) JOIN keeps only the rows that match in both tables.
Why use it: Data is split into several tables so nothing is repeated. JOIN puts it back together in one result.

03_join.sql

Oracle lets you alias a table, but without AS.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Join

Select e.name and d.department_name from employees e joined to departments d on e.department_id = d.id.

Step 4 Create a view

What it is: A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own.
Why use it: It hides a long query behind a short name, and it can hide private columns, such as salary, from some users.

Step 5 Users and roles

What it is: A user is a login. A role is a named set of privileges that you give to many users at once. GRANT gives a privilege and REVOKE takes it away.
Why use it: Each person gets only the access they need (least privilege), and you manage access once per role, not once per person.

Step 6 Backup and restore

What it is: A backup copies the database to a file. A restore loads that file back.
Why use it: It protects you from a failed disk, deleted data or ransomware. A backup you have never restored is not tested.

terminal

Oracle Data Pump (expdp and impdp) exports and imports a schema. DATA_PUMP_DIR is a folder on the database server. The tool asks for the password. For whole-database backups, DBAs use RMAN.

Practise it part by part

Export

Import

Step 7 Indexing

What it is: An index is a sorted lookup structure on a column, like the index at the back of a book.
Why use it: It makes WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY fast on big tables. The cost: slower inserts and updates, and extra disk space.

What it is: A trigger is code that runs by itself when a row is inserted, updated or deleted.
Why use it: It enforces a rule or records a change every time, even when the application forgets to.

Insert 'Amina' with department 1 and no salary, select her row, then COMMIT;.

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss after a failure. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore the database and resume operations.

In short: RPO = how often you save changes. RTO = how fast you can restore. Example: RPO 15 min means log backups every 15 min; RTO 1 hour means a tested restore that finishes in under 1 hour.

How to implement it (RPO 15 min, RTO 1 hour):

-- 1. Turn on archive log mode (once, as SYSDBA)
SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE; STARTUP MOUNT; ALTER DATABASE ARCHIVELOG; ALTER DATABASE OPEN;
-- 2. Full backup every night (RMAN, scheduled)
BACKUP DATABASE PLUS ARCHIVELOG;
-- 3. Every 15 min (RMAN, scheduled)                                 → RPO
BACKUP ARCHIVELOG ALL;
-- 4. Restore to a point in time (RMAN, database mounted)            → RTO
RUN { SET UNTIL TIME "TO_DATE('2026-10-26 09:59:59','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')";
      RESTORE DATABASE; RECOVER DATABASE; }
ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;

Then copy every backup to another server, and do a timed test restore each month: that time is your real RTO.

09_recovery.sql

Archive log mode keeps copies of the redo logs. With RMAN backups that lets you recover to a moment before the crash. Connect as a DBA.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Is archiving on?

Write SELECT log_mode FROM v$database;. The answer should be ARCHIVELOG.

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

What it is: Find the slow query, read its execution plan (how the database runs it), then fix the cause, most often a missing index.
Why use it: Slow queries are the most common complaint a DBA gets.

10_performance.sql

EXPLAIN PLAN saves the plan and DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY prints it. Look for TABLE ACCESS FULL versus INDEX RANGE SCAN.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Read the plan

Write EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name = 'John'; then SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);.

Fix it

Create idx_name_salary on employees (name, salary). Then select only name, salary where name = 'John'.

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

What it is:
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even with no match on the right. Missing values come back as NULL. Use it to find, for example, departments with no employees.
  • Three tables: chain one JOIN after another, each with its own ON.
  • GROUP BY turns many rows into one row per group, so you can COUNT, SUM or AVG each group. Example: staff per department.
  • HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY. WHERE filters rows before grouping. Example: HAVING COUNT(e.id) > 1 keeps departments with more than one person.
Order the database runs it: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.
Why use it: most reports are "how many / how much per group", and interviewers ask for them often.

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Connect as company_db for this step. Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name.

Practise it part by part

Add a projects table

Create projects with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, project_name VARCHAR2(80) and department_id NUMBER REFERENCES departments(id). Insert Payroll System (department 1) and Recruitment Drive (department 2) with two statements, then COMMIT;.

What it is: Change a view's query, see which views depend on a table, and drop a view you no longer need.
Why use it: When a table changes, the views built on it can break. You need to know what depends on what before you change anything.

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: Oracle lets you drop a table that a view uses, and marks the view INVALID. Check with SELECT object_name, status FROM user_objects WHERE object_type = 'VIEW';.

What it is: Take privileges back with REVOKE, put one role inside another, and drop roles that are no longer used.
Why use it: People change jobs and leave. Their access must be removed cleanly, and nested roles keep large setups simple.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

What it is: A trigger that writes who changed what, and when, into a separate audit table.
Why use it: It answers "who changed this salary?". Audits and security rules often require it.

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

:OLD is the row before the change and :NEW is the row after. A trigger runs inside your transaction, so the audit row is saved or rolled back together with the update.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Create salary_audit with an identity id, employee_id NUMBER, old_salary and new_salary (both NUMBER(10,2)), and changed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT SYSTIMESTAMP.

Audit trigger

Create or replace after_update_salary AFTER UPDATE OF salary ON employees FOR EACH ROW. In BEGIN ... END; insert :OLD.id, :OLD.salary, :NEW.salary into salary_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary). Finish with /.

Test and remove

Update John's salary to 900000, COMMIT;, select everything from salary_audit, then DROP TRIGGER after_update_salary;.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss after a failure. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore the database and resume operations. The business sets these two numbers, and you choose the tools to meet them.

DBA practical example: a bank. Suppose a bank has RPO = 5 minutes and RTO = 15 minutes. This means:
  • The bank cannot lose more than 5 minutes of transactions.
  • The database must be restored within 15 minutes.
To meet this, a nightly backup is not enough. The bank needs log backups at least every 5 minutes (or a standby server that copies every change as it happens), and a tested restore or automatic failover that finishes in under 15 minutes.
TargetWhat it meansWhat you need
RPO 24 hoursYou can lose one day of data.One full backup every night.
RPO 1 hourYou can lose one hour.A nightly full backup plus log backups every hour.
RPO near 0You can lose almost nothing.A standby server that copies every change as it happens.
RTO 4 hoursBack online within 4 hours.Restore from backup, if a test restore proves it fits.
RTO 1 hourBack online within 1 hour.A fast restore (small database, fast disks), or a standby server.
RTO a few minutesAlmost no downtime.Automatic failover to a standby server.
Work it out. Your RTO is 1 hour. The database backup is 60 GB, the restore runs at 30 GB per hour, and checking the data takes 30 minutes. Real recovery time = restore (2 hours) + checking (30 minutes) = 2 hours 30 minutes. You miss the target. The fix is a smaller or faster restore, or a standby server. Rule: RPO = time since the last backup or log. RTO = time to detect + get a server + restore + check.

recovery.sql

Point-in-time recovery needs archive log mode, so Oracle keeps every redo log. Run this as SYSDBA. It restarts the database, so do it on a test server.

Then recover with RMAN. In an rman target / session, with the database mounted, run RUN { SET UNTIL TIME "TO_DATE('2026-10-26 09:59:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')"; RESTORE DATABASE; RECOVER DATABASE; } and finish with ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;. Time the RESTORE step: that is your real RTO.

Step 16 Change data and tables

Interviewers often ask for the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. You practise on a scratch table, temp_staff, so your real employees table stays safe.

CommandWhat it removesWHERE?Undo?
DELETEThe rows you choose, or all rows, one by one.YesYes, until you commit (see Step 18).
TRUNCATEEvery row at once. The table and its columns stay.NoNo. It commits at once.
DROP TABLEThe whole table: rows, columns and indexes.NoUsually yes: the table goes to the recycle bin and FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP brings it back. DROP TABLE ... PURGE skips the bin.

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Step 18 Transactions and locking

What it is: A transaction is a group of changes that succeed or fail together, as one. A lock is the "busy" sign the database puts on a row while a transaction is using it.
Why use it: The transaction keeps the data right when something fails halfway. The lock keeps it right when many users work at the same time.

How they work together

  1. Start: make your first change. Oracle starts the transaction by itself. Your changes are now private: nobody else sees them yet.
  2. Change: every UPDATE or DELETE locks the rows it touches. Another session that wants to change the same row must wait.
  3. Finish: COMMIT; saves every change for good, and ROLLBACK undoes them all. Either way the locks come off, and the waiting session goes on.

Example. Amina sends 200 to Juma. The transaction makes sure the money leaves Amina and reaches Juma together, or not at all. The lock makes sure nobody else changes those two balances while it happens. The longer a transaction stays open, the longer others wait, so keep transactions short.

Deadlock. Session 1 locks Amina and then wants Juma. Session 2 locks Juma and then wants Amina. Each waits for the other forever, so the database stops one of them (the victim) and rolls it back. Avoid it by touching rows in the same order everywhere.

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The classic example is a bank transfer. ACID is the checklist interviewers expect.

LetterMeaningIn the bank transfer
A: AtomicityAll the changes in the transaction happen, or none do.Amina is never charged without Juma being paid.
C: ConsistencyThe data moves from one valid state to another. Constraints stay true.The total money in the two accounts stays the same.
I: IsolationTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work.Another user never sees the money gone from Amina but not yet in Juma.
D: DurabilityAfter COMMIT the data survives a crash.The transfer is still there after a power cut.

Isolation levels say what one transaction may see of another. The table follows the SQL standard; real databases can be stricter.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. Oracle runs READ COMMITTED by default and offers only that, SERIALIZABLE and READ ONLY. It never allows dirty reads. A transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and DDL such as CREATE TABLE commits by itself. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Accounts table

You are still connected as company_db. Create accounts with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR2(50) and balance NUMBER(10,2). Insert Amina 1000 and Juma 500 with two statements, then COMMIT;.

Transfer and COMMIT

Move 200 from Amina to Juma as one transaction: begin with nothing: Oracle starts a transaction by itself at your first change, subtract 200 from Amina, add 200 to Juma, then COMMIT;. Both changes are saved together.

A mistake and ROLLBACK

Begin again and subtract 900 from Amina. Select everything: her balance is now negative. Then ROLLBACK; and select again: the change is gone.

SAVEPOINT

Begin, subtract 100 from Amina, then set a savepoint called after_debit. Add 1000 to Juma by mistake and go back to the savepoint with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_debit;. Add the right 100 to Juma and COMMIT;.

Isolation level

Write SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; (it must be the first statement of a transaction, which is why the last COMMIT came just before), select everything and commit.

Clean up

Drop accounts.

Locking in practice

The transactions above changed rows one session at a time. Here two sessions want the same row, and locks make them take turns.

LockWhat it meansHow you ask for it
Shared (S)A read lock. Others may read the row, but nobody may change it.LOCK TABLE seats IN SHARE MODE (Oracle has no shared row lock)
Exclusive (X)A write lock. Nobody else may change or lock the row. Every UPDATE and DELETE takes one.SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Row lock or table lockLock only the rows you touch (many users at once) or the whole table (one user at a time).LOCK TABLE seats IN EXCLUSIVE MODE
Do not waitFail at once, or skip the rows someone else holds, instead of waiting.NOWAIT, SKIP LOCKED
Lock timeoutHow long a session waits for a lock before it gives up with an error.FOR UPDATE WAIT 5 (waits forever by default)
Pessimistic or optimisticPessimistic: lock the row first, then change it. Optimistic: lock nothing, but change the row only if its row_version is still the one you read.WHERE row_version = 0

See a lock with your own eyes (test server only). Run part 1 of the file below first, then:

  1. In window 1 run SELECT * FROM seats WHERE seat_no = 'A1' FOR UPDATE;. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2 run UPDATE seats SET booked_by = 'Juma' WHERE seat_no = 'A1';. It waits: window 1 holds the row.
  3. In window 1 run COMMIT;. Window 2 finishes at once. A1 now belongs to Juma, until part 2 books it for Amina.

18b_locking.sql

Book cinema seats safely: lock one row, read with a shared lock, skip busy rows, set a wait limit, lock a whole table, and use a version number instead of a lock.

In this database. Readers never wait and never block: a plain SELECT takes no lock. Only UPDATE, DELETE and FOR UPDATE lock rows, and Oracle never turns row locks into a table lock. Every lock ends at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. NOWAIT fails with ORA-00054, and WAIT 5 with ORA-30006. Expected: after part 2, A1 is booked by Amina. Part 4 returns A2 and A3, the free seats. In part 7 the first UPDATE says 1 row updated and the second 0 rows updated. At the end: A1 Amina 0, A2 Juma 1, A3 empty 0.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Seats table

You are still connected as company_db. Create seats with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, seat_no VARCHAR2(5) NOT NULL UNIQUE, booked_by VARCHAR2(50) and row_version NUMBER DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL. Insert the seats A1, A2 and A3 with three statements, then COMMIT;.

Pessimistic lock: FOR UPDATE

Lock seat A1 with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, book it for Amina, then COMMIT;. Nobody can take A1 between your read and your update.

Shared lock: SHARE MODE

Lock the table IN SHARE MODE (others can read it, nobody can change it), read seat A3, then COMMIT;.

Skip the busy rows

Lock every free seat that nobody else holds: WHERE booked_by IS NULL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Then COMMIT;.

Do not wait forever

Lock A1 FOR UPDATE WAIT 5 (give up after 5 seconds), then COMMIT;. FOR UPDATE NOWAIT would fail at once instead.

Table lock

Lock the whole table with LOCK TABLE seats IN EXCLUSIVE MODE;, clear the booking of A3, then COMMIT;.

Optimistic lock: row_version

Book A2 for Juma only WHERE seat_no = 'A2' AND row_version = 0, adding 1 to row_version. Then try the same for Neema, COMMIT; and SELECT * FROM seats;.

Clean up

Drop seats.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

A user phones: "the system is frozen". Usually one session holds a lock and others wait for it. You list the sessions, find who blocks whom, and end the blocker.

ProblemWhat you seeWhat you do
BlockingA statement waits, and v$session.blocking_session names the blockerKill the blocker, or ask its owner to commit or roll back.
DeadlockORA-00060: deadlock detected while waiting for resourceOracle rolls back one statement and writes a trace file. Run the work again and look at the trace to see which rows clashed.
Idle in a transactionA session did an update and never committed, so others wait on it.Ask the owner to commit or roll back. If you cannot, end the session.

Make a block on purpose (test server only), so you have something to find:

  1. In window 1, as company_db, run UPDATE employees SET salary = salary WHERE name = 'John';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2, as company_db, run the same UPDATE. It waits.
  3. In window 3, connected to the pluggable database as a DBA, run the statements below, find window 1's sid and serial# and kill it. Window 2 then finishes.

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. The v$ views and ALTER SYSTEM need DBA rights, so run this file as a DBA, not as company_db. The killed session shows as KILLED until Oracle finishes rolling it back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

List the sessions

Select sid, serial#, username, status, osuser, machine from v$session where username IS NOT NULL.

Find the blocker

Select sid, serial#, username, blocking_session, wait_class, seconds_in_wait from v$session where blocking_session IS NOT NULL. The blocking_session column holds the sid of the blocker.

End the blocker

Write ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION '123,4567' IMMEDIATE;. The two numbers are the blocker's sid and serial#, which you read from v$session.

Locks that wait or block

Select sid, type, lmode, request, block from v$lock where request > 0 OR block = 1.

Step 20 Stored procedures

What it is: A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved inside the database. You call it by name and pass it parameters.
Why use it: You write the logic once and reuse it, one call replaces many statements, and users can be allowed to run it without direct access to the tables.

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named PL/SQL block saved inside the database. You run it with EXEC instead of retyping the statements. Run this as company_db in SQL*Plus or SQLcl.

  • CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE – saves the procedure, replacing an older version with the same name.
  • p_dept IN NUMBER / p_total OUT NUMBER – parameters: IN brings a value in, OUT sends one back.
  • AS BEGIN … END; – the PL/SQL body. / on its own line runs the block.
  • SELECT … INTO – puts a query result into a variable.
  • VARIABLE / EXEC / PRINT – make a SQL*Plus variable, run the procedure, show the value.
  • user_objects / DROP PROCEDURE – list your procedures and whether they are VALID / delete one.
Your company_db user needs the right to create procedures. As a DBA run GRANT CREATE PROCEDURE TO company_db; once.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

raise_salary

Create or replace raise_salary(p_dept IN NUMBER, p_pct IN NUMBER). Its body updates salary to salary * (1 + p_pct / 100) for that department, then COMMIT;. Finish with /.

count_employees

Create or replace count_employees(p_dept IN NUMBER, p_total OUT NUMBER) that counts the department's employees INTO p_total. Finish with /.

Call them

Run raise_salary(1, 10). Declare VARIABLE total NUMBER, run count_employees(1, :total) and PRINT total.

List and drop

Select object_name, status from user_objects where object_type = 'PROCEDURE', then drop count_employees.

Step 21 Window functions

What it is: A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) but, unlike GROUP BY, still shows every row.
Why use it: Rankings, running totals and "top earner in each department" become one short query.

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add sample rows

Add Mary (1, 900000), Peter (1, 700000), Asha (2, 600000) and Neema (2, 650000) with one INSERT each, then COMMIT;.

Rank everyone

Select name, department_id, salary with ROW_NUMBER() as row_num, RANK() as rnk and DENSE_RANK() as dense_rnk, all OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).

Per department

Add PARTITION BY department_id: RANK() by salary as dept_rank, SUM(salary) as dept_total and AVG(salary) as dept_avg.

Previous, next, running total

Ordered by salary: LAG(salary) as prev_salary, LEAD(salary) as next_salary, and a running SUM(salary) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW as running_total.

Top earner per department

In a subquery ranked, number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn. Outside, keep rn = 1.

Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (v$session (the blocking_session column), then ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

What is the difference between a shared and an exclusive lock?

A shared (read) lock lets others read the row but not change it, and many sessions can hold one at the same time. An exclusive (write) lock lets only its owner change the row. Every UPDATE and DELETE takes an exclusive lock until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Pessimistic or optimistic locking?

Pessimistic locking locks the row before you change it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Use it when clashes are common, such as the last seat on a bus. Optimistic locking takes no lock: each row has a version number, and the UPDATE works only WHERE row_version = the value you read. If 0 rows change, someone else was first, so read again and retry. Use it when clashes are rare.

SQL Server 2019 or newer (the free Developer or Express edition works). Use SSMS or sqlcmd. Remember: GO ends a batch, and a few statements (CREATE VIEW, CREATE TRIGGER) must be the first in their batch.

Practise on a test server only. These commands create and delete things. Never run them on a live database, and never type a real password into this page.

Start here Install SQL Server and log in

A database has two parts. The server is the program that stores the data and runs in the background. The client is the tool you type in (a command-line program or a window like Workbench). So you install the server and a client, start the server, and then log in with the client.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

What it is: A database is a container for your data. A table stores the data in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet where every column has a fixed type.
Why use it: Every other step needs a place to keep the data.

01_create.sql

Run this in SSMS or sqlcmd. GO is not SQL: it is a tool command that ends a batch and sends it to the server.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. SQL Server uses IDENTITY(1,1) instead of AUTO_INCREMENT.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Write CREATE DATABASE company_db; GO USE company_db; GO, each on its own line.

departments table

Create departments with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY and department_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL.

employees table

Create employees with id (same style), name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES departments(id) and salary DECIMAL(10,2). End with GO.

Step 2 Insert and query data

What it is: INSERT adds rows. SELECT reads them. WHERE keeps only the rows you want, and ORDER BY sorts them.
Why use it: This is the daily work: putting data in and getting answers out.

02_insert_query.sql

Add rows, then read them back with WHERE and ORDER BY.

  • USE – picks the database the next commands run in.
  • GO – ends a batch, so SQL Server runs everything above it first.
  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Insert

Write USE company_db; then GO. Insert IT and Human Resources into departments(department_name) in one statement. Then insert John, department 1, salary 800000 into employees(name, department_id, salary).

Select

Write SELECT * FROM employees;, then select name, salary where salary > 500000 ordered by salary DESC.

Step 3 JOIN

What it is: A JOIN combines rows from two tables using a matching column, for example employees.department_id = departments.id. A plain (inner) JOIN keeps only the rows that match in both tables.
Why use it: Data is split into several tables so nothing is repeated. JOIN puts it back together in one result.

03_join.sql

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Join

Write USE company_db; then select e.name and d.department_name from employees e joined to departments d on e.department_id = d.id.

Step 4 Create a view

What it is: A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own.
Why use it: It hides a long query behind a short name, and it can hide private columns, such as salary, from some users.

04_view.sql

CREATE VIEW must be the first statement in its batch, so it sits between two GO lines.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

View

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create employee_view as SELECT name, salary FROM employees, then GO, then select everything from the view.

Step 5 Users and roles

What it is: A user is a login. A role is a named set of privileges that you give to many users at once. GRANT gives a privilege and REVOKE takes it away.
Why use it: Each person gets only the access they need (least privilege), and you manage access once per role, not once per person.

05_users.sql

SQL Server has two levels. A login lets someone connect to the server. A user maps that login to one database, where the permissions are granted.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Login

Create the login analyst WITH PASSWORD = 'Str0ng_Pass!'.

User and grant

Write USE company_db;, create the user analyst FOR LOGIN analyst, then GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo TO analyst;.

Role

Create the role report_reader, grant it SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo, then ALTER ROLE report_reader ADD MEMBER analyst;.

Step 6 Backup and restore

What it is: A backup copies the database to a file. A restore loads that file back.
Why use it: It protects you from a failed disk, deleted data or ransomware. A backup you have never restored is not tested.

06_backup.sql

Backups are T-SQL commands. The path is on the SQL Server machine, and the SQL Server service account must be able to write to it. Create the folder first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Backup

Write BACKUP DATABASE company_db TO DISK = 'C:\Backup\company_db.bak' WITH INIT;.

Restore

Write USE master;, then RESTORE DATABASE company_db FROM DISK = 'C:\Backup\company_db.bak' WITH REPLACE;.

Step 7 Indexing

What it is: An index is a sorted lookup structure on a column, like the index at the back of a book.
Why use it: It makes WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY fast on big tables. The cost: slower inserts and updates, and extra disk space.

07_index.sql

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create and check

Write USE company_db;. Create idx_name on employees (name), then run EXEC sp_helpindex 'employees';.

Step 8 Triggers

What it is: A trigger is code that runs by itself when a row is inserted, updated or deleted.
Why use it: It enforces a rule or records a change every time, even when the application forgets to.

08_trigger.sql

SQL Server has no BEFORE trigger. An AFTER INSERT trigger fixes the row just after it is saved. The inserted table holds the new rows. A simpler way is a default: salary DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 0.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Trigger

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create after_insert_employee ON employees AFTER INSERT AS. In BEGIN ... END update e setting e.salary = 0 from employees e joined to inserted i on e.id = i.id where i.salary IS NULL. End with GO.

Test it

Insert 'Amina' with department 1 and no salary, then select her row.

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss after a failure. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore the database and resume operations.

In short: RPO = how often you save changes. RTO = how fast you can restore. Example: RPO 15 min means log backups every 15 min; RTO 1 hour means a tested restore that finishes in under 1 hour.

How to implement it (RPO 15 min, RTO 1 hour):

-- 1. Full recovery model, so the log can be backed up
ALTER DATABASE company_db SET RECOVERY FULL;
-- 2. Full backup every night (SQL Server Agent job)
BACKUP DATABASE company_db TO DISK = 'D:\Backup\full.bak' WITH INIT, CHECKSUM;
-- 3. Log backup every 15 min (SQL Server Agent job)                 → RPO
BACKUP LOG company_db TO DISK = 'D:\Backup\log_0945.trn';
-- 4. Restore: full, then logs up to the failure                     → RTO
RESTORE DATABASE company_db FROM DISK = 'D:\Backup\full.bak' WITH NORECOVERY, REPLACE;
RESTORE LOG company_db FROM DISK = 'D:\Backup\log_0945.trn' WITH STOPAT = '2026-10-26 09:59:59', RECOVERY;

Then copy every backup to another server, and do a timed test restore each month: that time is your real RTO.

09_recovery.sql

In the FULL recovery model you can back up the transaction log, for example every 15 minutes, which sets the RPO. The log backup needs an earlier full backup (Step 6).

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Full recovery and log backup

Write ALTER DATABASE company_db SET RECOVERY FULL;, then BACKUP LOG company_db TO DISK = 'C:\Backup\company_log.trn';.

Check the model

Select name, recovery_model_desc from sys.databases where name = 'company_db'.

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

What it is: Find the slow query, read its execution plan (how the database runs it), then fix the cause, most often a missing index.
Why use it: Slow queries are the most common complaint a DBA gets.

10_performance.sql

SET STATISTICS IO ON shows how many pages a query reads. Fewer reads after the index means it worked. In SSMS you can also turn on "Include Actual Execution Plan".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Measure

Write USE company_db;, SET STATISTICS IO ON;, then SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name = 'John';.

Fix it

Create idx_name_salary on employees (name, salary). Then select only name, salary where name = 'John'.

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

What it is:
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even with no match on the right. Missing values come back as NULL. Use it to find, for example, departments with no employees.
  • Three tables: chain one JOIN after another, each with its own ON.
  • GROUP BY turns many rows into one row per group, so you can COUNT, SUM or AVG each group. Example: staff per department.
  • HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY. WHERE filters rows before grouping. Example: HAVING COUNT(e.id) > 1 keeps departments with more than one person.
Order the database runs it: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.
Why use it: most reports are "how many / how much per group", and interviewers ask for them often.

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name (NULL). A plain JOIN would hide it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add a projects table

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create projects with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, project_name VARCHAR(80) and department_id INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES departments(id). Insert Payroll System (department 1) and Recruitment Drive (department 2) in one statement.

LEFT JOIN

Select d.department_name and e.name from departments d with a LEFT JOIN employees e on e.department_id = d.id. A LEFT JOIN keeps every department, even one with no employee.

Join three tables

Select e.name, d.department_name and p.project_name from employees e. JOIN departments d on e.department_id = d.id, then JOIN projects p on p.department_id = d.id.

JOIN with GROUP BY

Select d.department_name and COUNT(e.id) AS staff from departments d with a LEFT JOIN employees e on e.department_id = d.id, grouped by d.department_name.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

What it is: Change a view's query, see which views depend on a table, and drop a view you no longer need.
Why use it: When a table changes, the views built on it can break. You need to know what depends on what before you change anything.

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: SQL Server lets you drop a table a view uses, and the view then fails. Create the view WITH SCHEMABINDING and SQL Server will refuse to drop the table under it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create a view over a join

Create dept_staff as the department-and-staff-count query (the GROUP BY query from Step 11), then select everything from it.

Change a view

Replace employee_view so it also shows department_id. SQL Server uses ALTER VIEW. End with GO.

What does a view depend on?

Select table_name from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEW_TABLE_USAGE where view_name = 'employee_view'.

Drop a view

Write DROP VIEW dept_staff;.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

What it is: Take privileges back with REVOKE, put one role inside another, and drop roles that are no longer used.
Why use it: People change jobs and leave. Their access must be removed cleanly, and nested roles keep large setups simple.

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: a role must have no members before you can drop it. The database user must be dropped before its login is no longer needed.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Take away a direct privilege

Write USE company_db;. Revoke SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo from analyst. Then select dp.name AS role_name and m.name AS member_name from sys.database_role_members rm, joined to sys.database_principals dp on rm.role_principal_id = dp.principal_id and to sys.database_principals m on rm.member_principal_id = m.principal_id.

DENY beats GRANT

Write DENY SELECT ON dbo.employees TO analyst;. A deny wins over a grant from any role. Then REVOKE SELECT ON dbo.employees FROM analyst; removes the deny.

Clean up in order

Remove analyst from report_reader with ALTER ROLE ... DROP MEMBER, drop the role, drop the user. Then USE master; and drop the login.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

What it is: A trigger that writes who changed what, and when, into a separate audit table.
Why use it: It answers "who changed this salary?". Audits and security rules often require it.

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

SQL Server has no OLD and NEW. It gives two virtual tables: deleted (the rows before) and inserted (the rows after). The trigger runs once per statement, not once per row, so it may see many rows.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create salary_audit with an identity id, employee_id INT, old_salary and new_salary (both DECIMAL(10,2)), and changed_at DATETIME DEFAULT GETDATE(). End with GO.

Audit trigger

Create after_update_salary ON employees AFTER UPDATE AS. In BEGIN ... END; insert into salary_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary) the d.id, d.salary, i.salary from deleted d joined to inserted i on d.id = i.id where d.salary <> i.salary. End with GO.

Test and remove

Update John's salary to 900000, select everything from salary_audit, then DROP TRIGGER after_update_salary;.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss after a failure. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore the database and resume operations. The business sets these two numbers, and you choose the tools to meet them.

DBA practical example: a bank. Suppose a bank has RPO = 5 minutes and RTO = 15 minutes. This means:
  • The bank cannot lose more than 5 minutes of transactions.
  • The database must be restored within 15 minutes.
To meet this, a nightly backup is not enough. The bank needs log backups at least every 5 minutes (or a standby server that copies every change as it happens), and a tested restore or automatic failover that finishes in under 15 minutes.
TargetWhat it meansWhat you need
RPO 24 hoursYou can lose one day of data.One full backup every night.
RPO 1 hourYou can lose one hour.A nightly full backup plus log backups every hour.
RPO near 0You can lose almost nothing.A standby server that copies every change as it happens.
RTO 4 hoursBack online within 4 hours.Restore from backup, if a test restore proves it fits.
RTO 1 hourBack online within 1 hour.A fast restore (small database, fast disks), or a standby server.
RTO a few minutesAlmost no downtime.Automatic failover to a standby server.
Work it out. Your RTO is 1 hour. The database backup is 60 GB, the restore runs at 30 GB per hour, and checking the data takes 30 minutes. Real recovery time = restore (2 hours) + checking (30 minutes) = 2 hours 30 minutes. You miss the target. The fix is a smaller or faster restore, or a standby server. Rule: RPO = time since the last backup or log. RTO = time to detect + get a server + restore + check.

11_rpo.sql

Combine a full, a differential and a log backup. Then restore to a point in time with STOPAT. The paths are on the SQL Server machine.

Run the restore from master: USE master; first, because you cannot restore a database you are using. Time the restore: that is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Differential backup

Write BACKUP DATABASE company_db TO DISK = 'C:\Backup\company_diff.bak' WITH DIFFERENTIAL;. It saves only what changed since the last full backup.

Restore to a time

Restore the full backup WITH NORECOVERY, REPLACE. Then RESTORE LOG from C:\Backup\company_log.trn WITH STOPAT = '2026-10-26 09:59:00', RECOVERY;.

Step 16 Change data and tables

Interviewers often ask for the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. You practise on a scratch table, temp_staff, so your real employees table stays safe.

CommandWhat it removesWHERE?Undo?
DELETEThe rows you choose, or all rows, one by one.YesYes, until you commit (see Step 18).
TRUNCATEEvery row at once. The table and its columns stay.NoYes, inside a transaction. It also restarts the IDENTITY counter.
DROP TABLEThe whole table: rows, columns and indexes.NoYes, inside a transaction you roll back. Otherwise restore from a backup.

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Scratch table

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create temp_staff with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) and salary DECIMAL(10,2). Insert Amina 500000, Juma 600000 and Neema 700000 into temp_staff (name, salary) with one statement.

UPDATE

Raise Juma's salary by 10% with salary = salary * 1.10 and a WHERE on the name. Then select everything to see the change.

DELETE

Delete Neema with a WHERE, then select everything again.

ALTER TABLE

Add a column with ALTER TABLE temp_staff ADD phone VARCHAR(20);, then GO. Remove it with ALTER TABLE temp_staff DROP COLUMN phone;, then GO.

TRUNCATE and DROP

Empty the table with TRUNCATE TABLE temp_staff;, then remove the table itself with DROP TABLE temp_staff;.

Step 17 Constraints

A constraint is a rule the database enforces for you, so bad data cannot get in.

ConstraintWhat it doesIn this step

FOREIGN KEYThe value must exist in another table.tasks.department_id
UNIQUENo two rows may share the value.email

When you run the three bad inserts, these are the errors to look for:

Rule brokenMessage (the wording may differ a little)
UNIQUEMsg 2627: Violation of UNIQUE KEY constraint ... Cannot insert duplicate key
NOT NULLMsg 515: Cannot insert the value NULL into column 'name'

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Table with rules

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create contacts with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, age INT CHECK (age >= 18) and status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'active'.

A good row

Insert Amina (amina@example.com, age 30) giving only the email, name and age. Select everything: the status column was filled in by DEFAULT.

Three bad rows

Write three inserts that each break one rule, and watch each one fail: the same email again (UNIQUE), a row with no name (NOT NULL), and age 15 (CHECK). Use Juma 31, Neema 25 and Baraka 15.

Cascade table

Create tasks with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, department_id INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES departments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE and task VARCHAR(100).

Test the cascade

Insert a department called Temp. Insert one task for it with INSERT ... SELECT id, 'Test task' FROM departments WHERE .... Delete the department, then select everything from tasks: the task is gone too.

Clean up

Drop tasks, then contacts.

Step 18 Transactions and locking

What it is: A transaction is a group of changes that succeed or fail together, as one. A lock is the "busy" sign the database puts on a row while a transaction is using it.
Why use it: The transaction keeps the data right when something fails halfway. The lock keeps it right when many users work at the same time.

How they work together

  1. Start: run BEGIN TRANSACTION;. Your changes are now private: nobody else sees them yet.
  2. Change: every UPDATE or DELETE locks the rows it touches. Another session that wants to change the same row must wait.
  3. Finish: COMMIT TRANSACTION; saves every change for good, and ROLLBACK undoes them all. Either way the locks come off, and the waiting session goes on.

Example. Amina sends 200 to Juma. The transaction makes sure the money leaves Amina and reaches Juma together, or not at all. The lock makes sure nobody else changes those two balances while it happens. The longer a transaction stays open, the longer others wait, so keep transactions short.

Deadlock. Session 1 locks Amina and then wants Juma. Session 2 locks Juma and then wants Amina. Each waits for the other forever, so the database stops one of them (the victim) and rolls it back. Avoid it by touching rows in the same order everywhere.

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The classic example is a bank transfer. ACID is the checklist interviewers expect.

LetterMeaningIn the bank transfer
A: AtomicityAll the changes in the transaction happen, or none do.Amina is never charged without Juma being paid.
C: ConsistencyThe data moves from one valid state to another. Constraints stay true.The total money in the two accounts stays the same.
I: IsolationTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work.Another user never sees the money gone from Amina but not yet in Juma.
D: DurabilityAfter COMMIT the data survives a crash.The transfer is still there after a power cut.

Isolation levels say what one transaction may see of another. The table follows the SQL standard; real databases can be stricter.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. SQL Server runs READ COMMITTED by default and also offers SNAPSHOT. Each statement commits alone unless you BEGIN TRANSACTION. Add SET XACT_ABORT ON; in real code so a runtime error rolls the whole transaction back. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Accounts table

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create accounts with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR(50) and balance DECIMAL(10,2). Insert Amina 1000 and Juma 500 in one statement.

Transfer and COMMIT

Move 200 from Amina to Juma as one transaction: begin with BEGIN TRANSACTION;, subtract 200 from Amina, add 200 to Juma, then COMMIT TRANSACTION;. Both changes are saved together.

A mistake and ROLLBACK

Begin again and subtract 900 from Amina. Select everything: her balance is now negative. Then ROLLBACK TRANSACTION; and select again: the change is gone.

SAVEPOINT

Begin, subtract 100 from Amina, then set a savepoint called after_debit. Add 1000 to Juma by mistake and go back to the savepoint with ROLLBACK TRANSACTION after_debit;. Add the right 100 to Juma and COMMIT TRANSACTION;.

Isolation level

Set SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;, then begin a transaction, select everything and commit it.

Clean up

Drop accounts.

Locking in practice

The transactions above changed rows one session at a time. Here two sessions want the same row, and locks make them take turns.

LockWhat it meansHow you ask for it
Shared (S)A read lock. Others may read the row, but nobody may change it.WITH (HOLDLOCK)
Exclusive (X)A write lock. Nobody else may change or lock the row. Every UPDATE and DELETE takes one.WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK)
Row lock or table lockLock only the rows you touch (many users at once) or the whole table (one user at a time).WITH (TABLOCKX)
Do not waitFail at once, or skip the rows someone else holds, instead of waiting.WITH (READPAST), WITH (NOWAIT)
Lock timeoutHow long a session waits for a lock before it gives up with an error.SET LOCK_TIMEOUT 5000 (waits forever by default)
Pessimistic or optimisticPessimistic: lock the row first, then change it. Optimistic: lock nothing, but change the row only if its row_version is still the one you read.WHERE row_version = 0

See a lock with your own eyes (test server only). Run part 1 of the file below first, then:

  1. In window 1 run BEGIN TRANSACTION; and SELECT * FROM seats WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) WHERE seat_no = 'A1';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2 run UPDATE seats SET booked_by = 'Juma' WHERE seat_no = 'A1';. It waits: window 1 holds the row.
  3. In window 1 run COMMIT TRANSACTION;. Window 2 finishes at once. A1 now belongs to Juma, until part 2 books it for Amina.

18b_locking.sql

Book cinema seats safely: lock one row, read with a shared lock, skip busy rows, set a wait limit, lock a whole table, and use a version number instead of a lock.

In this database. SQL Server asks for locks with table hints in WITH (...). Under the default READ COMMITTED, even a plain SELECT takes short shared locks, unless READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on. When one statement holds about 5,000 locks on a table, SQL Server swaps them for one table lock (lock escalation). UPDLOCK stops the deadlock where two sessions both read and then update. A lock timeout fails with error 1222. Expected: after part 2, A1 is booked by Amina. Part 4 returns A2, the first free seat. In part 7 the first @@ROWCOUNT is 1 and the second is 0, because row_version is already 1. At the end: A1 Amina 0, A2 Juma 1, A3 empty 0.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Seats table

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create seats with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, seat_no VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL UNIQUE, booked_by VARCHAR(50) and row_version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, then GO. Insert the seats A1, A2 and A3 in one statement.

Pessimistic lock: UPDLOCK

Begin a transaction. Lock seat A1 with WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK), book it for Amina, then COMMIT TRANSACTION;. Nobody can take A1 between your read and your update.

Shared lock: HOLDLOCK

Begin, read seat A3 WITH (HOLDLOCK) (the shared lock stays until the end, so nobody can change it), then commit.

Skip the busy rows

Begin and take the first free seat that nobody else holds: SELECT TOP 1 * FROM seats WITH (UPDLOCK, READPAST, ROWLOCK) WHERE booked_by IS NULL ORDER BY id. Then commit.

Do not wait forever

Set SET LOCK_TIMEOUT 5000; (milliseconds). Begin, lock A1 WITH (UPDLOCK), then commit.

Table lock

Begin, clear the booking of A3 with UPDATE seats WITH (TABLOCKX) so the whole table is locked, then commit.

Optimistic lock: row_version

Book A2 for Juma only WHERE seat_no = 'A2' AND row_version = 0, adding 1 to row_version, and show SELECT @@ROWCOUNT;. Then try the same for Neema and show @@ROWCOUNT again. Finish with SELECT * FROM seats;.

Clean up

Drop seats.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

A user phones: "the system is frozen". Usually one session holds a lock and others wait for it. You list the sessions, find who blocks whom, and end the blocker.

ProblemWhat you seeWhat you do
BlockingA query hangs, and blocking_session_id names the blockerKill the blocker, or ask its owner to commit.
DeadlockError 1205: Transaction was deadlocked ... and has been chosen as the deadlock victimSQL Server rolls the victim back for you. Run it again. The system_health event session records the deadlock graph.
Idle in a transactionA session did an update and never committed, so others wait on it.Ask the owner to commit or roll back. If you cannot, end the session.

Make a block on purpose (test server only), so you have something to find:

  1. In window 1 run BEGIN TRANSACTION; and UPDATE employees SET salary = salary WHERE name = 'John';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2 run the same UPDATE. It waits.
  3. In window 3, as an admin, run the statements below, find window 1's session_id and kill it. Window 2 then finishes.

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. Reading the sys.dm_ views needs the VIEW SERVER STATE permission. The older shortcut EXEC sp_who2; shows a BlkBy column that names the blocker. Killing a session rolls back its open transaction.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

List the sessions

Select session_id, login_name, status, host_name, program_name from sys.dm_exec_sessions where is_user_process = 1.

Find the blocker

Select session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, command from sys.dm_exec_requests where blocking_session_id <> 0.

End the blocker

End the blocker with KILL 55;. Use the blocking_session_id you found in place of 55.

Locks that are waiting

Select request_session_id, resource_type, request_mode, request_status from sys.dm_tran_locks where request_status = 'WAIT'.

Step 20 Stored procedures

What it is: A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved inside the database. You call it by name and pass it parameters.
Why use it: You write the logic once and reuse it, one call replaces many statements, and users can be allowed to run it without direct access to the tables.

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of T-SQL saved inside the database. You run it with EXEC instead of retyping the statements.

  • CREATE PROCEDURE name @param TYPE – saves the procedure. Parameters start with @.
  • AS BEGIN … END – the statements the procedure runs.
  • @total INT OUTPUT – an output parameter that sends a value back.
  • GO – ends the batch. CREATE PROCEDURE must be the first statement in its batch.
  • EXEC / DECLARE – run a procedure / make a variable to catch the OUTPUT value.
  • sys.procedures / DROP PROCEDURE – list the procedures / delete one.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

raise_salary

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create raise_salary @dept INT, @pct DECIMAL(5,2) that multiplies salary by (1 + @pct / 100) for that department. End the batch with GO.

count_employees

Create count_employees @dept INT, @total INT OUTPUT that sets @total = COUNT(*) for the department. End with GO.

Call them

Run raise_salary with @dept = 1, @pct = 10. Declare @t INT, run count_employees with @total = @t OUTPUT, and select @t AS total.

List and drop

Select name, create_date from sys.procedures, then drop count_employees.

Step 21 Window functions

What it is: A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) but, unlike GROUP BY, still shows every row.
Why use it: Rankings, running totals and "top earner in each department" become one short query.

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add sample rows

Write USE company_db; and GO, then add Mary (1, 900000), Peter (1, 700000), Asha (2, 600000) and Neema (2, 650000) in one INSERT.

Rank everyone

Select name, department_id, salary with ROW_NUMBER() as row_num, RANK() as rnk and DENSE_RANK() as dense_rnk, all OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).

Per department

Add PARTITION BY department_id: RANK() by salary as dept_rank, SUM(salary) as dept_total and AVG(salary) as dept_avg.

Previous, next, running total

Ordered by salary: LAG(salary) as prev_salary, LEAD(salary) as next_salary, and a running SUM(salary) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW as running_total.

Top earner per department

In a subquery ranked, number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn. Outside, keep rn = 1.

Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (sys.dm_exec_requests (the blocking_session_id column) or sp_who2, then KILL), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

What is the difference between a shared and an exclusive lock?

A shared (read) lock lets others read the row but not change it, and many sessions can hold one at the same time. An exclusive (write) lock lets only its owner change the row. Every UPDATE and DELETE takes an exclusive lock until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Pessimistic or optimistic locking?

Pessimistic locking locks the row before you change it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Use it when clashes are common, such as the last seat on a bus. Optimistic locking takes no lock: each row has a version number, and the UPDATE works only WHERE row_version = the value you read. If 0 rows change, someone else was first, so read again and retry. Use it when clashes are rare.

The big question. One realistic ticket that needs everything from the other steps: tables and constraints, data, joins, a view, users, an index, a trigger, a transaction, a backup, a recovery plan and a frozen system. You analyse it first, then build it file by file. Finish the other steps in this database first, or use them as a reference.

Practise on a test server only. This creates a new database called shop_db (separate from company_db), users and a backup. Never run it on a live system, and never type a real password into this page.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The ticket from the shop manager. You are the new DBA at KijijiShop, a small online shop. Build its database, shop_db.
  1. Store customers (name, a unique email, phone), products (name, category, a price above zero, stock that never goes below zero), orders (customer, status that starts as "new", date) and the items of each order (product, quantity above zero, the price at the time). Deleting an order must delete its items.
  2. Load sample data: 3 customers, 4 products, 2 orders with their items.
  3. Raise the price of every "Drinks" product by 10%. Delete the cancelled order. Add a loyalty_points column to customers, starting at 0.
  4. Reports: each order with the customer name and its total; customers who never ordered; categories with revenue above 2000; products nobody has bought.
  5. The sales team must not see customer emails: give them a view of order totals and a read-only user. A clerk user may add and change orders, but not delete anything.
  6. Orders are searched by date all day: make that fast.
  7. Every price change must be recorded: who it was, the old price and the new price.
  8. Placing an order must be all or nothing: the order, its items and the stock change are saved together, or none of them is.
  9. Take a backup, and prove you can restore it.
  10. The business wants to lose at most 1 hour of data and be back within 1 hour. What backup plan do you need?
  11. Monday morning the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Method: how to attack a big question

  1. Read the whole ticket once before you type anything.
  2. Underline the nouns. They become tables and columns. Underline the verbs and the rules ("never", "must", "only"). They become statements and constraints.
  3. Draw the relationships. Where a thing "has many" of another, the many side gets a foreign key. Where both sides have many, add a table in the middle.
  4. Order the work by what depends on what. Parent tables before child tables, tables before data, data before reports, reports before the view that uses them.
  5. Write one file for each group of lines, run it, and check the result with a SELECT before moving on.
  6. Answer the lines that are not code (backup plan, a frozen system) in plain words, with the exact commands you would use.

The design that falls out of line 1

RelationshipKindHow you build it
customers and ordersOne customer has many ordersA foreign key orders.customer_id
orders and order_itemsOne order has many itemsA foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE
products and order_itemsOne product appears in many itemsA foreign key order_items.product_id
orders and productsMany to manySolved by the order_items table in the middle
Why unit_price is stored on each item. Prices change (line 3 raises them). An old order must still show what the customer actually paid, so the item keeps a copy of the price from the day of the order. Without it, a price rise would silently change old totals.

Step 2 Build the tables

01_shop_create.sql

Turn the nouns and rules of line 1 into four tables.

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database shop_db and switch to it with USE shop_db;.

customers

Create customers with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE and phone VARCHAR(20).

products

Order totals

Write USE shop_db; first. Select o.id, the customer c.name and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total from orders o. Add JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id and JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id, then GROUP BY o.id, c.name.
