Step 8 Backup and restore

terminal

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Back up

Dump shop_db with mysqldump -u root -p into shop_backup.sql.

Restore

Load the file back into shop_db with mysql -u root -p shop_db < shop_backup.sql.

Step 9 Answer the last lines in words

Lines 10 and 11 have no code to type. In an interview you answer them out loud, so practise saying them. Open each answer only after you have tried.

Line 10: lose at most 1 hour, back within 1 hour. What plan do you need?

RPO 1 hour needs more than a nightly backup: a nightly full backup plus the binary log (point-in-time recovery with mysqlbinlog), taken at least every hour. RTO 1 hour means the restore must finish in an hour, so time a real restore. If the database is too big to restore in time, make the backup smaller or faster, or keep a standby server. The business sets the two numbers; you choose the tools.

Line 11: the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Do not restart anything yet. Look at the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST and sys.innodb_lock_waits to find the blocker, then KILL it), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that fails, end that one session. Then find out why it held the lock so far (a forgotten open transaction, a long job) and fix the cause.

Walk me through your design.

Four tables. customers and products are the things. orders belongs to one customer. order_items sits between orders and products because an order has many products and a product is in many orders. Each rule from the ticket is a constraint, so the data protects itself.

Why does an order item store the price?

Prices change. The item keeps the price from the day of the order, so old orders and reports still show what the customer paid.

Why is placing an order a transaction?

It changes three things: the order, its items and the stock. If one fails, the others must be undone, or the shop would sell stock it does not have. That is atomicity.

How do you make sure the clerk cannot delete anything?

Grant only SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the tables the job needs, and never DELETE. Nobody gets more than the job needs.

Step 10 Check that it worked

  • Run SHOW TABLES; in shop_db. You should see customers, products, orders, order_items, price_audit and the view order_summary.
  • Insert a customer with an email that already exists, and a product with price 0. Both must fail.
  • The order report shows order 1 for Amina with a total of 4200.
  • Connect as shop_reader: SELECT * FROM order_summary; works, but SELECT * FROM customers; on customers fails.
  • Change a product price: a row appears in price_audit with the old and new price.
  • The failing 100-rice order leaves no new order, and the Rice 5kg stock is 18.
  • Take the backup, delete a row, restore, and confirm the row is back.

Method: how to attack a big question

  1. Read the whole ticket once before you type anything.
  2. Underline the nouns. They become tables and columns. Underline the verbs and the rules ("never", "must", "only"). They become statements and constraints.
  3. Draw the relationships. Where a thing "has many" of another, the many side gets a foreign key. Where both sides have many, add a table in the middle.
  4. Order the work by what depends on what. Parent tables before child tables, tables before data, data before reports, reports before the view that uses them.
  5. Write one file for each group of lines, run it, and check the result with a SELECT before moving on.
  6. Answer the lines that are not code (backup plan, a frozen system) in plain words, with the exact commands you would use.

The design that falls out of line 1

RelationshipKindHow you build it
customers and ordersOne customer has many ordersA foreign key orders.customer_id

products and order_itemsOne product appears in many itemsA foreign key order_items.product_id
orders and productsMany to manySolved by the order_items table in the middle
Why unit_price is stored on each item. Prices change (line 3 raises them). An old order must still show what the customer actually paid, so the item keeps a copy of the price from the day of the order. Without it, a price rise would silently change old totals.

Step 2 Build the tables

01_shop_create.sql

Turn the nouns and rules of line 1 into four tables.

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database shop_db and switch to it with \c shop_db.

customers

Create customers with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE and phone VARCHAR(20).

products

Create products with the id, name, category, a price that must be above zero, and a stock that defaults to 0 and may not go below zero.

orders

Create orders with the id, customer_id (required, a foreign key to customers(id)), status (required, default 'new') and order_date (a DATE).

order_items

Create order_items with the id, order_id (a foreign key to orders(id) with ON DELETE CASCADE), product_id (a foreign key to products(id)), quantity (above zero) and unit_price (required).

Step 3 Add data and change it

02_shop_data.sql

Lines 2 and 3 of the ticket: sample data, a price rise, a delete and a new column.

Run this on a fresh database so the ids start at 1, because the item rows use ids 1 to 3. The item keeps the old price (unit_price) even though the product price rose.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Customers and products

You are connected to shop_db. Insert Amina, Juma and Neema (name, email, phone), then Cola and Juice (Drinks, 1500 and 2000, stock 50 and 30), Bread (Food, 1200, stock 40) and Rice 5kg (Food, 9000, stock 20). One statement for each table.

Orders and items

Insert order 1 (customer 1, 'paid', 2026-10-01) and order 2 (customer 2, 'cancelled', 2026-10-02). Then the items: order 1 has Cola x2 at 1500 and Bread x1 at 1200; order 2 has Juice x1 at 2000.

Price rise and cancelled order

Raise Drinks prices by 10% with price = price * 1.10. Delete the cancelled order with a WHERE on status. Then select everything from order_items: the cancelled order's item is gone too.

New column

Add loyalty_points to customers as INT with DEFAULT 0.

Step 4 Reports

03_shop_reports.sql

Line 4 of the ticket: four reports with joins, grouping and a subquery.

Expected results: order 1 for Amina totals 4200. Juma and Neema never ordered (Juma's only order was cancelled and deleted). Only Drinks passes the 2000 line (3000). Juice and Rice 5kg were never bought. A HAVING filters groups after the sum, a WHERE filters rows before it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Order totals

You are connected to shop_db. Select o.id, the customer c.name and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total from orders o. Add JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id and JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id, then GROUP BY o.id, c.name.

Customers who never ordered

Select c.name from customers c with a LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id on orders, keeping only the rows where o.id IS NULL.

Revenue above 2000

Select p.category and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as revenue from order_items i joined to products p. Group by category and keep only groups with HAVING SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) > 2000.

Products nobody bought

Select name from products where id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items).

Step 5 A view and two users

04_shop_security.sql

Line 5 of the ticket: hide the emails behind a view, and give each user only what the job needs.

The sales team gets the view, not the tables, so emails stay hidden. The clerk can read and change what an order needs and nothing else: no DELETE. Grant the least that works.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

The view

Create the view order_summary: o.id AS order_id, c.name as customer, o.status and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total, from orders o joined to customers c and order_items i, grouped by o.id, c.name, o.status.

Read-only user

Create the role shop_reader with LOGIN and PASSWORD 'Str0ng_Pass!'. Grant CONNECT on the database, USAGE on the schema public, and SELECT on order_summary only.

Clerk user

Create shop_clerk the same way with CONNECT and USAGE. Grant SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on orders, SELECT, INSERT on order_items, and SELECT, UPDATE on products. No DELETE anywhere.

Step 6 Index and audit trigger

05_shop_speed_audit.sql

Lines 6 and 7 of the ticket: speed up the date search, and record every price change.

On a table this small the database may still scan the whole table. That is normal: the index pays off when the table has thousands of rows. The trigger logs only real price changes, so the stock updates in Step 7 add nothing to the audit.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Index

You are connected to shop_db. Create idx_orders_date on orders(order_date).

Check the index

List the indexes of orders from pg_indexes, then ask for the plan with EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2026-10-01';.

Audit table

Create price_audit with id, product_id, old_price and new_price, and a changed_at timestamp that defaults to now.

Audit trigger

Write the function log_price_change() that inserts OLD.id, OLD.price, NEW.price into price_audit and returns NEW. Then create the trigger after_update_price AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW that runs it.

Test it

Set Cola's price to 1700, then select everything from price_audit. One row shows 1650 and 1700.

Step 7 Place an order safely

06_shop_order.sql

Line 8 of the ticket: an order, its items and the stock change are saved together or not at all.

Expected: two orders remain (1 and the good new one), and Rice 5kg stock is 18. MAX(id) finds the new order on a practice server with one user. In a real application read the new id with RETURNING id. After the failing statement PostgreSQL refuses everything until the ROLLBACK.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

A good order

You are connected to shop_db. Begin with BEGIN;. Insert an order for customer 3 ('new', '2026-10-05'). Insert its item with INSERT ... SELECT (SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders), id, 2, price FROM products WHERE name = 'Rice 5kg', so the order id and the price come from the data. Take 2 off the stock of Rice 5kg, then COMMIT;.

An order that must fail

Begin again. Insert an order for customer 3 dated '2026-10-06', insert an item for 100 Rice 5kg, then take 100 off the stock. The stock CHECK (stock >= 0) stops that last statement. Finish with ROLLBACK; so the order and the item disappear.

Check the result

Select everything from orders, then name and stock from products.

Step 8 Backup and restore

terminal

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Back up

Write a custom-format dump with pg_dump -U postgres -F c -f shop_backup.dump shop_db to shop_backup.dump.

Restore

Restore it with pg_restore -U postgres -d shop_db --clean shop_backup.dump.

Step 9 Answer the last lines in words

Lines 10 and 11 have no code to type. In an interview you answer them out loud, so practise saying them. Open each answer only after you have tried.

Line 10: lose at most 1 hour, back within 1 hour. What plan do you need?

RPO 1 hour needs more than a nightly backup: a nightly full backup plus continuous WAL archiving (point-in-time recovery), taken at least every hour. RTO 1 hour means the restore must finish in an hour, so time a real restore. If the database is too big to restore in time, make the backup smaller or faster, or keep a standby server. The business sets the two numbers; you choose the tools.

Line 11: the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Do not restart anything yet. Look at the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids, then pg_terminate_backend), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that fails, end that one session. Then find out why it held the lock so far (a forgotten open transaction, a long job) and fix the cause.

Walk me through your design.

Four tables. customers and products are the things. orders belongs to one customer. order_items sits between orders and products because an order has many products and a product is in many orders. Each rule from the ticket is a constraint, so the data protects itself.

Why does an order item store the price?

Prices change. The item keeps the price from the day of the order, so old orders and reports still show what the customer paid.

Why is placing an order a transaction?

It changes three things: the order, its items and the stock. If one fails, the others must be undone, or the shop would sell stock it does not have. That is atomicity.

How do you make sure the clerk cannot delete anything?

Grant only SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the tables the job needs, and never DELETE. Nobody gets more than the job needs.

  • Run \dt in shop_db. You should see customers, products, orders, order_items, price_audit and the view order_summary.
  • Insert a customer with an email that already exists, and a product with price 0. Both must fail.
  • The order report shows order 1 for Amina with a total of 4200.
  • Connect as shop_reader: SELECT * FROM order_summary; works, but SELECT * FROM customers; on customers fails.
  • Change a product price: a row appears in price_audit with the old and new price.
  • The failing 100-rice order leaves no new order, and the Rice 5kg stock is 18.
  • Take the backup, delete a row, restore, and confirm the row is back.

Practise on a test server only. This creates a new database called shop_db (separate from company_db), users and a backup. Never run it on a live system, and never type a real password into this page.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The ticket from the shop manager. You are the new DBA at KijijiShop, a small online shop. Build its database, shop_db.
  1. Store customers (name, a unique email, phone), products (name, category, a price above zero, stock that never goes below zero), orders (customer, status that starts as "new", date) and the items of each order (product, quantity above zero, the price at the time). Deleting an order must delete its items.
  2. Load sample data: 3 customers, 4 products, 2 orders with their items.
  3. Raise the price of every "Drinks" product by 10%. Delete the cancelled order. Add a loyalty_points column to customers, starting at 0.
  4. Reports: each order with the customer name and its total; customers who never ordered; categories with revenue above 2000; products nobody has bought.
  5. The sales team must not see customer emails: give them a view of order totals and a read-only user. A clerk user may add and change orders, but not delete anything.
  6. Orders are searched by date all day: make that fast.
  7. Every price change must be recorded: who it was, the old price and the new price.
  8. Placing an order must be all or nothing: the order, its items and the stock change are saved together, or none of them is.
  9. Take a backup, and prove you can restore it.
  10. The business wants to lose at most 1 hour of data and be back within 1 hour. What backup plan do you need?
  11. Monday morning the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Do not start with SQL. Start by turning the ticket into a plan. This table shows how each line maps to what you already practised.

Method: how to attack a big question

  1. Read the whole ticket once before you type anything.
  2. Underline the nouns. They become tables and columns. Underline the verbs and the rules ("never", "must", "only"). They become statements and constraints.
  3. Draw the relationships. Where a thing "has many" of another, the many side gets a foreign key. Where both sides have many, add a table in the middle.
  4. Order the work by what depends on what. Parent tables before child tables, tables before data, data before reports, reports before the view that uses them.
  5. Write one file for each group of lines, run it, and check the result with a SELECT before moving on.
  6. Answer the lines that are not code (backup plan, a frozen system) in plain words, with the exact commands you would use.

The design that falls out of line 1

RelationshipKindHow you build it
customers and ordersOne customer has many ordersA foreign key orders.customer_id
orders and order_itemsOne order has many itemsA foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE
products and order_itemsOne product appears in many itemsA foreign key order_items.product_id
orders and productsMany to manySolved by the order_items table in the middle
Why unit_price is stored on each item. Prices change (line 3 raises them). An old order must still show what the customer actually paid, so the item keeps a copy of the price from the day of the order. Without it, a price rise would silently change old totals.

Step 2 Build the tables

01_shop_create.sql

Turn the nouns and rules of line 1 into four tables.

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database shop_db, then GO. Switch to it with USE shop_db;, then GO.

customers

Create customers with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE and phone VARCHAR(20).

products

Create products with the id, name, category, a price that must be above zero, and a stock that defaults to 0 and may not go below zero.

orders

Create orders with the id, customer_id (required, a foreign key to customers(id)), status (required, default 'new') and order_date (a DATE).

order_items

Create order_items with the id, order_id (a foreign key to orders(id) with ON DELETE CASCADE), product_id (a foreign key to products(id)), quantity (above zero) and unit_price (required).

Step 3 Add data and change it

02_shop_data.sql

Lines 2 and 3 of the ticket: sample data, a price rise, a delete and a new column.

Run this on a fresh database so the ids start at 1, because the item rows use ids 1 to 3. The item keeps the old price (unit_price) even though the product price rose.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Customers and products

Write USE shop_db; and GO first. Insert Amina, Juma and Neema (name, email, phone), then Cola and Juice (Drinks, 1500 and 2000, stock 50 and 30), Bread (Food, 1200, stock 40) and Rice 5kg (Food, 9000, stock 20). One statement for each table.

Orders and items

Insert order 1 (customer 1, 'paid', 2026-10-01) and order 2 (customer 2, 'cancelled', 2026-10-02). Then the items: order 1 has Cola x2 at 1500 and Bread x1 at 1200; order 2 has Juice x1 at 2000.

Price rise and cancelled order

Raise Drinks prices by 10% with price = price * 1.10. Delete the cancelled order with a WHERE on status. Then select everything from order_items: the cancelled order's item is gone too.

New column

Add loyalty_points to customers as INT with DEFAULT 0.

Step 4 Reports

03_shop_reports.sql

Line 4 of the ticket: four reports with joins, grouping and a subquery.

Expected results: order 1 for Amina totals 4200. Juma and Neema never ordered (Juma's only order was cancelled and deleted). Only Drinks passes the 2000 line (3000). Juice and Rice 5kg were never bought. A HAVING filters groups after the sum, a WHERE filters rows before it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Order totals

Write USE shop_db; and GO first. Select o.id, the customer c.name and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total from orders o. Add JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id and JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id, then GROUP BY o.id, c.name.

Customers who never ordered

Select c.name from customers c with a LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id on orders, keeping only the rows where o.id IS NULL.

Revenue above 2000

Select p.category and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as revenue from order_items i joined to products p. Group by category and keep only groups with HAVING SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) > 2000.

Products nobody bought

Select name from products where id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items).

Step 5 A view and two users

04_shop_security.sql

Line 5 of the ticket: hide the emails behind a view, and give each user only what the job needs.

A view must be the first statement in its batch, so it sits between two GO lines. The sales team gets the view, not the tables, so emails stay hidden. The clerk has no DELETE. Grant the least that works.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

The view

Write USE shop_db; and GO, then: Create the view order_summary: o.id AS order_id, c.name as customer, o.status and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total, from orders o joined to customers c and order_items i, grouped by o.id, c.name, o.status. Finish with GO.

Read-only user

Create the login shop_reader with PASSWORD = 'Str0ng_Pass!', the user shop_reader for that login, and grant SELECT on order_summary only.

Clerk user

Do the same for shop_clerk. Grant SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on orders, SELECT, INSERT on order_items, and SELECT, UPDATE on products. No DELETE anywhere.

Step 6 Index and audit trigger

05_shop_speed_audit.sql

Lines 6 and 7 of the ticket: speed up the date search, and record every price change.

On a table this small the database may still scan the whole table. That is normal: the index pays off when the table has thousands of rows. The trigger logs only real price changes, so the stock updates in Step 7 add nothing to the audit.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Index

Write USE shop_db; and GO first. Create idx_orders_date on orders(order_date).

Check the index

Show the indexes with EXEC sp_helpindex 'orders';.

Audit table

Create price_audit with id, product_id, old_price and new_price, and a changed_at timestamp that defaults to now.

Audit trigger

Create the trigger after_update_price on products AFTER UPDATE. Insert d.id, d.price, i.price from deleted d joined to inserted i on the id, where d.price <> i.price. End with GO.

Test it

Set Cola's price to 1700, then select everything from price_audit. One row shows 1650 and 1700.

Step 7 Place an order safely

06_shop_order.sql

Line 8 of the ticket: an order, its items and the stock change are saved together or not at all.

Expected: two orders remain (1 and the good new one), and Rice 5kg stock is 18. MAX(id) finds the new order on a practice server with one user. In a real application read the new id with SCOPE_IDENTITY(). In real code add SET XACT_ABORT ON; so any error rolls the whole transaction back by itself.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

A good order

Write USE shop_db; and GO first. Begin with BEGIN TRANSACTION;. Insert an order for customer 3 ('new', '2026-10-05'). Insert its item with INSERT ... SELECT (SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders), id, 2, price FROM products WHERE name = 'Rice 5kg', so the order id and the price come from the data. Take 2 off the stock of Rice 5kg, then COMMIT TRANSACTION;.

An order that must fail

Begin again. Insert an order for customer 3 dated '2026-10-06', insert an item for 100 Rice 5kg, then take 100 off the stock. The stock CHECK (stock >= 0) stops that last statement. Finish with ROLLBACK TRANSACTION; so the order and the item disappear.

Check the result

Select everything from orders, then name and stock from products.

Step 8 Backup and restore

07_shop_backup.sql

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Back up

Back up shop_db to the file 'C:\Backup\shop_db.bak' with WITH INIT.

Restore

Switch to master, then restore shop_db from the same file with WITH REPLACE.

Step 9 Answer the last lines in words

Lines 10 and 11 have no code to type. In an interview you answer them out loud, so practise saying them. Open each answer only after you have tried.

Line 10: lose at most 1 hour, back within 1 hour. What plan do you need?

RPO 1 hour needs more than a nightly backup: a nightly full backup plus transaction log backups (full recovery model), taken at least every hour. RTO 1 hour means the restore must finish in an hour, so time a real restore. If the database is too big to restore in time, make the backup smaller or faster, or keep a standby server. The business sets the two numbers; you choose the tools.

Line 11: the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Do not restart anything yet. Look at the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (sys.dm_exec_requests (blocking_session_id) or sp_who2, then KILL), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that fails, end that one session. Then find out why it held the lock so far (a forgotten open transaction, a long job) and fix the cause.

Walk me through your design.

Four tables. customers and products are the things. orders belongs to one customer. order_items sits between orders and products because an order has many products and a product is in many orders. Each rule from the ticket is a constraint, so the data protects itself.

Why does an order item store the price?

Prices change. The item keeps the price from the day of the order, so old orders and reports still show what the customer paid.

Why is placing an order a transaction?

It changes three things: the order, its items and the stock. If one fails, the others must be undone, or the shop would sell stock it does not have. That is atomicity.

How do you make sure the clerk cannot delete anything?

Grant only SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the tables the job needs, and never DELETE. Nobody gets more than the job needs.

Step 10 Check that it worked

  • Run SELECT name FROM sys.tables; in shop_db. You should see customers, products, orders, order_items, price_audit and the view order_summary.
  • Insert a customer with an email that already exists, and a product with price 0. Both must fail.
  • The order report shows order 1 for Amina with a total of 4200.
  • Connect as shop_reader: SELECT * FROM order_summary; works, but SELECT * FROM customers; on customers fails.
  • Change a product price: a row appears in price_audit with the old and new price.
  • The failing 100-rice order leaves no new order, and the Rice 5kg stock is 18.
  • Take the backup, delete a row, restore, and confirm the row is back.

Big question: a government recruitment portal. This is Task 1 from your question sheet: a database for an online job portal where applicants apply for public-service vacancies, get shortlisted, sit interviews and are placed. You build the schema, seed it, answer every question on the sheet, add an index and an audit trigger, and show one applicant's whole journey. Every query here is written for MySQL.

Practise on a test server only. This creates a new database called recruit_db, an audit table and a trigger. Never run it on a live system, and never type a real password or a real National ID into this page.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

Task 1, as given. Tables: Applicants (ApplicantID, FullName, Email, Phone, NationalID, PasswordHash, RegistrationDate), Applications (ApplicationID, ApplicantID, VacancyID, AppliedDate, ApplicationStatus, ShortlistStatus, LastUpdated), Vacancies (VacancyID, JobTitle, PublicInstitution, Cadre, NumberOfPosts, AdvertDate, ClosingDate, Status), Placements (PlacementID, ApplicationID, Institution, PlacementDate, PlacementStatus) and InterviewResults (ResultID, ApplicationID, InterviewType, InterviewDate, Score, ResultStatus).
  1. Section A.1 Create the schema with data types, primary keys, foreign keys, unique NationalID and Email, one application per applicant per vacancy, CHECK constraints on status fields, and indexes on the columns the API filters and joins on. Supply it as schema.sql.
  2. Section A.2 Seed at least 10 realistic records per major table: vacancies that are Open, Closed and past their closing date; applicants with and without applications; at least one applicant who reached placement.
  3. i Total successfully submitted applications. ii Average applications per vacancy, including vacancies with zero. iii / Q3 Vacancies that never received an application. iv / Q4 Vacancies still Open after their closing date. v / Q2 Top five vacancies with their rank. vi Recruitment funnel per public institution. vii Overall placement rate. viii / Q5 Vacancy with the most applications.
  4. Joins: Q1 applicants with submitted applications, Q6 name, vacancy, date and status, Q7 shortlisted applicants, Q8 interview totals, Q9 more than one vacancy, Q10 never submitted, Q11 selected but not placed.
  5. x / Q12 Show a complete application journey.
  6. Index joins / Q12 practical: create an index on applications(vacancy_id) and compare the execution plan before and after.
  7. ix / Q13: an audit table and a trigger that records application status changes.

The sheet numbers some questions twice (i to x, then Q1 to Q13). This table puts each one in a single file, so nothing is done twice.

The design

APPLICANTS 1 ───< APPLICATIONS >─── 1 VACANCIES
                       │ 1
             ┌─────────┴──────────┐
             *                   0..1
     INTERVIEW_RESULTS        PLACEMENTS

UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id)   one application per applicant per vacancy
UNIQUE (placements.application_id)  an application is placed at most once
One rule to agree before any query: what counts as "submitted"? In this design an application is submitted when its status is Submitted, Selected or Rejected. A Draft was never sent, and a Withdrawn was pulled back. Every report below uses that same list, so the numbers agree with each other. Write the definition down in an interview: it shows you asked what the business means.

Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. MySQL already builds an index for every foreign key, so interview_results.application_id and applications.vacancy_id are indexed for free. A separate index on applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database recruit_db and switch to it with USE recruit_db;.

applicants

Create applicants with an identity applicant_id, full_name, email, phone, national_id, password_hash and registration_date DATE. Make email and national_id unique with named constraints.

vacancies

Create vacancies with the id, job_title, public_institution, cadre, number_of_posts (above zero), advert_date, closing_date (not before the advert date) and status ('Open' or 'Closed', default 'Open').

applications

Create applications with the id, applicant_id and vacancy_id (both required foreign keys), applied_date, application_status (Draft, Submitted, Withdrawn, Selected, Rejected), shortlist_status (Pending, Shortlisted, Not Shortlisted) and last_updated. Add UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id).

interview_results

Create interview_results with the id, application_id (foreign key), interview_type (Written, Oral, Practical), interview_date, score from 0 to 100, and result_status (Passed or Failed).

placements

Create placements with the id, application_id (foreign key, unique), institution, placement_date and placement_status (Placed, Reported, Declined; default Placed).

Indexes

Index the columns the API filters on: idx_vac_status_close on vacancies (status, closing_date), idx_vac_institution on vacancies (public_institution), and idx_app_status on applications (application_status).

The password hashes are fake placeholders: a real system stores a bcrypt or Argon2 hash made by the application, never a password. Placements has only 2 rows on purpose: only selected applicants can be placed, and Q11 needs one selected applicant who is not placed yet. Step 4 The headline numbers

03_kpis.sql

Questions i, ii and vii.

Expected: 13 submitted applications, an average of 1.30 per vacancy (13 over 10 vacancies) and a placement rate of 15.38% (2 of 13). The status filter for ii sits in the ON condition, not in WHERE: a WHERE would throw away the vacancies with zero applications, and the average would wrongly become 13 over 7. * 1.0 turns whole-number division into decimal division on every database.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

i. Submitted applications

Write USE recruit_db; first. Count the rows in applications whose status is in ('Submitted', 'Selected', 'Rejected'), named submitted_applications.

ii. Average per vacancy

In a derived table per_vacancy, count submitted applications for every vacancy with vacancies v LEFT JOIN applications a, keeping the status test inside the ON. Outside, take AVG(app_count * 1.0), rounded to 2 places.

vii. Placement rate

From submitted applications a LEFT JOIN placements p, divide COUNT(p.placement_id) by COUNT(a.application_id), times 100.0, rounded to 2 places.

Step 5 Vacancy reports

04_vacancy_reports.sql

Questions iii/Q3, iv/Q4, v/Q2 and viii/Q5.

Expected: iii returns vacancies 8, 9 and 10. iv returns 6 and 7 (on 2026-10-26; later dates add more). v returns seven rows, not five: Accountant II and Nurse Officer II tie on 3 and both get rank 1, then two vacancies share rank 3 and three share rank 5. RANK() keeps ties honest; ROW_NUMBER() would cut them at random and DENSE_RANK() would give 1, 1, 2, 2, 3. viii returns the same two leaders, because a maximum can be shared. CURRENT_DATE gets today's date in MySQL.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

iii. Never received an application

Write USE recruit_db; first. Select the vacancy id, title, institution and status from vacancies v, LEFT JOIN applications a on the vacancy id, keeping rows where a.application_id IS NULL.

iv. Open after closing date

Select id, title and closing date from vacancies where status = 'Open' and closing_date < CURRENT_DATE.

v. Top five with rank

In a derived table ranked, count submitted applications per vacancy and add RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(a.application_id) DESC) AS rnk. Outside, keep rnk <= 5 and order by rnk, vacancy_id.

viii. The maximum

Count submitted applications per vacancy and keep the groups whose count equals MAX(cnt) of the per-vacancy counts, using HAVING.

Step 6 The recruitment funnel

05_funnel.sql

Question vi: per public institution, how many applications go in at the top, and how many survive each stage.

Why DISTINCT? An application with two interview rows appears twice after the join, so a plain COUNT would count Amina twice. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts it once. CASE ... END returns NULL when the condition is false, and COUNT ignores NULLs, so each column counts only its own stage. Expected: Ministry of Finance 3, 2, 1, 1; Office of the Attorney General 1, 1, 1, 1; e-Government Authority 2, 2, 1, 0.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Funnel query

Write USE recruit_db; first. Group by v.public_institution. Count distinct submitted applications, distinct shortlisted ones, distinct ones with a 'Passed' interview, and distinct placed ones. Join applications, then LEFT JOIN interview_results and placements.

Step 9 Index on applications(vacancy_id): before and after

08_index.sql

The "index joins" question and the Q12 practical: same query, two plans. The query joins applications to applicants for one vacancy.

Read the type and key columns. Before: ALL on a, a full table scan. After: ref using idx_app_vacancy. MySQL had quietly made fk_app_vacancy for the foreign key, which is why the "before" needs IGNORE INDEX to show a table with no index. Once your own index exists, MySQL may drop its automatic one.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Before

Write USE recruit_db;. Ask for the plan with EXPLAIN on the join query, adding IGNORE INDEX (fk_app_vacancy) after applications a, so MySQL behaves as if the column had no index.

Create the index

Create idx_app_vacancy on applications (vacancy_id), then list the indexes with SHOW INDEX FROM applications;.

After

Run the same EXPLAIN without the hint.

Step 10 Audit trigger on applications

09_audit.sql

Question ix and Q13: every change of application_status is recorded with who made it and when, even if someone changes it outside the application.

Expected: exactly one audit row, application 13 from Submitted to Selected. The second update changes only the shortlist, so the trigger writes nothing. Because application 13 is now Selected and has no placement, Q11 from Step 7 would now also list Neema Kileo: run it again and see.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Write USE recruit_db; first. Create application_audit with an identity audit_id, application_id, old_status, new_status, changed_by and changed_at defaulting to now.

Trigger

Create trg_application_status_audit AFTER UPDATE ON applications FOR EACH ROW that inserts OLD.application_id, OLD.application_status, NEW.application_status and CURRENT_USER() into the audit table, only WHERE OLD.application_status <> NEW.application_status.

Test it

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < CURRENT_DATE;, and run it every night as a MySQL EVENT. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. MySQL indexes them automatically.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

One rule to agree before any query: what counts as "submitted"? In this design an application is submitted when its status is Submitted, Selected or Rejected. A Draft was never sent, and a Withdrawn was pulled back. Every report below uses that same list, so the numbers agree with each other. Write the definition down in an interview: it shows you asked what the business means.

Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. PostgreSQL does not index foreign key columns for you, so interview_results.application_id gets its own index. applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Database

Create the database recruit_db and connect to it with \c recruit_db.

applicants

Create applicants with an identity applicant_id, full_name, email, phone, national_id, password_hash and registration_date DATE. Make email and national_id unique with named constraints.

vacancies

Create vacancies with the id, job_title, public_institution, cadre, number_of_posts (above zero), advert_date, closing_date (not before the advert date) and status ('Open' or 'Closed', default 'Open').

applications

Create applications with the id, applicant_id and vacancy_id (both required foreign keys), applied_date, application_status (Draft, Submitted, Withdrawn, Selected, Rejected), shortlist_status (Pending, Shortlisted, Not Shortlisted) and last_updated. Add UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id).

interview_results

Create interview_results with the id, application_id (foreign key), interview_type (Written, Oral, Practical), interview_date, score from 0 to 100, and result_status (Passed or Failed).

placements

Create placements with the id, application_id (foreign key, unique), institution, placement_date and placement_status (Placed, Reported, Declined; default Placed).

Indexes

Index the columns the API filters on: idx_vac_status_close on vacancies (status, closing_date), idx_vac_institution on vacancies (public_institution), and idx_app_status on applications (application_status). Also idx_result_app on interview_results (application_id).

Step 9 Index on applications(vacancy_id): before and after

08_index.sql

The "index joins" question and the Q12 practical: same query, two plans. The query joins applications to applicants for one vacancy.

Before: Seq Scan on applications. After: Index Scan or Bitmap Index Scan on idx_app_vacancy. With only 15 rows PostgreSQL rightly prefers a sequential scan, so enable_seqscan = off tells this one session to avoid it if it can, which proves the index is usable. On a table with thousands of rows the planner picks the index by itself.

After

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < CURRENT_DATE;, and run it every night as pg_cron or an operating-system cron job. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. PostgreSQL does not index them for you, so you add the index yourself.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < TRUNC(SYSDATE);, and run it every night as a DBMS_SCHEDULER job. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. Oracle does not index them for you, so you add the index yourself.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

The design

APPLICANTS 1 ───< APPLICATIONS >─── 1 VACANCIES
                       │ 1
             ┌─────────┴──────────┐
             *                   0..1
     INTERVIEW_RESULTS        PLACEMENTS

UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id)   one application per applicant per vacancy
UNIQUE (placements.application_id)  an application is placed at most once
One rule to agree before any query: what counts as "submitted"? In this design an application is submitted when its status is Submitted, Selected or Rejected. A Draft was never sent, and a Withdrawn was pulled back. Every report below uses that same list, so the numbers agree with each other. Write the definition down in an interview: it shows you asked what the business means.

Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. SQL Server does not index foreign key columns for you, so interview_results.application_id gets its own index. applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database recruit_db, then GO. Switch to it with USE recruit_db;, then GO.

applicants

Create applicants with an identity applicant_id, full_name, email, phone, national_id, password_hash and registration_date DATE. Make email and national_id unique with named constraints.

vacancies

Create vacancies with the id, job_title, public_institution, cadre, number_of_posts (above zero), advert_date, closing_date (not before the advert date) and status ('Open' or 'Closed', default 'Open').

applications

Create applications with the id, applicant_id and vacancy_id (both required foreign keys), applied_date, application_status (Draft, Submitted, Withdrawn, Selected, Rejected), shortlist_status (Pending, Shortlisted, Not Shortlisted) and last_updated. Add UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id).

interview_results

Create interview_results with the id, application_id (foreign key), interview_type (Written, Oral, Practical), interview_date, score from 0 to 100, and result_status (Passed or Failed).

placements

Create placements with the id, application_id (foreign key, unique), institution, placement_date and placement_status (Placed, Reported, Declined; default Placed).

Indexes

Index the columns the API filters on: idx_vac_status_close on vacancies (status, closing_date), idx_vac_institution on vacancies (public_institution), and idx_app_status on applications (application_status). Also idx_result_app on interview_results (application_id).

  1. Draw an ERD with the entities Applicants, Workstations and Assessments.
  2. Create the database and populate each table with at least 10 rows.
  3. Find the most used workstation (Q1) and the workstations never used (Q2). Show every workstation with its usage count, including unused ones (Q3).
  4. Find the average score per workstation (Q4), the highest-scoring applicant (Q5), applicants with no assessment (Q6), applicant, assessment and workstation details together (Q7), and applicants scoring above the overall average (Q8). Produce other join questions too.
  5. Q9: create a view that hides sensitive applicant data and shows only what recruitment officers need.
  6. Q10: do a full backup, restore it to another database, and verify that the data and constraints are preserved, secure, scalable and follow the business rules.

Workstations and applicants have a many-to-many relationship: one applicant can use several workstations over time, and one workstation serves many applicants. Assessments is the table in the middle, and it also carries the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

+--------------------+          +----------------------------+          +----------------------+
| APPLICANTS         |          | ASSESSMENTS                |          | WORKSTATIONS         |
+--------------------+          +----------------------------+          +----------------------+
| PK applicant_id    |1        *| PK assessment_id           |*        1| PK workstation_id    |
|    full_name       |----------| FK applicant_id            |----------|    station_code  UQ  |
|    email       UQ  |          | FK workstation_id          |          |    centre_name       |
|    phone           |          |    assessment_type         |          |    room              |
|    national_id UQ  |          |    assessment_date         |          |    status            |
|    date_of_birth   |          |    session_slot            |          +----------------------+
+--------------------+          |    score (0 to 100)        |
                                +----------------------------+
UQ (applicant_id, assessment_type)                   one attempt per test type
UQ (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot)   one person per seat per session
Business ruleHow the database enforces it
An applicant is identified by email and National IDUNIQUE (email), UNIQUE (national_id)
A score is between 0 and 100CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
One attempt per assessment typeUNIQUE (applicant_id, assessment_type)
A workstation seats one person per sessionUNIQUE (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot)
Every assessment belongs to a real applicant and workstationTwo FOREIGN KEYs
Officers never see National IDs, birth dates or emailsA view plus GRANT SELECT on the view only

Step 2 Create the database

01_assess_schema.sql

One table per entity, with the business rules as constraints.

No extra index is needed for the foreign keys: uq_one_attempt starts with applicant_id and uq_station_slot starts with workstation_id, so each foreign key column already leads an index. The one extra index is on assessment_date, because officers search by day.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database assess_db and switch to it with USE assess_db;.

applicants

Create applicants with an identity id, full_name, email (unique), phone, national_id (unique) and date_of_birth.

workstations

Create workstations with the id, a unique station_code, centre_name, room and status (Active, Maintenance, Retired; default Active).

assessments

Create assessments with the id, the two foreign keys, assessment_type, assessment_date, session_slot (Morning or Afternoon) and score (0 to 100). Add UNIQUE (applicant_id, assessment_type) and UNIQUE (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot).

Index for date searches

Create idx_ass_date on assessments (assessment_date).

Step 3 Populate the tables

02_assess_seed.sql

12 applicants, 10 workstations and 12 assessments. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: DSM-01 is used three times (the most). ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01 are never used. Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo have no assessment. Amina Juma and Baraka Mwakyusa sat at DSM-01 on the same day in different sessions, which the unique rule allows.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Applicants

Write USE assess_db; first. Insert the 12 applicants: name, email, phone, a 20-digit National ID and date of birth.

Workstations

Insert the 10 workstations: code, centre, room and status.

Assessments

Insert the 12 assessments: applicant id, workstation id, type, date, session and score.

Step 4 Workstation usage

03_usage.sql

Q1, Q2 and Q3.

Expected: Q1 DSM-01 with 3. Q2 ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01. Q3 all 10 workstations, the unused ones with 0. COUNT(s.assessment_id) counts only real matches, so an unused station gives 0; COUNT(*) would give 1, because the LEFT JOIN still returns one row with NULLs.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Q1. Most used

Write USE assess_db; first. Count assessments per workstation and keep the group whose count equals the MAX of the per-station counts.

Q2. Never used

workstations w LEFT JOIN assessments s and keep rows where s.assessment_id IS NULL.

Q3. Usage including unused

The same LEFT JOIN, grouped, with COUNT(s.assessment_id) AS times_used, ordered by times_used DESC, w.station_code.

Step 5 Scores

04_scores.sql

Q4, Q5 and Q8.

Expected: Q4 DSM-03 first with 88.00. Q5 Rehema Mollel, 91. Q8 the overall average is 72.92, so Amina Juma (85), Neema Kileo (74), Rehema Mollel (91), Halima Said (77) and Peter Ngowi (85) are above it. score * 1.0 matters: the average of whole numbers is otherwise cut to a whole number.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Q4. Average per workstation

Write USE assess_db; first. Group assessments by workstation and show ROUND(AVG(s.score * 1.0), 2) AS avg_score, highest first.

Q5. Highest scorer

Show name, type and score where s.score = (SELECT MAX(score) FROM assessments).

Q8. Above the overall average

Average each applicant's scores and keep those with HAVING greater than the average of all assessments.

Step 6 Join questions

05_joins.sql

Q6, Q7 and two extra join questions of the kind interviewers add.

Expected: Q6 Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo. Q7 twelve rows. Centres: Dar es Salaam 3 stations and 6 tests, Arusha 2 and 0, Mbeya 1 and 0. The self-join returns DSM-01 on 2026-10-05: Amina Juma then Baraka Mwakyusa. s2.assessment_id > s1.assessment_id stops each pair appearing twice and a row pairing with itself.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Q6. No assessment

Write USE assess_db; first. applicants a LEFT JOIN assessments s and keep s.assessment_id IS NULL.

Q7. Applicant, assessment and workstation

Join assessments s to applicants a and workstations w, ordered by date and station.

Extra: tests per centre

Per centre_name, count distinct stations and assessments, keeping centres with none.

Extra: shared seat on the same day (self-join)

Join assessments to itself as s1 and s2 on the same workstation and date, with s2.assessment_id > s1.assessment_id.

Step 7 Hide sensitive data with a view

06_officer_view.sql

Q9 and item v: officers see names, centres and scores, a masked phone, and nothing else.

Hidden: email, National ID, date of birth and most of the phone. The view alone is not security: a user who can read applicants can still see everything. The protection comes from granting the officer SELECT on the view and nothing on the tables.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

The view

Write USE assess_db; first. Create officer_assessment_view with the applicant id, name, CONCAT(LEFT(a.phone, 4), '******') AS masked_phone, station code, centre, type, date and score, from assessments s joined to applicants a and workstations w.

Look at it

Select everything from the view.

The officer account

Create the account recruit_officer and grant it SELECT on the view only.

Step 8 Back up, restore to another database, verify

terminal

Q10: dump assess_db and load it into a new database assess_restore. Run these in a normal terminal, not inside the mysql client.

A dump made without --databases holds no USE line, so you can load it into any database name. --routines and --triggers keep stored code; views are always included.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Back up

Dump assess_db with --routines and --triggers into assess_backup.sql.

Restore to a new database

Create assess_restore with mysql -u root -p -e, then load the file into it.

08_verify_restore.sql

Now prove the copy is good: the same row counts, the same constraints and indexes, and the rules still refuse bad data.

Expected: 12, 10 and 12 rows, the same constraint and index list as assess_db, and all four inserts fail: duplicate email (uq_ta_email), a seat already taken that session (uq_station_slot), a score of 120 (chk_ass_score) and an applicant that does not exist (fk_ass_applicant). The last line still shows 12 assessments. If any insert succeeds, the restore lost a rule.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Switch to the copy and count

Write USE assess_restore;. Then count the rows of the three tables in one SELECT.

List the constraints and indexes

List the constraints of the restored database, then the indexes of assessments.

Try to break the rules

Write four inserts that must each fail: a duplicate email, applicant 11 on DSM-01 on 2026-10-05 Morning, a score of 120, and applicant 99.

Count again

Count the assessments: still 12.

Step 9 Explain it: secure, scalable, business rules

How do you show that the restored database is "secure"?

The officer still has SELECT on the view and nothing on the tables, so National IDs and birth dates stay hidden. Log in as the officer: the view works and SELECT * FROM applicants; fails. MySQL accounts are server-wide ('recruit_officer'@'localhost'), so they are not in the dump. On a new server, create the account and the grant again.

How is the design "scalable"?

Identity keys never collide, every foreign key column leads an index (through the two composite unique constraints), and the date column has its own index. Reports join on indexed integer keys, so they stay fast as the tables grow.

How do you prove the business rules still hold after a restore?

You try to break each one and expect an error: a duplicate email, a double-booked seat, a score out of range and a missing applicant. A restore that silently lost a constraint is caught at once.

Why is assessments the table in the middle?

Applicants and workstations are many-to-many. A relational database stores that with a junction table, and here the junction table also holds the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

Why does Q2 use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and not NOT IN?

NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery ever contains a NULL. The LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern, or NOT EXISTS, has no such trap.

Is a view enough to hide data?

No. A view only chooses columns. The hiding works because the officer is granted the view and denied the tables. For stronger protection add column-level privileges, row-level security, or masking at the database level.

Step 10 Check that it worked

  • The three tables hold 12, 10 and 12 rows, and the ERD rules match the constraints you listed.
  • Q1 returns DSM-01 (3). Q2 returns ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01. Q3 lists all 10 stations.
  • Q5 returns Rehema Mollel (91). Q8 returns five applicants above 72.92.
  • As recruit_officer, the view works but SELECT on the table is refused.
  • In assess_restore every count matches and all four bad inserts fail.

Step 9 Explain it: secure, scalable, business rules

How do you show that the restored database is "secure"?

The officer still has SELECT on the view and nothing on the tables, so National IDs and birth dates stay hidden. Log in as the officer: the view works and SELECT * FROM applicants; fails. With a DBA export the users and grants come along. On a new server you check them with DBA_TAB_PRIVS.

How is the design "scalable"?

Identity keys never collide, every foreign key column leads an index (through the two composite unique constraints), and the date column has its own index. Reports join on indexed integer keys, so they stay fast as the tables grow.

How do you prove the business rules still hold after a restore?

You try to break each one and expect an error: a duplicate email, a double-booked seat, a score out of range and a missing applicant. A restore that silently lost a constraint is caught at once.

Why is assessments the table in the middle?

Applicants and workstations are many-to-many. A relational database stores that with a junction table, and here the junction table also holds the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

Why does Q2 use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and not NOT IN?

NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery ever contains a NULL. The LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern, or NOT EXISTS, has no such trap.

Is a view enough to hide data?

No. A view only chooses columns. The hiding works because the officer is granted the view and denied the tables. For stronger protection add column-level privileges, row-level security, or masking at the database level.

  • Q5 returns Rehema Mollel (91). Q8 returns five applicants above 72.92.
  • As recruit_officer, the view works but SELECT on the table is refused.
  • In assess_restore every count matches and all four bad inserts fail.

Big question: an assessment centre. This is Task 2 from your question sheet. Applicants sit computer-based assessments at workstations in regional centres. You draw the ERD, build and seed the database, answer the usage and score questions, hide sensitive data behind a view, then back it up, restore it as a second database and prove the rules survived. Every query here is written for SQL Server.

Step 1 Read the question and draw the ERD

Task 2, as given.
  1. Draw an ERD with the entities Applicants, Workstations and Assessments.
  2. Create the database and populate each table with at least 10 rows.
  3. Find the most used workstation (Q1) and the workstations never used (Q2). Show every workstation with its usage count, including unused ones (Q3).
  4. Find the average score per workstation (Q4), the highest-scoring applicant (Q5), applicants with no assessment (Q6), applicant, assessment and workstation details together (Q7), and applicants scoring above the overall average (Q8). Produce other join questions too.
  5. Q9: create a view that hides sensitive applicant data and shows only what recruitment officers need.
  6. Q10: do a full backup, restore it to another database, and verify that the data and constraints are preserved, secure, scalable and follow the business rules.

Workstations and applicants have a many-to-many relationship: one applicant can use several workstations over time, and one workstation serves many applicants. Assessments is the table in the middle, and it also carries the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

+--------------------+          +----------------------------+          +----------------------+
| APPLICANTS         |          | ASSESSMENTS                |          | WORKSTATIONS         |
+--------------------+          +----------------------------+          +----------------------+
| PK applicant_id    |1        *| PK assessment_id           |*        1| PK workstation_id    |
|    full_name       |----------| FK applicant_id            |----------|    station_code  UQ  |
|    email       UQ  |          | FK workstation_id          |          |    centre_name       |
|    phone           |          |    assessment_type         |          |    room              |
|    national_id UQ  |          |    assessment_date         |          |    status            |
|    date_of_birth   |          |    session_slot            |          +----------------------+
+--------------------+          |    score (0 to 100)        |
                                +----------------------------+
UQ (applicant_id, assessment_type)                   one attempt per test type
UQ (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot)   one person per seat per session
Business ruleHow the database enforces it
An applicant is identified by email and National IDUNIQUE (email), UNIQUE (national_id)
A score is between 0 and 100CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
One attempt per assessment typeUNIQUE (applicant_id, assessment_type)
A workstation seats one person per sessionUNIQUE (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot)
Every assessment belongs to a real applicant and workstationTwo FOREIGN KEYs
Officers never see National IDs, birth dates or emailsA view plus GRANT SELECT on the view only

How do you show that the restored database is "secure"?

How is the design "scalable"?

Identity keys never collide, every foreign key column leads an index (through the two composite unique constraints), and the date column has its own index. Reports join on indexed integer keys, so they stay fast as the tables grow.

How do you prove the business rules still hold after a restore?

You try to break each one and expect an error: a duplicate email, a double-booked seat, a score out of range and a missing applicant. A restore that silently lost a constraint is caught at once.

Why is assessments the table in the middle?

Applicants and workstations are many-to-many. A relational database stores that with a junction table, and here the junction table also holds the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery ever contains a NULL. The LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern, or NOT EXISTS, has no such trap.

Is a view enough to hide data?

Big question: a retail database. This is the Database Administrator task from your question sheet. You build XXXX_RETAIL with five tables, set the delete rules, archive the products, write the grants an admin would give, add a view, a trigger and a procedure, tune a join with indexes, and finally lose a table and restore it with its keys. Every query here is written for MySQL.

Practise on a test server only. XXXX stands for your own initials; this page writes it as xxxx_retail. Never run the drop and restore steps on a live system.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The task, as given.
  1. Create the database XXXX_RETAIL.
  2. Create the tables categories, products, orders, customers and order_items.
  3. Insert data into the tables.
  4. Delete an order's items when the order is deleted (ON DELETE CASCADE). Refuse to delete a product that other rows still point to (ON DELETE RESTRICT).
  5. Create XXXX_RETAIL.archives as a copy of XXXX_RETAIL.products.
  6. Show the grants: all privileges to retail_admin; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on orders and order_items to the user; SELECT only on all tables to the user; revoke UPDATE on orders; a role with SELECT on all tables, granted to the user.
  7. Views, triggers and stored procedures.
  8. Join orders, order_items and products: explain the query, create indexes, explain it again.
  9. Back up each table, delete one table, and restore it from the backup together with its primary and foreign keys.

Two one-to-many chains meet in order_items: a customer places many orders and an order has many items; a category holds many products and a product appears in many items. The arrows show what each delete rule does.

+----------------+        +-------------------+        +----------------+
| CUSTOMERS      |1      *| ORDERS            |1      *| ORDER_ITEMS    |
| PK customer_id |--------| PK order_id       |--------| PK order_item_id
|    email   UQ  |        | FK customer_id    | CASCADE| FK order_id    |
+----------------+        |    order_date     |        | FK product_id  |
                          |    status         |        |    quantity    |
+----------------+        +-------------------+        |    unit_price  |
| CATEGORIES     |1      *+-------------------+1      *+----------------+
| PK category_id |--------| PRODUCTS          |----------------^
|    name    UQ  |RESTRICT| PK product_id     | RESTRICT
+----------------+        | FK category_id    |
                          |    price, stock   |
                          +-------------------+
Business ruleHow the database enforces it
Deleting an order removes its itemsfk_item_order … ON DELETE CASCADE
A product that was sold cannot be deletedfk_item_product with RESTRICT
A category with products cannot be deletedfk_product_category with RESTRICT
Prices and stock are never negative; quantities are positiveCHECK constraints
A sale reduces stockThe trigger trg_item_stock

Step 6 Grant and revoke privileges

05_privileges.sql

Item 6. You are not asked to create the accounts, only to show the statements an admin would run. The user is 'retail_user'@'localhost'.

  • GRANT … ON … TO – gives a privilege on a table (or all tables) to a user or role.
  • REVOKE … ON … FROM – takes a privilege back. Only that privilege goes; the others stay.
  • CREATE ROLE – makes a named bundle of privileges. Grant to the role once, then give the role to many users.
  • GRANT role TO user – gives a user everything the role holds.
Write these; do not run them unless you are an admin on a test server where retail_admin and retail_user already exist. xxxx_retail.* means every table in the database. After item iv, the user can still insert and delete orders but not change them.

iii. Read every table

Grant SELECT only, on all tables, to the user.

iv. Take UPDATE on orders back

Revoke UPDATE on orders from the user.

v. A read-only role

Create the role retail_reader, grant it SELECT on all tables, and give it to the user.

A one-statement trigger needs no DELIMITER; the procedure has a BEGIN … END block, so it does.

Use them

Step 8 Join, explain, index, explain again

07_join_explain.sql

Item 8: one query over orders, order_items and products, its plan before and after the indexes.

  • EXPLAIN – shows how the database will find the rows (the plan) instead of, or as well as, running the query.
  • CREATE INDEX – builds a sorted lookup on a column, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading every row.
  • JOIN … ON – matches rows of two tables on a key; the columns in ON are the first candidates for an index.
Expected: 6 rows, for orders 3, 4 and 5. In the type column, ALL means a full table scan; ref or range means an index is used. MySQL already created an index for each foreign key in Step 4 (SHOW INDEX shows them), so the joins on order_id and product_id are covered. The missing one is the date filter. With only a few rows the optimizer may still choose a full scan, because reading a tiny table is cheaper than using an index; on real volumes the second plan switches to the indexes.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write USE xxxx_retail; first. Join orders o, order_items oi and products p for orders from 2026-10-05, with quantity * unit_price AS line_total.

i. Explain it

Show the plan of the same query.

ii. Create the indexes

Add the indexes the query needs.

iii. Explain it again

Step 10 Restore the table with its keys

09_restore_table.sql

Item 9 ii. Copy the rows back from bak_order_items, then add back what a copy never carries: the primary key, the foreign keys with their delete rules, the CHECK, the trigger and the indexes.

MODIFY with AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY restores the primary key and the auto-numbering in one go. Expected at the end: 10 rows, a primary key, two foreign keys and the CHECK in the list, and the delete of product 1 fails again, which proves RESTRICT is back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Copy the rows back

Write USE xxxx_retail; first. Recreate order_items from bak_order_items.

Primary key

Restore the primary key on order_item_id and its automatic numbering.

Foreign keys and CHECK

Add chk_item_qty back, then fk_item_order (CASCADE) and fk_item_product (RESTRICT).

Trigger, indexes

Create the trigger trg_item_stock again. MySQL makes the foreign key indexes for you.

Prove it

Count the rows, list the constraints of order_items, and try to delete product 1 (it must fail).

Step 11 Explain it

Why CASCADE for order items but RESTRICT for products?

An order item means nothing without its order, so it should go with it. A product is part of the sales history: deleting it would leave items pointing at nothing, or wipe old sales. Refuse the delete and mark the product inactive, or move it to the archive, instead.

What does CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT copy?

The columns and the rows. It does not copy the primary key, foreign keys, CHECK constraints, indexes, triggers or defaults. That is why the archive and the backup tables have none, and why Step 10 adds them back by hand.

Why grant through a role?

You grant the privileges to the role once. Each new user gets them with one statement, and revoking from the role changes every member at once. It also shows clearly who can do what.

The user has REVOKE UPDATE on orders. Can they still update orders?

Not through the direct grant. But if a role they hold had UPDATE on orders, they still could. Revoke removes only the grant you name, so check the roles too.

What do you look for in the plan?

Full scans of big tables, and which join method is used. After the indexes, the date filter and the joins should use index lookups. On tiny tables a full scan can still be the cheapest plan, so test on realistic volumes.

Is a table copy a real backup?

No. It lives in the same database on the same disk, so it is lost with the server. It is a quick undo before a risky change. A real backup is a dump or a backup file kept somewhere else: mysqldump, pg_dump, Data Pump or BACKUP DATABASE.

Step 12 Check that it worked

  • After Step 3 the five tables hold 4, 5, 8, 6 and 10 rows.
  • Deleting order 6 removed its item, and deleting product 1 was refused.
  • archives holds 8 rows and has no primary key.
  • After the procedure call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock and order 4 totals 138000.
  • The second plan uses the new indexes (or would, on a bigger table).
  • The restored order_items has 10 rows, its primary key, both foreign keys and the CHECK, and product 1 still cannot be deleted.
