  • The restored order_items has 10 rows, its primary key, both foreign keys and the CHECK, and product 1 still cannot be deleted.

Big question: a retail database. This is the Database Administrator task from your question sheet. You build XXXX_RETAIL with five tables, set the delete rules, archive the products, write the grants an admin would give, add a view, a trigger and a procedure, tune a join with indexes, and finally lose a table and restore it with its keys. Every query here is written for SQL Server.

Practise on a test server only. XXXX stands for your own initials; this page writes it as xxxx_retail. Never run the drop and restore steps on a live system.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The task, as given.
  1. Create the database XXXX_RETAIL.
  2. Create the tables categories, products, orders, customers and order_items.
  3. Insert data into the tables.
  4. Delete an order's items when the order is deleted (ON DELETE CASCADE). Refuse to delete a product that other rows still point to (ON DELETE RESTRICT).
  5. Create XXXX_RETAIL.archives as a copy of XXXX_RETAIL.products.
  6. Show the grants: all privileges to retail_admin; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on orders and order_items to the user; SELECT only on all tables to the user; revoke UPDATE on orders; a role with SELECT on all tables, granted to the user.
  7. Views, triggers and stored procedures.
  8. Join orders, order_items and products: explain the query, create indexes, explain it again.
  9. Back up each table, delete one table, and restore it from the backup together with its primary and foreign keys.

Two one-to-many chains meet in order_items: a customer places many orders and an order has many items; a category holds many products and a product appears in many items. The arrows show what each delete rule does.

+----------------+        +-------------------+        +----------------+
| CUSTOMERS      |1      *| ORDERS            |1      *| ORDER_ITEMS    |
| PK customer_id |--------| PK order_id       |--------| PK order_item_id
|    email   UQ  |        | FK customer_id    | CASCADE| FK order_id    |
+----------------+        |    order_date     |        | FK product_id  |
                          |    status         |        |    quantity    |
+----------------+        +-------------------+        |    unit_price  |
| CATEGORIES     |1      *+-------------------+1      *+----------------+
| PK category_id |--------| PRODUCTS          |----------------^
|    name    UQ  |RESTRICT| PK product_id     | RESTRICT
+----------------+        | FK category_id    |
                          |    price, stock   |
                          +-------------------+
Business ruleHow the database enforces it
Deleting an order removes its itemsfk_item_order … ON DELETE CASCADE
A product that was sold cannot be deletedfk_item_product with RESTRICT
A category with products cannot be deletedfk_product_category with RESTRICT
Prices and stock are never negative; quantities are positiveCHECK constraints
A sale reduces stockThe trigger trg_item_stock

Step 2 Create the database and the five tables

01_retail_schema.sql

Items 1 and 2. Parents first: categories and customers must exist before the tables that point to them.

fk_product_category already refuses to delete a category that still has products: ON DELETE NO ACTION (SQL Server's name for restrict). The two foreign keys of order_items are added in Step 4, because they are item 4 of the question.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Step 4 Delete rules: CASCADE and RESTRICT

03_delete_rules.sql

Item 4. Delete an order and its items go with it. Try to delete a product that was sold and the database refuses.

Expected: the first count is 1, the second is 0. The product delete fails with error 547 (conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint), and the Smartphone is still there. SQL Server has no RESTRICT keyword: NO ACTION, the default, gives the same result.

Test RESTRICT

Step 5 Archive the products

04_archive.sql

Item 5: a copy of products, with every row, in a new table archives.

Expected: 8 rows. SQL Server has no CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT: SELECT * INTO does the same job, and its full name is database.schema.table. The copy gets the columns and rows only: no primary key, no foreign key, no CHECK and no index. Step 9 uses the same idea for the backup, which is why Step 10 has to add the keys back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Step 6 Grant and revoke privileges

05_privileges.sql

Item 6. You are not asked to create the accounts, only to show the statements an admin would run. The user is retail_user.

  • GRANT … ON … TO – gives a privilege on a table (or all tables) to a user or role.
  • REVOKE … ON … FROM – takes a privilege back. Only that privilege goes; the others stay.
  • CREATE ROLE – makes a named bundle of privileges. Grant to the role once, then give the role to many users.
  • ALTER ROLE … ADD MEMBER – gives a user everything the role holds.
Write these; do not run them unless you are an admin on a test server where retail_admin and retail_user already exist. CONTROL ON DATABASE is SQL Server's "all privileges" (the old GRANT ALL keyword is deprecated). SCHEMA::dbo covers every table in the dbo schema, including tables added later. After item iv, the user can still insert and delete orders but not change them.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

i. Everything to retail_admin

ii. Change orders and order_items

iii. Read every table

Grant SELECT only, on all tables, to the user.

iv. Take UPDATE on orders back

Revoke UPDATE on orders from the user.

v. A read-only role

Create the role retail_reader, grant it SELECT on all tables, and give it to the user.

Step 7 View, trigger and stored procedure

06_view_trigger_proc.sql

Item 7. A view with each order's total, a trigger that takes sold items out of stock, and a procedure that adds an item at the current price.

Expected: the view lists orders 1 to 5 (order 6 was deleted in Step 4) with totals 620000, 76000, 60000, 120000 and 486000. After the call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock (not 194: the trigger only acts on rows inserted after it was created) and order 4 totals 138000. A SQL Server trigger fires once per statement, not per row, so it joins to the inserted table, which holds every inserted row. Each CREATE VIEW/TRIGGER/PROCEDURE must be the first statement in its batch, hence the GO lines.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

The view

The trigger

Create trg_item_stock: after each insert on order_items, subtract the quantity from that product's stock.

The procedure

Create add_order_item with an order id, product id and quantity. It inserts the item with the product's current price.

Use them

Add 1 × product 3 to order 4, then check the stock and the order total.

Step 8 Join, explain, index, explain again

07_join_explain.sql

Item 8: one query over orders, order_items and products, its plan before and after the indexes.

  • SET SHOWPLAN_TEXT ON – shows how the database will find the rows (the plan) instead of, or as well as, running the query.
  • CREATE INDEX – builds a sorted lookup on a column, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading every row.
  • JOIN … ON – matches rows of two tables on a key; the columns in ON are the first candidates for an index.
Expected: 6 rows, for orders 3, 4 and 5. Table Scan or Clustered Index Scan means a full scan; Index Seek means an index is used. In SSMS you can press Ctrl+L for the graphical plan instead. SQL Server does not index foreign key columns for you, so you add one for each join column and one for the date filter. With only a few rows the optimizer may still choose a full scan, because reading a tiny table is cheaper than using an index; on real volumes the second plan switches to the indexes.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

The join

Write USE xxxx_retail; first. Join orders o, order_items oi and products p for orders from 2026-10-05, with quantity * unit_price AS line_total. End with GO.

i. Explain it

Show the plan of the same query.

ii. Create the indexes

Add the indexes the query needs.

iii. Explain it again

Show the plan again and compare.

Step 9 Back up every table, then lose one

08_backup_tables.sql

Item 9 i. Copy each table into a bak_ table, then drop order_items, the table with the two foreign keys.

Expected: bak_order_items holds 10 rows. Dropping a table also drops its indexes and its trigger. The view order_summary stays but fails until the table is back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Copy every table

Write USE xxxx_retail; first. Copy each of the five tables into bak_<table> with SELECT * INTO, and count the items copy.

Drop a table

Drop order_items.

Step 10 Restore the table with its keys

09_restore_table.sql

Item 9 ii. Copy the rows back from bak_order_items, then add back what a copy never carries: the primary key, the foreign keys with their delete rules, the CHECK, the trigger and the indexes.

SELECT * INTO kept the IDENTITY property and the NOT NULL columns, so only the primary key is missing. Expected at the end: 10 rows, a primary key, two foreign keys and the CHECK in the list, and the delete of product 1 fails again, which proves RESTRICT is back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Copy the rows back

Write USE xxxx_retail; first. Recreate order_items from bak_order_items.

Primary key

Restore the primary key on order_item_id.

Foreign keys and CHECK

Add chk_item_qty back, then fk_item_order (CASCADE) and fk_item_product (NO ACTION).

Trigger, indexes

Write GO, then create the trigger again, then the two indexes.

Prove it

Count the rows, list the constraints of order_items, and try to delete product 1 (it must fail).

Step 11 Explain it

Why CASCADE for order items but RESTRICT for products?

An order item means nothing without its order, so it should go with it. A product is part of the sales history: deleting it would leave items pointing at nothing, or wipe old sales. Refuse the delete and mark the product inactive, or move it to the archive, instead.

What does CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT copy?

The columns and the rows. It does not copy the primary key, foreign keys, CHECK constraints, indexes, triggers or defaults. That is why the archive and the backup tables have none, and why Step 10 adds them back by hand.

Why grant through a role?

You grant the privileges to the role once. Each new user gets them with one statement, and revoking from the role changes every member at once. It also shows clearly who can do what.

The user has REVOKE UPDATE on orders. Can they still update orders?

Not through the direct grant. But if a role they hold had UPDATE on orders, they still could. Revoke removes only the grant you name, so check the roles too.

What do you look for in the plan?

Full scans of big tables, and which join method is used. After the indexes, the date filter and the joins should use index lookups. On tiny tables a full scan can still be the cheapest plan, so test on realistic volumes.

Is a table copy a real backup?

No. It lives in the same database on the same disk, so it is lost with the server. It is a quick undo before a risky change. A real backup is a dump or a backup file kept somewhere else: mysqldump, pg_dump, Data Pump or BACKUP DATABASE.

Step 12 Check that it worked

  • After Step 3 the five tables hold 4, 5, 8, 6 and 10 rows.
  • Deleting order 6 removed its item, and deleting product 1 was refused.
  • archives holds 8 rows and has no primary key.
  • After the procedure call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock and order 4 totals 138000.
  • The second plan uses the new indexes (or would, on a bigger table).
  • The restored order_items has 10 rows, its primary key, both foreign keys and the CHECK, and product 1 still cannot be deleted.

Big question: the Ajira recruitment exam. This is the DBA practical exam: you log in with your exam number, load the seed file, then answer scenario questions on the seven topics the exam covers: queries, subqueries, rank functions, triggers, procedures, transactions and user control. Every answer uses only the tables and data in the seed, and every query is written for MySQL 8.

Practise on a test server only. The seed drops and recreates every table in ajira_recruitment_db. The last file creates roles and users. Never type a real password or a real National ID into this page.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

What the exam gives you.
  • A seed file, seed.sql, for a recruitment portal: regions, employers, candidates, vacancies, applications, education, work experience and an application status history. Each table has 10 rows.
  • Scenario questions on: 1 queries, 2 subqueries, 3 rank functions, 4 triggers, 5 procedures, 6 transactions, 7 user control.
  • The scenarios are not given in advance. AI can show you the type of question, but in the exam you must read the scenario and work out the SQL yourself. Practise until you can write each file below without looking.
Login. In the exam terminal, at the C/library/user/student> prompt, log in with your exam number as the user name:
mysql -u psrs_26_12422_01091 -p
Enter password: GODFREY
The user name is your exam number: PSRS/26/12422/01091 is typed as psrs_26_12422_01091. The password is your last name in capital letters: GODFREY.
TopicWhat the scenario asks forFileStep

The design

REGIONS 1 ───< EMPLOYERS 1 ───< VACANCIES
   │ 1                              │ 1
   └──────< CANDIDATES 1 ───< APPLICATIONS >─── (one per candidate per vacancy)
               │ 1    │ 1           │ 1
               │      │             └───< APPLICATION_STATUS_HISTORY
               │      └───< WORK_EXPERIENCE   (end_date NULL = still working there)
               └───< EDUCATION                (grade_or_gpa is text: 'GPA 3.8' or 'Credit')
Three traps in this seed. middle_name is NULL for Baraka and Kelvin, so CONCAT(first, ' ', middle, ' ', last) returns NULL for them: use CONCAT_WS. grade_or_gpa is text, so you cut out the number with SUBSTRING and CAST before you compare or rank it, and skip the Diploma rows that say Credit. chk_vacancy_posts refuses posts_available = 0, so filling the last post must close the vacancy instead.

Which JOIN? A simple decision guide.
Your requirementJOIN to consider

01_queries.sql

Scenario: the Recruitment Secretariat wants quick reports for a meeting.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Open vacancies with employer and region

What to do: List every open job with its employer and region. Earliest closing date first.

How: Switch to ajira_recruitment_db. List vacancy_title, employer_name, region_name and application_deadline for every vacancy whose status is Open, earliest deadline first. Join vacancies v to employers e, then to regions r through the employer.

New words:
  • USE db picks the database to work in, so you can write vacancies instead of ajira_recruitment_db.vacancies.
You should see: 10 rows. First: Database Administrator II (closes 2027-02-28). Last: Junior Data Analyst (closes 2027-03-28).

Full names and ages

What to do: Show each candidate's full name and age.

How: Show candidate_id, the full name as full_name built with CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, middle_name, last_name), and the age today as age with TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, date_of_birth, CURDATE()). Oldest first.

New words:
  • CONCAT_WS(separator, a, b, c) "concat with separator": joins the texts with the separator between them and skips NULLs. CONCAT_WS(' ', 'Baraka', NULL, 'Kassim') → Baraka Kassim.
  • TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, start, end) counts how many whole units (YEAR, MONTH, DAY) lie between two dates. TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, '2000-12-01', '2026-10-29') → 25: the 26th birthday has not come yet, so it is not counted. That is exactly how age works.
  • CURDATE() today's date, without the time, for example 2026-10-29.
You should see: 10 names. Baraka Kassim and Kelvin Mhando have no middle name, but their names must still show, not NULL. Oldest at the top: Hassan Ali Mfaume.

What to do: For each type of employer, count the employers and add up their posts.

How: For each employer_type, show the number of employers as employers and the total posts_available as total_posts. LEFT JOIN the vacancies, count with COUNT(DISTINCT e.employer_id), biggest total first.

New words:
  • COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts each different value once. An employer with 3 vacancies appears in 3 joined rows, but is counted as 1.
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the first table, even when the second table has no match. The second table's columns are then NULL.

  • CURDATE() today's date, without the time, for example 2026-10-29.

Step 5 Rank functions

03_ranking.sql

Scenario: the selection panel wants candidates and vacancies in order, with ties handled fairly.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Rank candidates by GPA

What to do: Put the Bachelor candidates in order of GPA, best first, numbered three ways.

How: Switch to ajira_recruitment_db. In a CTE g, take first name, last name and the GPA as a number gpa (rows LIKE 'GPA%' only). Then show RANK(), DENSE_RANK() and ROW_NUMBER() over gpa DESC as rnk, dense_rnk and row_num. Break the ROW_NUMBER tie with last_name.

New words:
  • USE db picks the database to work in, so you can write vacancies instead of ajira_recruitment_db.vacancies.
  • WITH name AS (...) a CTE: a named result you build first and then select from, like a derived table but easier to read.
  • CAST(x AS DECIMAL(3,2)) changes the type of a value. CAST('3.8' AS DECIMAL(3,2)) → the number 3.80, which you can compare, average and sort. DECIMAL(3,2) means 3 digits in all, 2 after the point.
  • SUBSTRING(text, start) takes the text from position start to the end. Positions start at 1, so SUBSTRING('GPA 3.8', 5) → 3.8.
  • LIKE 'GPA%' matches a text pattern. % means "anything here", so 'GPA%' matches every text that starts with GPA.
  • RANK() numbers the rows in order. Ties share a number and the next number is skipped: 1, 2, 2, 4.
  • OVER (ORDER BY ...) turns the function into a window function: it works across the rows in this order, but keeps every row (unlike GROUP BY).
  • DENSE_RANK() like RANK, but no number is skipped after a tie: 1, 2, 2, 3.
  • ROW_NUMBER() gives every row its own number, even on a tie: 1, 2, 3, 4. Add a tie-breaker to ORDER BY so the order is not random.
You should see: The table below. Neema and Asha tie at 3.6: RANK gives both 4 and jumps to 6, DENSE_RANK gives both 4 and goes on with 5, ROW_NUMBER gives 4 and 5.
first_namelast_namegparnkdense_rnkrow_num

Rank vacancies inside each employer type

What to do: Rank the jobs by number of posts inside each employer type. The numbering starts again for each type.

How: Show employer_type, vacancy_title, posts_available and RANK() with PARTITION BY e.employer_type, most posts first, as rank_in_type.

  • PARTITION BY x splits the rows into groups inside OVER, and the numbering starts again at 1 in each group.
You should see: MDA: ICT Officer II 1, Database Administrator II 2, Database Technician 2
LGA: Records Management Assistant 1, Human Resources Officer 2, Accountant II 2, Procurement Officer 4

Private: Junior Data Analyst 1

Top vacancy in each region

What to do: Find the job with the most posts in each region.

How: In a CTE ranked, number the vacancies with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the employer's region_id, most posts first, tie broken by vacancy_title, as rn. Keep rn = 1 and show region name, vacancy title and posts.

You should see: Dar es Salaam: Records Management Assistant (4)
Dodoma: Database Technician (2; it ties with Human Resources Officer and wins by alphabet)
Arusha: Procurement Officer (1)

Running total of posts

What to do: Add up the posts job by job, in order of closing date (a running total).

How: Show vacancy_title, application_deadline, posts_available and SUM(posts_available) OVER (ORDER BY application_deadline) as running_posts.

New words:
  • SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY ...) a running total: each row shows the sum of itself and all rows before it.
You should see: 2, 5, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 19, 21

Step 6 Triggers

04_triggers.sql

Scenario: every status change must be recorded automatically, and nobody may apply to a vacancy that is not open.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit trigger

What to do: Make a trigger that writes a history row every time an application's status changes.

How: Switch to ajira_recruitment_db and set DELIMITER //. Create trg_application_status AFTER UPDATE ON applications. When OLD.application_status <> NEW.application_status, insert into application_status_history the id, old and new status, NOW(), CURRENT_USER() and 'Status changed'.

New words:
  • USE db picks the database to work in, so you can write vacancies instead of ajira_recruitment_db.vacancies.
  • DELIMITER // changes the "end of statement" mark from ; to //, so the ;s inside BEGIN ... END do not end the CREATE too early. DELIMITER ; puts it back.
  • AFTER UPDATE / BEFORE INSERT ... FOR EACH ROW when the trigger fires: after every changed row, or before every new row is saved.
  • OLD. and NEW. inside a trigger, OLD.column is the value before the change and NEW.column the value after it (or the row being inserted).
  • NOW() today's date and the time right now, for example 2026-10-29 09:15:00.
  • CURRENT_USER() the account you are logged in as, for example psrs_26_12422_01091@localhost.
You should see: Query OK. Nothing to see until you test it.

Test the audit trigger

What to do: Test it: move application 2 to Interview, then look at its history.

How: Move application 2 to Interview, then select old_status, new_status and changed_by from the history of application 2.

You should see: 2 rows: Submitted → Shortlisted (from the seed) and Shortlisted → Interview (new, with your login in changed_by)

Refuse closed vacancies

What to do: Make a trigger that blocks an application to a job that is not Open or is past its closing date.

How: Create trg_application_open_only BEFORE INSERT ON applications. Read the vacancy's status and deadline INTO two declared variables. If the status is not Open or DATE(NEW.application_date) is after the deadline, SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' with the message Vacancy is not open for applications.

New words:
  • DECLARE name TYPE makes a variable that lives only inside this BEGIN ... END.
  • SELECT ... INTO variables puts the values found by the SELECT into variables instead of showing them.
  • DATE(x) keeps only the date part of a date and time: DATE('2026-10-29 09:15') → 2026-10-29.
  • SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' raises your own error: the statement stops and the client sees MESSAGE_TEXT. 45000 is the code for "error made by the user".
You should see: Query OK.

Test the refusal

What to do: Test it: close job 5, try to apply to it, then open it again.

How: Close vacancy 5, try to insert an application from candidate 2 to vacancy 5 dated NOW(), then open vacancy 5 again.

You should see: The insert fails with ERROR 1644 (45000): Vacancy is not open for applications. The two updates work.

Step 7 Procedures

05_procedures.sql

Scenario: the portal needs one call to apply for a job, a report per employer type, and a count it can read back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

apply_for_vacancy

What to do: Make a procedure that applies a candidate for a job: it adds the application and a history row. Use it so Amani applies for job 9.

How: Switch to ajira_recruitment_db and set DELIMITER //. Create apply_for_vacancy(IN p_candidate INT, IN p_vacancy INT, IN p_letter TEXT): insert a Submitted application dated NOW(), then a history row for LAST_INSERT_ID() from NULL to Submitted by System with Application received. Call it for candidate 1 and vacancy 9, then list candidate 1's applications.

New words:
  • USE db picks the database to work in, so you can write vacancies instead of ajira_recruitment_db.vacancies.
  • DELIMITER // changes the "end of statement" mark from ; to //, so the ;s inside BEGIN ... END do not end the CREATE too early. DELIMITER ; puts it back.
  • IN and OUT parameters IN passes a value into the procedure. OUT gives a value back to the caller.
  • NOW() today's date and the time right now, for example 2026-10-29 09:15:00.
  • LAST_INSERT_ID() the AUTO_INCREMENT id of the row you just inserted, so the history row can point to the new application.
  • CALL name(...) runs a stored procedure.
You should see: Amani now has 2 applications (jobs 1 and 9); the new one is number 11. Running the call again fails, because she has already applied (uq_candidate_vacancy).

vacancy_report

What to do: Make a procedure that lists the jobs of one employer type and how many people applied. Run it for MDA.

How: Create vacancy_report(IN p_type VARCHAR(20)) that lists, for one employer type, each vacancy title, employer name and COUNT(a.application_id) AS applications (a LEFT JOIN, so a vacancy with no application shows 0), most first. Call it for MDA.

New words:
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the first table, even when the second table has no match. The second table's columns are then NULL.
You should see: Database Technician 2, Database Administrator II 1, ICT Officer II 1

count_applications

What to do: Make a procedure that counts one candidate's applications and gives the number back. Run it for Amani.

How: Create count_applications(IN p_candidate INT, OUT p_total INT) that counts the candidate's applications INTO p_total. Call it for candidate 1 into @total and select it.

New words:
  • @total a session variable: it keeps its value until you log out. The OUT parameter is written into it.
You should see: @total = 2

Step 8 Transactions

06_transactions.sql

Scenario: selecting a candidate and using up a post must happen together or not at all.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Select a candidate safely

What to do: Select the candidate for job 9 and take one of its posts, both together.

How: Switch to ajira_recruitment_db. In one transaction, set application 9 to Selected and take one post from vacancy 9, then COMMIT and show vacancy 9's posts_available.

New words:
  • USE db picks the database to work in, so you can write vacancies instead of ajira_recruitment_db.vacancies.
  • START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT groups statements so they count together. COMMIT saves them all for good.
You should see: Job 9 now has 1 post. The history gets Shortlisted → Selected from the trigger.

Undo a mistake

What to do: Delete all the history, look at it, then undo.

How: Start a transaction, delete every row of application_status_history, count it, ROLLBACK, and count it again.

New words:
  • ROLLBACK undoes everything since START TRANSACTION that was not committed.
You should see: The count is 0, then after ROLLBACK it is back to 13 (if you did every step in order).

Keep half of the work

What to do: Extend job 1's closing date by 7 days, cancel the job, then undo only the cancel.

How: Extend vacancy 1's deadline by 7 days with DATE_ADD, set SAVEPOINT deadline_extended, cancel the vacancy, roll back to the savepoint, COMMIT, then show its deadline and status.

New words:
  • DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL 7 DAY) adds time to a date: DATE_ADD('2027-02-28', INTERVAL 7 DAY) → 2027-03-07.
  • SAVEPOINT name a bookmark inside a transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes only the work after the bookmark.
You should see: Closing date 2027-03-07, status still Open.

An error inside a transaction

What to do: Try to select the candidate for job 5, which has only 1 post. Taking it would leave 0 posts, which the table does not allow.

How: Try to select application 5 and take the only post of vacancy 5. The second update breaks chk_vacancy_posts, so end with ROLLBACK and check application 5.

You should see: The second update fails: Check constraint 'chk_vacancy_posts' is violated. After ROLLBACK, application 5 is still Rejected.

Step 9 User control

07_user_control.sql

Scenario: HR viewers may read vacancies and candidates without personal data; recruiters may also record applications.

Creating roles and users needs CREATE ROLE and CREATE USER rights. If your exam login lacks them, write the statements anyway and explain them.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

A view without personal data

What to do: Make a view of the candidates without private data: no National ID, email, phone or date of birth.

How: Switch to ajira_recruitment_db. Create v_candidate_public with only candidate_id, first_name, last_name, gender and region_id: no National ID, email, phone or date of birth.

New words:
  • USE db picks the database to work in, so you can write vacancies instead of ajira_recruitment_db.vacancies.
  • CREATE VIEW saves a SELECT under a name. It looks like a table, but shows only the columns you chose.
You should see: Query OK. Selecting from the view shows 5 columns.

Roles

What to do: Make two roles. hr_viewer reads jobs and the view. hr_officer can also add and change applications and run apply_for_vacancy.

How: Create roles hr_viewer and hr_officer. Give hr_viewer SELECT on vacancies and on the view. Give hr_officer SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on applications, EXECUTE on apply_for_vacancy, and the role hr_viewer itself.

New words:
  • CREATE ROLE a named bundle of rights. Give rights to the role once, then give the role to users.
  • GRANT ... ON ... TO gives a right (SELECT, INSERT, EXECUTE ...) on a table or procedure to a user or role.
You should see: Query OK.

Users

What to do: Make the users viewer1 and recruiter1 and give each a role.

How: Create 'viewer1'@'localhost' with password Viewer#2026 and 'recruiter1'@'localhost' with Recruit#2026. Grant them hr_viewer and hr_officer, and make the roles active at login with SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL.

New words:
  • 'user'@'localhost' a MySQL account is a name plus the computer it may log in from. localhost means only from this server.
  • IDENTIFIED BY sets the account's password.
  • SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL makes the granted roles switch on by themselves at login. Without it the user must run SET ROLE first.
You should see: Query OK. This needs the right to create users.

Check and take back

What to do: Look at recruiter1's rights, then take UPDATE away from hr_officer.

How: Show recruiter1's grants USING 'hr_officer', revoke UPDATE on applications from hr_officer, and show the role's grants again.

New words:
  • SHOW GRANTS FOR ... USING role lists the rights of a user or role. USING also shows the rights that come through that role.
  • REVOKE ... FROM takes a right away. Taking it from a role takes it from every user of that role.
You should see: After the revoke, hr_officer has only SELECT and INSERT on applications. Logged in as viewer1, the view works but SELECT * FROM candidates fails with ERROR 1142.

Clean up

What to do: Delete the users and the roles.

How: Drop both users, then both roles.

New words:
  • DROP USER / DROP ROLE deletes the account or the role and its rights.
You should see: Query OK.

Step 10 Explain it

Why CONCAT_WS and not CONCAT?

CONCAT returns NULL if any part is NULL, so Baraka and Kelvin, who have no middle name, would get no name at all. CONCAT_WS skips NULL parts.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER?

Neema and Asha both have 3.6. RANK gives both 4 and skips to 6. DENSE_RANK gives both 4 and goes on with 5. ROW_NUMBER gives 4 and 5, so you must add a tie-breaker such as last_name or the order is random.

Subquery or JOIN?

IN and NOT EXISTS answer "is there a matching row?" without repeating rows. A JOIN repeats a candidate once per match. NOT EXISTS is also safe when the inner column has NULLs; NOT IN is not.

Why SIGNAL in a trigger?

SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' stops the insert with your own message. The rule then holds for every client: the portal, a script or a DBA at the console.

Does an error roll back the transaction?

No. In MySQL a failed statement is undone, but earlier statements in the same transaction stay until you COMMIT or ROLLBACK. That is why Step 8 ends with ROLLBACK.

Why grant through roles and a view?

The view hides the National ID, email, phone and date of birth. Roles hold the privileges once: each new user gets them with one GRANT, and one REVOKE on the role changes every member.

Done The Ajira exam practice is complete

  • Every table had 10 rows after the seed.
  • Each query file matches its expected result.
  • Application 2 has 2 history rows, and the closed vacancy refused an application.
  • Amani has 2 applications, and vacancy 9 has 1 post left.
  • viewer1 can read the view but not candidates.

Start here Install MySQL and log in

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

terminal

The server must be running before you can log in.

Run the net start commands in Command Prompt opened as Administrator. Service names can differ, so open services.msc to see the exact name on your computer. On Linux use sudo systemctl start mysql. On macOS with Homebrew use brew services start mysql.

terminal

This is the command-line login. You type your password when asked. It stays hidden while you type.

On a fresh Ubuntu server, sudo mysql may log you in as root without a password. Your prompt changes to mysql> when you are in.

first_commands.sql

Once you are in, run these to prove the login works and see where you are.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

01_create.sql

Run this in the mysql client as root.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task.

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Add rows, then read them back with WHERE and ORDER BY.

  • USE – picks the database the next commands run in.
  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Step 3 JOIN

03_join.sql

An INNER JOIN keeps only the rows that match on both sides. Give each table a short alias.

Step 4 Create a view

04_view.sql

A view that hides everything except name and salary.

Step 5 Users and roles

05_users.sql

Always give the full account name 'user'@'host'. In the task, TO 'analyst' alone would mean 'analyst'@'%', a different account.

Step 6 Backup and restore

terminal

The most common MySQL backup tool is mysqldump. It writes SQL that rebuilds your tables and data. Run these in a normal terminal, not inside the mysql client.

  • -u root – the MySQL username.
  • -p – ask for the password.
  • company_db – the database to back up. Add a table name after it to back up only that table.
  • > – save the output to a file. < feeds a file back in to restore.
  • --all-databases – back up every database, including users and permissions. Useful for DBA work.
  • --single-transaction – takes a consistent copy of InnoDB tables without locking them, so users can keep working.
  • --routines – includes stored procedures and functions.
  • --triggers – includes triggers (on by default, but writing it makes it clear).
To restore one database, it must exist first: run CREATE DATABASE company_db; in mysql if it is missing. For a live database, add the options below. \ at the end of a line means the command continues on the next line (Linux and macOS; in Windows PowerShell use `, or write it all on one line).

backup_drill

Interview practical: create data, back it up, delete the database by accident, then restore it. The SQL lines run in the mysql client; the mysqldump and mysql -u root -p lines run in a terminal.

Careful. DROP DATABASE deletes everything in it, including your Step 1–5 tables. If company_db already exists, CREATE DATABASE fails: drop it first or use a test machine.

Step 7 Indexing

07_index.sql

Step 8 Triggers

08_trigger.sql

A BEFORE INSERT trigger changes the new row before it is saved. NEW is the row being inserted.

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

09_recovery.sql

The binary log records every change. With a full backup plus the binary log you can recover to a moment just before a crash, so the RPO drops from minutes to nearly zero.

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

10_performance.sql

Read the plan first. type: ALL in the output means a full table scan.

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name. A plain JOIN would hide it.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: MySQL lets you drop a table that a view uses. The view stays but fails with an error when you query it. Check dependencies before you drop anything.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: the user gets the role's rights only while the role is granted and active. Drop the role and the rights go with it.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

OLD is the row before the change and NEW is the row after. A DELETE trigger has only OLD; an INSERT trigger has only NEW.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

terminal

Test the restore time (your real RTO) with time, and replay the binary log up to one minute before the crash (point-in-time recovery).

The .sql backup restores the data as of 09:45. The binary log then replays every change from 09:45 to 09:59, so the RPO is one minute, not fifteen. time works on Linux and macOS; in PowerShell use Measure-Command.

Step 16 Change data and tables

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Step 17 Constraints

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement. CHECK is enforced from MySQL 8.0.16. MySQL 8 runs in strict mode by default, which is why the missing name is an error.

Step 18 Transactions and locking

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. InnoDB (the normal MySQL engine) runs REPEATABLE READ by default, and autocommit is on: each statement commits alone unless you start a transaction. MyISAM tables have no transactions. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

18b_locking.sql

Book cinema seats safely: lock one row, read with a shared lock, skip busy rows, set a wait limit, lock a whole table, and use a version number instead of a lock.

In this database. InnoDB locks rows through the index. Without an index on seat_no it would lock every row it reads, which is why seat_no is UNIQUE. A plain SELECT takes no lock: it reads a snapshot. FOR SHARE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED need MySQL 8.0 (older: LOCK IN SHARE MODE). Expected: after part 2, A1 is booked by Amina. Part 4 returns A2, the first free seat. In part 7 the first ROW_COUNT() is 1 and the second is 0, because row_version is already 1. At the end: A1 Amina 0, A2 Juma 1, A3 empty 0.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. You need the PROCESS privilege to see other people's sessions (root has it). Killing a big transaction makes MySQL roll it back, which can take a while.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved inside the database. You run it with CALL instead of retyping the statements. Needs MySQL 5.0 or later; run it in the mysql client.

  • DELIMITER // – changes the end-of-statement mark, so the ; inside the procedure does not end the CREATE early. DELIMITER ; puts it back.
  • CREATE PROCEDURE name(...) – saves the procedure. IN parameters bring values in; OUT parameters send a value back.
  • BEGIN … END – wraps the statements the procedure runs.
  • SELECT … INTO p_total – puts a query result into a variable or OUT parameter.
  • CALL – runs the procedure. @total is a session variable that catches the OUT value.
  • SHOW PROCEDURE STATUS / DROP PROCEDURE – list the saved procedures / delete one.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row. Window functions need MySQL 8.0 or later.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Big question · Step 2 Build the tables

01_shop_create.sql

Turn the nouns and rules of line 1 into four tables.

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

02_shop_data.sql

Lines 2 and 3 of the ticket: sample data, a price rise, a delete and a new column.

Run this on a fresh database so the ids start at 1, because the item rows use ids 1 to 3. The item keeps the old price (unit_price) even though the product price rose.

Big question · Step 4 Reports

03_shop_reports.sql

Line 4 of the ticket: four reports with joins, grouping and a subquery.

Expected results: order 1 for Amina totals 4200. Juma and Neema never ordered (Juma's only order was cancelled and deleted). Only Drinks passes the 2000 line (3000). Juice and Rice 5kg were never bought. A HAVING filters groups after the sum, a WHERE filters rows before it.

04_shop_security.sql

Line 5 of the ticket: hide the emails behind a view, and give each user only what the job needs.

The sales team gets the view, not the tables, so emails stay hidden. The clerk can read and change what an order needs and nothing else: no DELETE. Grant the least that works.

Big question · Step 6 Index and audit trigger

05_shop_speed_audit.sql

Lines 6 and 7 of the ticket: speed up the date search, and record every price change.

MySQL already builds an index for every foreign key, which is why the new index is on the date, not on customer_id. On a table this small the database may still scan the whole table. That is normal: the index pays off when the table has thousands of rows. The trigger logs only real price changes, so the stock updates in Step 7 add nothing to the audit.

Big question · Step 7 Place an order safely

06_shop_order.sql

Line 8 of the ticket: an order, its items and the stock change are saved together or not at all.

Expected: two orders remain (1 and the good new one), and Rice 5kg stock is 18. MAX(id) finds the new order on a practice server with one user. In a real application read the new id with LAST_INSERT_ID().

Big question · Step 8 Backup and restore

terminal

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Big question Task 1, Recruitment

Big question · Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. MySQL already builds an index for every foreign key, so interview_results.application_id and applications.vacancy_id are indexed for free. A separate index on applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Big question · Step 3 seed.sql: realistic test data

seed.sql

Section A.2. Run it once on the fresh schema, so the ids start at 1: the applications refer to applicants and vacancies by those ids.

The password hashes are fake placeholders: a real system stores a bcrypt or Argon2 hash made by the application, never a password. Placements has only 2 rows on purpose: only selected applicants can be placed, and Q11 needs one selected applicant who is not placed yet. The dates are set around October 2026, so question iv depends on today's date when you run it.

Big question · Step 4 The headline numbers

03_kpis.sql

Questions i, ii and vii.

Expected: 13 submitted applications, an average of 1.30 per vacancy (13 over 10 vacancies) and a placement rate of 15.38% (2 of 13). The status filter for ii sits in the ON condition, not in WHERE: a WHERE would throw away the vacancies with zero applications, and the average would wrongly become 13 over 7. * 1.0 turns whole-number division into decimal division on every database.

Big question · Step 5 Vacancy reports

04_vacancy_reports.sql

Questions iii/Q3, iv/Q4, v/Q2 and viii/Q5.

Expected: iii returns vacancies 8, 9 and 10. iv returns 6 and 7 (on 2026-10-26; later dates add more). v returns seven rows, not five: Accountant II and Nurse Officer II tie on 3 and both get rank 1, then two vacancies share rank 3 and three share rank 5. RANK() keeps ties honest; ROW_NUMBER() would cut them at random and DENSE_RANK() would give 1, 1, 2, 2, 3. viii returns the same two leaders, because a maximum can be shared. CURRENT_DATE gets today's date in MySQL.

Big question · Step 6 The recruitment funnel

05_funnel.sql

Question vi: per public institution, how many applications go in at the top, and how many survive each stage.

Why DISTINCT? An application with two interview rows appears twice after the join, so a plain COUNT would count Amina twice. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts it once. CASE ... END returns NULL when the condition is false, and COUNT ignores NULLs, so each column counts only its own stage. Expected: Ministry of Finance 3, 2, 1, 1; Office of the Attorney General 1, 1, 1, 1; e-Government Authority 2, 2, 1, 0.

06_joins.sql

Q1 and Q6 to Q11. Each one practises a different kind of join.

Expected: Q1 eight applicants. Q7 seven shortlisted rows. Q8 seven rows, for example Amina Juma, Accountant II, 160, Passed. Q9 five applicants with 2 each. Q10 Elia Shirima (only a Draft), Peter Ngowi (Withdrawn), Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo. Q11 Juma Hassan, ICT Officer II. Q10 uses NOT EXISTS instead of a LEFT JOIN because the test also has a status condition: it reads as "there is no submitted application for this person".

Question x and Q12: follow one applicant from application to placement, across all five tables.

Expected for Amina Juma: two rows for Accountant II (Written 78, Oral 82, both at stage "5 Placed" at the Ministry of Finance) and one row for Nurse Officer II at stage "1 Applied". The interviews and placement are LEFT JOIN, so an application that has not reached those stages still shows. Change the email to follow anyone else.

Big question · Step 9 Index on applications(vacancy_id): before and after

08_index.sql

The "index joins" question and the Q12 practical: same query, two plans. The query joins applications to applicants for one vacancy.

Read the type and key columns. Before: ALL on a, a full table scan. After: ref using idx_app_vacancy. MySQL had quietly made fk_app_vacancy for the foreign key, which is why the "before" needs IGNORE INDEX to show a table with no index. Once your own index exists, MySQL may drop its automatic one.

Q1, Q2 and Q3.

Q4, Q5 and Q8.

Q9 and item v: officers see names, centres and scores, a masked phone, and nothing else.

terminal

A dump made without --databases holds no USE line, so you can load it into any database name. --routines and --triggers keep stored code; views are always included.

01_retail_schema.sql

Items 1 and 2. Parents first: categories and customers must exist before the tables that point to them.

fk_product_category already refuses to delete a category that still has products: ON DELETE RESTRICT. The two foreign keys of order_items are added in Step 4, because they are item 4 of the question.

Big question · Step 3 Insert the data

02_retail_seed.sql

Item 3: 4 categories, 5 customers, 8 products, 6 orders and 10 order items. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: order 6 is Cancelled and has one item (used to test CASCADE). Product 1, the Smartphone, is in two orders (used to test RESTRICT). Rehema Mollel has no order and the Pen Pack was never sold.

Big question · Step 4 Delete rules: CASCADE and RESTRICT

03_delete_rules.sql

Item 4. Delete an order and its items go with it. Try to delete a product that was sold and the database refuses.

Expected: the first count is 1, the second is 0. The product delete fails with error 1451 (Cannot delete or update a parent row), and the Smartphone is still there.

Big question · Step 5 Archive the products

04_archive.sql

Item 5: a copy of products, with every row, in a new table archives.

Expected: 8 rows. In MySQL the prefix xxxx_retail. is the database name. The copy gets the columns and rows only: no primary key, no foreign key, no CHECK and no index. Step 9 uses the same idea for the backup, which is why Step 10 has to add the keys back.

Big question · Step 6 Grant and revoke privileges

05_privileges.sql

Item 6. You are not asked to create the accounts, only to show the statements an admin would run. The user is 'retail_user'@'localhost'.

  • GRANT … ON … TO – gives a privilege on a table (or all tables) to a user or role.
  • REVOKE … ON … FROM – takes a privilege back. Only that privilege goes; the others stay.
  • CREATE ROLE – makes a named bundle of privileges. Grant to the role once, then give the role to many users.
  • GRANT role TO user – gives a user everything the role holds.
Write these; do not run them unless you are an admin on a test server where retail_admin and retail_user already exist. xxxx_retail.* means every table in the database. After item iv, the user can still insert and delete orders but not change them.

Big question · Step 7 View, trigger and stored procedure

06_view_trigger_proc.sql

Item 7. A view with each order's total, a trigger that takes sold items out of stock, and a procedure that adds an item at the current price.

Expected: the view lists orders 1 to 5 (order 6 was deleted in Step 4) with totals 620000, 76000, 60000, 120000 and 486000. After the call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock (not 194: the trigger only acts on rows inserted after it was created) and order 4 totals 138000. A one-statement trigger needs no DELIMITER; the procedure has a BEGIN … END block, so it does.

Big question · Step 8 Join, explain, index, explain again

07_join_explain.sql

Item 8: one query over orders, order_items and products, its plan before and after the indexes.

  • EXPLAIN – shows how the database will find the rows (the plan) instead of, or as well as, running the query.
  • CREATE INDEX – builds a sorted lookup on a column, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading every row.
  • JOIN … ON – matches rows of two tables on a key; the columns in ON are the first candidates for an index.
Expected: 6 rows, for orders 3, 4 and 5. In the type column, ALL means a full table scan; ref or range means an index is used. MySQL already created an index for each foreign key in Step 4 (SHOW INDEX shows them), so the joins on order_id and product_id are covered. The missing one is the date filter. With only a few rows the optimizer may still choose a full scan, because reading a tiny table is cheaper than using an index; on real volumes the second plan switches to the indexes.

Big question · Step 9 Back up every table, then lose one

08_backup_tables.sql

Item 9 i. Copy each table into a bak_ table, then drop order_items, the table with the two foreign keys.

Expected: bak_order_items holds 10 rows. Dropping a table also drops its indexes and its trigger. The view order_summary stays but fails until the table is back.

Big question · Step 10 Restore the table with its keys

09_restore_table.sql

Item 9 ii. Copy the rows back from bak_order_items, then add back what a copy never carries: the primary key, the foreign keys with their delete rules, the CHECK, the trigger and the indexes.

MODIFY with AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY restores the primary key and the auto-numbering in one go. Expected at the end: 10 rows, a primary key, two foreign keys and the CHECK in the list, and the delete of product 1 fails again, which proves RESTRICT is back.

Start here Install PostgreSQL and log in

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

terminal

The server must be running before you can log in.

Run the net start commands in Command Prompt opened as Administrator. Service names can differ, so open services.msc to see the exact name on your computer. On Linux use sudo systemctl start postgresql. On macOS with Homebrew use brew services start postgresql.

terminal

This is the command-line login. You type your password when asked. It stays hidden while you type.

On Linux the postgres account is an operating system user, so use sudo -u postgres psql the first time. Your prompt changes to postgres=# when you are in.

first_commands.sql

Once you are in, run these to prove the login works and see where you are.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

01_create.sql

Run this in psql as the postgres user. \c is a psql command that switches database.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. PostgreSQL has no AUTO_INCREMENT: use an identity column (or SERIAL).

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Same idea as MySQL. The data type for money is NUMERIC.

  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Step 3 JOIN

03_join.sql

Step 4 Create a view

04_view.sql

Step 5 Users and roles

05_users.sql

In PostgreSQL users and groups are both roles. A role needs CONNECT on the database, USAGE on the schema, and SELECT on the tables.

Step 6 Backup and restore

terminal

Run these in a normal terminal. The plain file is SQL text. The custom format (-F c) is compressed and lets pg_restore pick what to restore.

The target database must already exist. Create it first with createdb -U postgres company_db on a new server.

Step 7 Indexing

07_index.sql

Step 8 Triggers

08_trigger.sql

PostgreSQL needs two pieces: a trigger function that returns the changed row, and the trigger that calls it. $$ marks the start and end of the function body.

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

09_recovery.sql

WAL (write-ahead log) archiving plus a base backup lets you recover to any moment, which lowers the RPO. These commands show whether it is ready.

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

10_performance.sql

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real timings. Look for "Seq Scan" (reads the whole table) versus "Index Scan".

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name. A plain JOIN would hide it.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: PostgreSQL refuses DROP TABLE employees; while a view uses it. It says other objects depend on it. DROP TABLE employees CASCADE; would drop the view too, so use CASCADE with care.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: PostgreSQL will not drop a role that still holds privileges ("role cannot be dropped because some objects depend on it"). Revoke first, then drop.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

UPDATE OF salary fires only when the salary column is changed. In PostgreSQL, DROP TRIGGER must name the table.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

postgresql.conf

Turn on WAL archiving so every change is copied out. With a base backup plus the archive you can restore to any minute. Edit postgresql.conf and restart the service.

Test the restore time too (your real RTO): time psql -U postgres -d company_db -f backup.sql. Windows paths and copy differ from the Linux cp shown here.

Step 16 Change data and tables

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table (PostgreSQL needs TRUNCATE ... CASCADE). A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Step 17 Constraints

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Step 18 Transactions and locking

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. PostgreSQL runs READ COMMITTED by default and treats READ UNCOMMITTED like it. Each statement commits alone unless you BEGIN. If a statement fails inside a transaction, the rest is refused until you ROLLBACK. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

18b_locking.sql

Book cinema seats safely: lock one row, read with a shared lock, skip busy rows, set a wait limit, lock a whole table, and use a version number instead of a lock.

In this database. Readers never block writers: a plain SELECT takes no row lock. Row locks are kept in the row itself, so PostgreSQL never turns many row locks into a table lock. A lock that waits too long fails with error 55P03. RETURNING shows the rows the UPDATE changed. Expected: after part 2, A1 is booked by Amina. Part 4 returns A2, the first free seat. In part 7 the first UPDATE returns A2 with row_version 1 (UPDATE 1) and the second returns nothing (UPDATE 0). At the end: A1 Amina 0, A2 Juma 1, A3 empty 0.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. A normal user sees only their own sessions in full. postgres (a superuser) sees everything and can end any session.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved inside the database. In PostgreSQL a PROCEDURE does work and is run with CALL; a FUNCTION returns a value and is used inside SELECT. Procedures need PostgreSQL 11 or later.

  • CREATE PROCEDURE name(...) – saves the procedure with its parameters.
  • LANGUAGE plpgsql – the procedural language that allows BEGIN … END, variables and IF. LANGUAGE sql is for a plain query.
  • AS $$ … $$ – dollar quotes hold the body, so you do not have to escape quotes inside it.
  • CREATE FUNCTION … RETURNS INT – a function that gives back one value.
  • CALL / SELECT fn() – run a procedure / use a function.
  • pg_proc / DROP FUNCTION – the catalog of procedures and functions (prokind is p or f) / delete one.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Big question · Step 9 Index on applications(vacancy_id): before and after

08_index.sql

The "index joins" question and the Q12 practical: same query, two plans. The query joins applications to applicants for one vacancy.

Before: Seq Scan on applications. After: Index Scan or Bitmap Index Scan on idx_app_vacancy. With only 15 rows PostgreSQL rightly prefers a sequential scan, so enable_seqscan = off tells this one session to avoid it if it can, which proves the index is usable. On a table with thousands of rows the planner picks the index by itself.

Big question · Step 10 Audit trigger on applications

09_audit.sql

Question ix and Q13: every change of application_status is recorded with who made it and when, even if someone changes it outside the application.

Expected: exactly one audit row, application 13 from Submitted to Selected. The second update changes only the shortlist, so the trigger writes nothing. Because application 13 is now Selected and has no placement, Q11 from Step 7 would now also list Neema Kileo: run it again and see.

Big question Task 2, Assessments

Big question · Step 2 Create the database

01_assess_schema.sql

One table per entity, with the business rules as constraints.

No extra index is needed for the foreign keys: uq_one_attempt starts with applicant_id and uq_station_slot starts with workstation_id, so each foreign key column already leads an index. The one extra index is on assessment_date, because officers search by day.

Big question · Step 3 Populate the tables

02_assess_seed.sql

12 applicants, 10 workstations and 12 assessments. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: DSM-01 is used three times (the most). ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01 are never used. Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo have no assessment. Amina Juma and Baraka Mwakyusa sat at DSM-01 on the same day in different sessions, which the unique rule allows.

Big question · Step 4 Workstation usage

03_usage.sql

Q1, Q2 and Q3.

Expected: Q1 DSM-01 with 3. Q2 ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01. Q3 all 10 workstations, the unused ones with 0. COUNT(s.assessment_id) counts only real matches, so an unused station gives 0; COUNT(*) would give 1, because the LEFT JOIN still returns one row with NULLs.

Big question · Step 5 Scores

04_scores.sql

Q4, Q5 and Q8.

Expected: Q4 DSM-03 first with 88.00. Q5 Rehema Mollel, 91. Q8 the overall average is 72.92, so Amina Juma (85), Neema Kileo (74), Rehema Mollel (91), Halima Said (77) and Peter Ngowi (85) are above it. score * 1.0 matters: the average of whole numbers is otherwise cut to a whole number.

Big question · Step 6 Join questions

05_joins.sql

Q6, Q7 and two extra join questions of the kind interviewers add.

Expected: Q6 Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo. Q7 twelve rows. Centres: Dar es Salaam 3 stations and 6 tests, Arusha 2 and 0, Mbeya 1 and 0. The self-join returns DSM-01 on 2026-10-05: Amina Juma then Baraka Mwakyusa. s2.assessment_id > s1.assessment_id stops each pair appearing twice and a row pairing with itself.

Big question · Step 7 Hide sensitive data with a view

06_officer_view.sql

Q9 and item v: officers see names, centres and scores, a masked phone, and nothing else.

Hidden: email, National ID, date of birth and most of the phone. The view alone is not security: a user who can read applicants can still see everything. The protection comes from granting the officer SELECT on the view and nothing on the tables.

Big question · Step 8 Back up, restore to another database, verify

terminal

Q10: dump assess_db in custom format and restore it into a new database assess_restore.

Roles such as recruit_officer belong to the whole server, not to one database, so the restored view keeps its grant on the same server. On a new server, create the role first or the grant is skipped with a warning.

08_verify_restore.sql

Now prove the copy is good: the same row counts, the same constraints and indexes, and the rules still refuse bad data.

Expected: 12, 10 and 12 rows, the same constraint and index list as assess_db, and all four inserts fail: duplicate email (uq_ta_email), a seat already taken that session (uq_station_slot), a score of 120 (chk_ass_score) and an applicant that does not exist (fk_ass_applicant). The last line still shows 12 assessments. If any insert succeeds, the restore lost a rule.

Big question Task 3, Retail

Big question · Step 2 Create the database and the five tables

01_retail_schema.sql

Items 1 and 2. Parents first: categories and customers must exist before the tables that point to them.

fk_product_category already refuses to delete a category that still has products: ON DELETE RESTRICT. The two foreign keys of order_items are added in Step 4, because they are item 4 of the question.

Big question · Step 3 Insert the data

02_retail_seed.sql

Item 3: 4 categories, 5 customers, 8 products, 6 orders and 10 order items. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: order 6 is Cancelled and has one item (used to test CASCADE). Product 1, the Smartphone, is in two orders (used to test RESTRICT). Rehema Mollel has no order and the Pen Pack was never sold.

Big question · Step 4 Delete rules: CASCADE and RESTRICT

03_delete_rules.sql

Item 4. Delete an order and its items go with it. Try to delete a product that was sold and the database refuses.

Expected: the first count is 1, the second is 0. The product delete fails with "violates foreign key constraint fk_item_product", and the Smartphone is still there.

Big question · Step 5 Archive the products

04_archive.sql

Item 5: a copy of products, with every row, in a new table archives.

Expected: 8 rows. In PostgreSQL a database is not a prefix you can write in a query, so the full name is public.archives (schema.table). The copy gets the columns and rows only: no primary key, no foreign key, no CHECK and no index. Step 9 uses the same idea for the backup, which is why Step 10 has to add the keys back.

Big question · Step 6 Grant and revoke privileges

05_privileges.sql

Item 6. You are not asked to create the accounts, only to show the statements an admin would run. The user is retail_user.

  • GRANT … ON … TO – gives a privilege on a table (or all tables) to a user or role.
  • REVOKE … ON … FROM – takes a privilege back. Only that privilege goes; the others stay.
  • CREATE ROLE – makes a named bundle of privileges. Grant to the role once, then give the role to many users.
  • GRANT role TO user – gives a user everything the role holds.
Write these; do not run them unless you are an admin on a test server where retail_admin and retail_user already exist. ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public covers every table that exists now. Tables created later need the grant again, or ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES. After item iv, the user can still insert and delete orders but not change them.

Big question · Step 7 View, trigger and stored procedure

06_view_trigger_proc.sql

Item 7. A view with each order's total, a trigger that takes sold items out of stock, and a procedure that adds an item at the current price.

Expected: the view lists orders 1 to 5 (order 6 was deleted in Step 4) with totals 620000, 76000, 60000, 120000 and 486000. After the call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock (not 194: the trigger only acts on rows inserted after it was created) and order 4 totals 138000. A PostgreSQL trigger always calls a function, so you write the function first.

Big question · Step 8 Join, explain, index, explain again

07_join_explain.sql

Item 8: one query over orders, order_items and products, its plan before and after the indexes.

  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE – shows how the database will find the rows (the plan) instead of, or as well as, running the query.
  • CREATE INDEX – builds a sorted lookup on a column, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading every row.
  • JOIN … ON – matches rows of two tables on a key; the columns in ON are the first candidates for an index.
Expected: 6 rows, for orders 3, 4 and 5. Seq Scan means a full table scan; Index Scan or Bitmap Index Scan means an index is used. ANALYZE also runs the query and shows the real time. PostgreSQL does not index foreign key columns for you, so you add one for each join column and one for the date filter. ANALYZE refreshes the statistics the planner uses. With only a few rows the optimizer may still choose a full scan, because reading a tiny table is cheaper than using an index; on real volumes the second plan switches to the indexes.

Big question · Step 9 Back up every table, then lose one

08_backup_tables.sql

Item 9 i. Copy each table into a bak_ table, then drop order_items, the table with the two foreign keys.

Expected: bak_order_items holds 10 rows. Dropping a table also drops its indexes and its trigger. CASCADE is needed because the view order_summary depends on the table; it drops the view too, and Step 10 makes it again.

Big question · Step 10 Restore the table with its keys

09_restore_table.sql

Item 9 ii. Copy the rows back from bak_order_items, then add back what a copy never carries: the primary key, the foreign keys with their delete rules, the CHECK, the trigger and the indexes.

The copy lost the primary key, the identity and every NOT NULL. The identity restarts at 100, above the copied ids, so new rows never collide. Expected at the end: 10 rows, a primary key, two foreign keys and the CHECK in the list, and the delete of product 1 fails again, which proves RESTRICT is back.
