Start here Install Oracle and log in

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

terminal

The server must be running before you can log in.

Run the net start commands in Command Prompt opened as Administrator. Service names can differ, so open services.msc to see the exact name on your computer. On Linux, start the database with the service script the installer created (for XE 21c: sudo /etc/init.d/oracle-xe-21c start).

terminal

This is the command-line login. You type your password when asked. It stays hidden while you type.

sqlplus / as sysdba lands in the root container (CDB$ROOT). To work in the pluggable database, run ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = XEPDB1;. Your prompt changes to SQL> when you are in.

first_commands.sql

Once you are in, run these to prove the login works and see where you are.

Step 1 Create the schema and tables

01_create.sql

In Oracle a schema is a user, so "create the database" means creating the user company_db as a DBA. Connect to a pluggable database such as XEPDB1 (Oracle XE) first. In a container database, Oracle may require common user names to start with C##; a pluggable database does not.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. Oracle uses VARCHAR2 and NUMBER. Identity columns need Oracle 12c or newer.

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Oracle does not accept a list of rows in one VALUES, so use one INSERT per row. Oracle does not save changes until you COMMIT.

  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • COMMIT – saves your inserts for good. Without it, other sessions cannot see the new rows.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Step 3 JOIN

03_join.sql

Oracle lets you alias a table, but without AS.

Step 4 Create a view

04_view.sql

Step 5 Users and roles

05_users.sql

Connect as a DBA (for example SYSTEM) for this file. The user needs CREATE SESSION to log in. Because the tables belong to company_db, the grant names the owner.

Step 6 Backup and restore

terminal

Oracle Data Pump (expdp and impdp) exports and imports a schema. DATA_PUMP_DIR is a folder on the database server. The tool asks for the password. For whole-database backups, DBAs use RMAN.

Step 7 Indexing

07_index.sql

Connect as company_db. Oracle stores unquoted names in capitals, so the table appears as EMPLOYEES in the data dictionary.

Step 8 Triggers

08_trigger.sql

In Oracle the new row is :NEW. The / on its own line tells SQL*Plus to run the block.

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

09_recovery.sql

Archive log mode keeps copies of the redo logs. With RMAN backups that lets you recover to a moment before the crash. Connect as a DBA.

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

10_performance.sql

EXPLAIN PLAN saves the plan and DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY prints it. Look for TABLE ACCESS FULL versus INDEX RANGE SCAN.

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Connect as company_db for this step. Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: Oracle lets you drop a table that a view uses, and marks the view INVALID. Check with SELECT object_name, status FROM user_objects WHERE object_type = 'VIEW';.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: analyst reaches the table through senior_reader, then report_reader. Dropping a role in Oracle removes it from everyone automatically, so analyst loses the access at once.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

:OLD is the row before the change and :NEW is the row after. A trigger runs inside your transaction, so the audit row is saved or rolled back together with the update.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

recovery.sql

Point-in-time recovery needs archive log mode, so Oracle keeps every redo log. Run this as SYSDBA. It restarts the database, so do it on a test server.

Then recover with RMAN. In an rman target / session, with the database mounted, run RUN { SET UNTIL TIME "TO_DATE('2026-10-26 09:59:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')"; RESTORE DATABASE; RECOVER DATABASE; } and finish with ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;. Time the RESTORE step: that is your real RTO.

Step 16 Change data and tables

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Step 17 Constraints

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Step 18 Transactions and locking

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. Oracle runs READ COMMITTED by default and offers only that, SERIALIZABLE and READ ONLY. It never allows dirty reads. A transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and DDL such as CREATE TABLE commits by itself. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

18b_locking.sql

Book cinema seats safely: lock one row, read with a shared lock, skip busy rows, set a wait limit, lock a whole table, and use a version number instead of a lock.

In this database. Readers never wait and never block: a plain SELECT takes no lock. Only UPDATE, DELETE and FOR UPDATE lock rows, and Oracle never turns row locks into a table lock. Every lock ends at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. NOWAIT fails with ORA-00054, and WAIT 5 with ORA-30006. Expected: after part 2, A1 is booked by Amina. Part 4 returns A2 and A3, the free seats. In part 7 the first UPDATE says 1 row updated and the second 0 rows updated. At the end: A1 Amina 0, A2 Juma 1, A3 empty 0.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. The v$ views and ALTER SYSTEM need DBA rights, so run this file as a DBA, not as company_db. The killed session shows as KILLED until Oracle finishes rolling it back.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named PL/SQL block saved inside the database. You run it with EXEC instead of retyping the statements. Run this as company_db in SQL*Plus or SQLcl.

  • CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE – saves the procedure, replacing an older version with the same name.
  • p_dept IN NUMBER / p_total OUT NUMBER – parameters: IN brings a value in, OUT sends one back.
  • AS BEGIN … END; – the PL/SQL body. / on its own line runs the block.
  • SELECT … INTO – puts a query result into a variable.
  • VARIABLE / EXEC / PRINT – make a SQL*Plus variable, run the procedure, show the value.
  • user_objects / DROP PROCEDURE – list your procedures and whether they are VALID / delete one.
Your company_db user needs the right to create procedures. As a DBA run GRANT CREATE PROCEDURE TO company_db; once.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Big question Task 1, Recruitment

Big question · Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. Oracle does not index foreign key columns for you, so interview_results.application_id gets its own index. applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Big question · Step 3 seed.sql: realistic test data

seed.sql

Section A.2. Run it once on the fresh schema, so the ids start at 1: the applications refer to applicants and vacancies by those ids.

The password hashes are fake placeholders: a real system stores a bcrypt or Argon2 hash made by the application, never a password. Placements has only 2 rows on purpose: only selected applicants can be placed, and Q11 needs one selected applicant who is not placed yet. The dates are set around October 2026, so question iv depends on today's date when you run it.

Big question · Step 4 The headline numbers

03_kpis.sql

Questions i, ii and vii.

Expected: 13 submitted applications, an average of 1.30 per vacancy (13 over 10 vacancies) and a placement rate of 15.38% (2 of 13). The status filter for ii sits in the ON condition, not in WHERE: a WHERE would throw away the vacancies with zero applications, and the average would wrongly become 13 over 7. * 1.0 turns whole-number division into decimal division on every database.

Big question · Step 5 Vacancy reports

04_vacancy_reports.sql

Questions iii/Q3, iv/Q4, v/Q2 and viii/Q5.

Expected: iii returns vacancies 8, 9 and 10. iv returns 6 and 7 (on 2026-10-26; later dates add more). v returns seven rows, not five: Accountant II and Nurse Officer II tie on 3 and both get rank 1, then two vacancies share rank 3 and three share rank 5. RANK() keeps ties honest; ROW_NUMBER() would cut them at random and DENSE_RANK() would give 1, 1, 2, 2, 3. viii returns the same two leaders, because a maximum can be shared. TRUNC(SYSDATE) gets today's date in Oracle.

Big question · Step 6 The recruitment funnel

05_funnel.sql

Question vi: per public institution, how many applications go in at the top, and how many survive each stage.

Why DISTINCT? An application with two interview rows appears twice after the join, so a plain COUNT would count Amina twice. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts it once. CASE ... END returns NULL when the condition is false, and COUNT ignores NULLs, so each column counts only its own stage. Expected: Ministry of Finance 3, 2, 1, 1; Office of the Attorney General 1, 1, 1, 1; e-Government Authority 2, 2, 1, 0.

08_verify_restore.sql

Now prove the copy is good: the same row counts, the same constraints and indexes, and the rules still refuse bad data.

Expected: 12, 10 and 12 rows, the same constraint and index list as assess_db, and all four inserts fail: duplicate email (uq_ta_email), a seat already taken that session (uq_station_slot), a score of 120 (chk_ass_score) and an applicant that does not exist (fk_ass_applicant). The last line still shows 12 assessments. If any insert succeeds, the restore lost a rule. Run this as a DBA: CURRENT_SCHEMA makes plain table names point at the restored schema.

Big question Task 3, Retail

Big question · Step 2 Create the database and the five tables

01_retail_schema.sql

Items 1 and 2. Parents first: categories and customers must exist before the tables that point to them.

fk_product_category already refuses to delete a category that still has products: no ON DELETE clause (Oracle's default already refuses the delete). The two foreign keys of order_items are added in Step 4, because they are item 4 of the question.

Big question · Step 3 Insert the data

02_retail_seed.sql

Item 3: 4 categories, 5 customers, 8 products, 6 orders and 10 order items. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: order 6 is Cancelled and has one item (used to test CASCADE). Product 1, the Smartphone, is in two orders (used to test RESTRICT). Rehema Mollel has no order and the Pen Pack was never sold.

Big question · Step 4 Delete rules: CASCADE and RESTRICT

03_delete_rules.sql

Item 4. Delete an order and its items go with it. Try to delete a product that was sold and the database refuses.

Expected: the first count is 1, the second is 0. The product delete fails with ORA-02292 (child record found), and the Smartphone is still there. Oracle has no ON DELETE RESTRICT keyword: leaving out ON DELETE gives exactly that behaviour.

Big question · Step 5 Archive the products

04_archive.sql

Item 5: a copy of products, with every row, in a new table archives.

Expected: 8 rows. In Oracle the prefix xxxx_retail. is the schema (the user that owns the tables). The copy gets the columns and rows only: no primary key, no foreign key, no CHECK and no index. Step 9 uses the same idea for the backup, which is why Step 10 has to add the keys back.

Big question · Step 6 Grant and revoke privileges

05_privileges.sql

Item 6. You are not asked to create the accounts, only to show the statements an admin would run. The user is retail_user.

  • GRANT … ON … TO – gives a privilege on a table (or all tables) to a user or role.
  • REVOKE … ON … FROM – takes a privilege back. Only that privilege goes; the others stay.
  • CREATE ROLE – makes a named bundle of privileges. Grant to the role once, then give the role to many users.
  • GRANT role TO user – gives a user everything the role holds.
Write these; do not run them unless you are an admin on a test server where retail_admin and retail_user already exist. Oracle grants object privileges one table at a time (Oracle 23ai adds GRANT SELECT ANY TABLE ON SCHEMA). GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES TO retail_admin would give system-wide power, far more than this schema. After item iv, the user can still insert and delete orders but not change them.

Big question · Step 7 View, trigger and stored procedure

06_view_trigger_proc.sql

Item 7. A view with each order's total, a trigger that takes sold items out of stock, and a procedure that adds an item at the current price.

Expected: the view lists orders 1 to 5 (order 6 was deleted in Step 4) with totals 620000, 76000, 60000, 120000 and 486000. After the call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock (not 194: the trigger only acts on rows inserted after it was created) and order 4 totals 138000. Write / on its own line after each trigger and procedure, so SQL*Plus runs the block. Oracle uses :NEW inside a trigger.

Big question · Step 8 Join, explain, index, explain again

07_join_explain.sql

Item 8: one query over orders, order_items and products, its plan before and after the indexes.

  • EXPLAIN PLAN FOR – shows how the database will find the rows (the plan) instead of, or as well as, running the query.
  • CREATE INDEX – builds a sorted lookup on a column, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading every row.
  • JOIN … ON – matches rows of two tables on a key; the columns in ON are the first candidates for an index.
Expected: 6 rows, for orders 3, 4 and 5. TABLE ACCESS FULL means a full scan; INDEX RANGE SCAN or TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID means an index is used. Oracle does not index foreign key columns for you, so you add one for each join column and one for the date filter. With only a few rows the optimizer may still choose a full scan, because reading a tiny table is cheaper than using an index; on real volumes the second plan switches to the indexes.

Big question · Step 9 Back up every table, then lose one

08_backup_tables.sql

Item 9 i. Copy each table into a bak_ table, then drop order_items, the table with the two foreign keys.

Expected: bak_order_items holds 10 rows. Dropping a table also drops its indexes and its trigger. PURGE skips the recycle bin, so you really have to use the backup (otherwise FLASHBACK TABLE order_items TO BEFORE DROP could bring it back).

Big question · Step 10 Restore the table with its keys

09_restore_table.sql

Item 9 ii. Copy the rows back from bak_order_items, then add back what a copy never carries: the primary key, the foreign keys with their delete rules, the CHECK, the trigger and the indexes.

The copy kept the NOT NULL columns but lost the primary key and the identity. Oracle cannot turn an existing column into an identity, so a sequence starting at 100 becomes its default. Expected at the end: 10 rows, a primary key, two foreign keys and the CHECK in the list, and the delete of product 1 fails again, which proves RESTRICT is back.

Start here Install SQL Server and log in

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

terminal

The server must be running before you can log in.

Run the net start commands in Command Prompt opened as Administrator. Service names can differ, so open services.msc to see the exact name on your computer. On Linux use sudo systemctl start mssql-server.

terminal

This is the command-line login. You type your password when asked. It stays hidden while you type.

In sqlcmd nothing runs until you type GO on its own line. Your prompt changes to 1> when you are in.

first_commands.sql

Once you are in, run these to prove the login works and see where you are.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

01_create.sql

Run this in SSMS or sqlcmd. GO is not SQL: it is a tool command that ends a batch and sends it to the server.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. SQL Server uses IDENTITY(1,1) instead of AUTO_INCREMENT.

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Add rows, then read them back with WHERE and ORDER BY.

  • USE – picks the database the next commands run in.
  • GO – ends a batch, so SQL Server runs everything above it first.
  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Step 3 JOIN

03_join.sql

Step 4 Create a view

04_view.sql

CREATE VIEW must be the first statement in its batch, so it sits between two GO lines.

Step 5 Users and roles

05_users.sql

SQL Server has two levels. A login lets someone connect to the server. A user maps that login to one database, where the permissions are granted.

Step 6 Backup and restore

06_backup.sql

Backups are T-SQL commands. The path is on the SQL Server machine, and the SQL Server service account must be able to write to it. Create the folder first.

Step 7 Indexing

07_index.sql

Step 8 Triggers

08_trigger.sql

SQL Server has no BEFORE trigger. An AFTER INSERT trigger fixes the row just after it is saved. The inserted table holds the new rows. A simpler way is a default: salary DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 0.

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

09_recovery.sql

In the FULL recovery model you can back up the transaction log, for example every 15 minutes, which sets the RPO. The log backup needs an earlier full backup (Step 6).

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

10_performance.sql

SET STATISTICS IO ON shows how many pages a query reads. Fewer reads after the index means it worked. In SSMS you can also turn on "Include Actual Execution Plan".

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name (NULL). A plain JOIN would hide it.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: SQL Server lets you drop a table a view uses, and the view then fails. Create the view WITH SCHEMABINDING and SQL Server will refuse to drop the table under it.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: a role must have no members before you can drop it. The database user must be dropped before its login is no longer needed.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

SQL Server has no OLD and NEW. It gives two virtual tables: deleted (the rows before) and inserted (the rows after). The trigger runs once per statement, not once per row, so it may see many rows.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

11_rpo.sql

Combine a full, a differential and a log backup. Then restore to a point in time with STOPAT. The paths are on the SQL Server machine.

Run the restore from master: USE master; first, because you cannot restore a database you are using. Time the restore: that is your real RTO.

Step 16 Change data and tables

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Step 17 Constraints

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Step 18 Transactions and locking

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. SQL Server runs READ COMMITTED by default and also offers SNAPSHOT. Each statement commits alone unless you BEGIN TRANSACTION. Add SET XACT_ABORT ON; in real code so a runtime error rolls the whole transaction back. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

18b_locking.sql

Book cinema seats safely: lock one row, read with a shared lock, skip busy rows, set a wait limit, lock a whole table, and use a version number instead of a lock.

In this database. SQL Server asks for locks with table hints in WITH (...). Under the default READ COMMITTED, even a plain SELECT takes short shared locks, unless READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on. When one statement holds about 5,000 locks on a table, SQL Server swaps them for one table lock (lock escalation). UPDLOCK stops the deadlock where two sessions both read and then update. A lock timeout fails with error 1222. Expected: after part 2, A1 is booked by Amina. Part 4 returns A2, the first free seat. In part 7 the first @@ROWCOUNT is 1 and the second is 0, because row_version is already 1. At the end: A1 Amina 0, A2 Juma 1, A3 empty 0.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. Reading the sys.dm_ views needs the VIEW SERVER STATE permission. The older shortcut EXEC sp_who2; shows a BlkBy column that names the blocker. Killing a session rolls back its open transaction.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of T-SQL saved inside the database. You run it with EXEC instead of retyping the statements.

  • CREATE PROCEDURE name @param TYPE – saves the procedure. Parameters start with @.
  • AS BEGIN … END – the statements the procedure runs.
  • @total INT OUTPUT – an output parameter that sends a value back.
  • GO – ends the batch. CREATE PROCEDURE must be the first statement in its batch.
  • EXEC / DECLARE – run a procedure / make a variable to catch the OUTPUT value.
  • sys.procedures / DROP PROCEDURE – list the procedures / delete one.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Big question KijijiShop

Big question · Step 2 Build the tables

01_shop_create.sql

Turn the nouns and rules of line 1 into four tables.

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Big question · Step 3 Add data and change it

02_shop_data.sql

Lines 2 and 3 of the ticket: sample data, a price rise, a delete and a new column.

Run this on a fresh database so the ids start at 1, because the item rows use ids 1 to 3. The item keeps the old price (unit_price) even though the product price rose.

Big question · Step 4 Reports

03_shop_reports.sql

Line 4 of the ticket: four reports with joins, grouping and a subquery.

Expected results: order 1 for Amina totals 4200. Juma and Neema never ordered (Juma's only order was cancelled and deleted). Only Drinks passes the 2000 line (3000). Juice and Rice 5kg were never bought. A HAVING filters groups after the sum, a WHERE filters rows before it.

Big question · Step 5 A view and two users

04_shop_security.sql

Line 5 of the ticket: hide the emails behind a view, and give each user only what the job needs.

A view must be the first statement in its batch, so it sits between two GO lines. The sales team gets the view, not the tables, so emails stay hidden. The clerk has no DELETE. Grant the least that works.

Big question · Step 6 Index and audit trigger

05_shop_speed_audit.sql

Lines 6 and 7 of the ticket: speed up the date search, and record every price change.

On a table this small the database may still scan the whole table. That is normal: the index pays off when the table has thousands of rows. The trigger logs only real price changes, so the stock updates in Step 7 add nothing to the audit.

Big question · Step 7 Place an order safely

06_shop_order.sql

Line 8 of the ticket: an order, its items and the stock change are saved together or not at all.

Expected: two orders remain (1 and the good new one), and Rice 5kg stock is 18. MAX(id) finds the new order on a practice server with one user. In a real application read the new id with SCOPE_IDENTITY(). In real code add SET XACT_ABORT ON; so any error rolls the whole transaction back by itself.

Big question · Step 8 Backup and restore

07_shop_backup.sql

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Big question Task 1, Recruitment

Big question · Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. SQL Server does not index foreign key columns for you, so interview_results.application_id gets its own index. applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Big question · Step 3 seed.sql: realistic test data

seed.sql

Section A.2. Run it once on the fresh schema, so the ids start at 1: the applications refer to applicants and vacancies by those ids.

The password hashes are fake placeholders: a real system stores a bcrypt or Argon2 hash made by the application, never a password. Placements has only 2 rows on purpose: only selected applicants can be placed, and Q11 needs one selected applicant who is not placed yet. The dates are set around October 2026, so question iv depends on today's date when you run it.

Big question · Step 4 The headline numbers

03_kpis.sql

Questions i, ii and vii.

Expected: 13 submitted applications, an average of 1.30 per vacancy (13 over 10 vacancies) and a placement rate of 15.38% (2 of 13). The status filter for ii sits in the ON condition, not in WHERE: a WHERE would throw away the vacancies with zero applications, and the average would wrongly become 13 over 7. * 1.0 turns whole-number division into decimal division, which SQL Server needs.

Big question · Step 5 Vacancy reports

04_vacancy_reports.sql

Questions iii/Q3, iv/Q4, v/Q2 and viii/Q5.

Expected: iii returns vacancies 8, 9 and 10. iv returns 6 and 7 (on 2026-10-26; later dates add more). v returns seven rows, not five: Accountant II and Nurse Officer II tie on 3 and both get rank 1, then two vacancies share rank 3 and three share rank 5. RANK() keeps ties honest; ROW_NUMBER() would cut them at random and DENSE_RANK() would give 1, 1, 2, 2, 3. viii returns the same two leaders, because a maximum can be shared. CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE) gets today's date in SQL Server.

Big question · Step 6 The recruitment funnel

05_funnel.sql

Question vi: per public institution, how many applications go in at the top, and how many survive each stage.

Why DISTINCT? An application with two interview rows appears twice after the join, so a plain COUNT would count Amina twice. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts it once. CASE ... END returns NULL when the condition is false, and COUNT ignores NULLs, so each column counts only its own stage. Expected: Ministry of Finance 3, 2, 1, 1; Office of the Attorney General 1, 1, 1, 1; e-Government Authority 2, 2, 1, 0.

Big question · Step 7 Join questions

06_joins.sql

Q1 and Q6 to Q11. Each one practises a different kind of join.

Expected: Q1 eight applicants. Q7 seven shortlisted rows. Q8 seven rows, for example Amina Juma, Accountant II, 160, Passed. Q9 five applicants with 2 each. Q10 Elia Shirima (only a Draft), Peter Ngowi (Withdrawn), Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo. Q11 Juma Hassan, ICT Officer II. Q10 uses NOT EXISTS instead of a LEFT JOIN because the test also has a status condition: it reads as "there is no submitted application for this person".

Big question · Step 8 The application journey

07_journey.sql

Question x and Q12: follow one applicant from application to placement, across all five tables.

Expected for Amina Juma: two rows for Accountant II (Written 78, Oral 82, both at stage "5 Placed" at the Ministry of Finance) and one row for Nurse Officer II at stage "1 Applied". The interviews and placement are LEFT JOIN, so an application that has not reached those stages still shows. Change the email to follow anyone else.

Big question · Step 9 Index on applications(vacancy_id): before and after

08_index.sql

The "index joins" question and the Q12 practical: same query, two plans. The query joins applications to applicants for one vacancy.

The plan rows show Clustered Index Scan on applications before, and Index Seek on idx_app_vacancy after, usually with a Key Lookup. The Messages tab shows the logical reads. In SSMS you can also press Ctrl+M (Include Actual Execution Plan) to see it as a picture. On 15 rows the optimizer may still scan, because that is cheaper; the index pays off as the table grows.

Big question · Step 10 Audit trigger on applications

09_audit.sql

Question ix and Q13: every change of application_status is recorded with who made it and when, even if someone changes it outside the application.

Expected: exactly one audit row, application 13 from Submitted to Selected. The second update changes only the shortlist, so the trigger writes nothing. Because application 13 is now Selected and has no placement, Q11 from Step 7 would now also list Neema Kileo: run it again and see.

Big question · Step 2 Create the database

01_assess_schema.sql

One table per entity, with the business rules as constraints.

No extra index is needed for the foreign keys: uq_one_attempt starts with applicant_id and uq_station_slot starts with workstation_id, so each foreign key column already leads an index. The one extra index is on assessment_date, because officers search by day.

12 applicants, 10 workstations and 12 assessments. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: DSM-01 is used three times (the most). ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01 are never used. Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo have no assessment. Amina Juma and Baraka Mwakyusa sat at DSM-01 on the same day in different sessions, which the unique rule allows.

Big question · Step 4 Workstation usage

03_usage.sql

Q1, Q2 and Q3.

Expected: Q1 DSM-01 with 3. Q2 ARU-01, ARU-02 and MBY-01. Q3 all 10 workstations, the unused ones with 0. COUNT(s.assessment_id) counts only real matches, so an unused station gives 0; COUNT(*) would give 1, because the LEFT JOIN still returns one row with NULLs.

Big question · Step 5 Scores

04_scores.sql

Q4, Q5 and Q8.

Expected: Q4 DSM-03 first with 88.00. Q5 Rehema Mollel, 91. Q8 the overall average is 72.92, so Amina Juma (85), Neema Kileo (74), Rehema Mollel (91), Halima Said (77) and Peter Ngowi (85) are above it. score * 1.0 matters most in SQL Server: the average of whole numbers is otherwise cut to a whole number.

Big question · Step 6 Join questions

05_joins.sql

Q6, Q7 and two extra join questions of the kind interviewers add.

Expected: Q6 Grace Lyimo and Omari Kombo. Q7 twelve rows. Centres: Dar es Salaam 3 stations and 6 tests, Arusha 2 and 0, Mbeya 1 and 0. The self-join returns DSM-01 on 2026-10-05: Amina Juma then Baraka Mwakyusa. s2.assessment_id > s1.assessment_id stops each pair appearing twice and a row pairing with itself.

Q9 and item v: officers see names, centres and scores, a masked phone, and nothing else.

Hidden: email, National ID, date of birth and most of the phone. The view alone is not security: a user who can read applicants can still see everything. The protection comes from granting the officer SELECT on the view and nothing on the tables.

RESTORE FILELISTONLY shows the logical file names (by default assess_db and assess_db_log). WITH MOVE gives the restored copy new file names, or it would clash with the original. Put the files in your SQL Server data folder on a real server; C:\Backup is fine for practice.

The last line still shows 12 assessments. If any insert succeeds, the restore lost a rule.

Items 1 and 2. Parents first: categories and customers must exist before the tables that point to them.

fk_product_category already refuses to delete a category that still has products: ON DELETE NO ACTION (SQL Server's name for restrict). The two foreign keys of order_items are added in Step 4, because they are item 4 of the question.

Big question · Step 3 Insert the data

02_retail_seed.sql

Item 3: 4 categories, 5 customers, 8 products, 6 orders and 10 order items. Run it once on the fresh tables, so the ids start at 1.

Planted cases: order 6 is Cancelled and has one item (used to test CASCADE). Product 1, the Smartphone, is in two orders (used to test RESTRICT). Rehema Mollel has no order and the Pen Pack was never sold.

Big question · Step 4 Delete rules: CASCADE and RESTRICT

03_delete_rules.sql

Item 4. Delete an order and its items go with it. Try to delete a product that was sold and the database refuses.

Expected: the first count is 1, the second is 0. The product delete fails with error 547 (conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint), and the Smartphone is still there. SQL Server has no RESTRICT keyword: NO ACTION, the default, gives the same result.

Big question · Step 5 Archive the products

04_archive.sql

Item 5: a copy of products, with every row, in a new table archives.

Expected: 8 rows. SQL Server has no CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT: SELECT * INTO does the same job, and its full name is database.schema.table. The copy gets the columns and rows only: no primary key, no foreign key, no CHECK and no index. Step 9 uses the same idea for the backup, which is why Step 10 has to add the keys back.

Big question · Step 6 Grant and revoke privileges

05_privileges.sql

Item 6. You are not asked to create the accounts, only to show the statements an admin would run. The user is retail_user.

  • GRANT … ON … TO – gives a privilege on a table (or all tables) to a user or role.
  • REVOKE … ON … FROM – takes a privilege back. Only that privilege goes; the others stay.
  • CREATE ROLE – makes a named bundle of privileges. Grant to the role once, then give the role to many users.
  • ALTER ROLE … ADD MEMBER – gives a user everything the role holds.
Write these; do not run them unless you are an admin on a test server where retail_admin and retail_user already exist. CONTROL ON DATABASE is SQL Server's "all privileges" (the old GRANT ALL keyword is deprecated). SCHEMA::dbo covers every table in the dbo schema, including tables added later. After item iv, the user can still insert and delete orders but not change them.

Big question · Step 7 View, trigger and stored procedure

06_view_trigger_proc.sql

Item 7. A view with each order's total, a trigger that takes sold items out of stock, and a procedure that adds an item at the current price.

Expected: the view lists orders 1 to 5 (order 6 was deleted in Step 4) with totals 620000, 76000, 60000, 120000 and 486000. After the call, Rice 5kg has 199 in stock (not 194: the trigger only acts on rows inserted after it was created) and order 4 totals 138000. A SQL Server trigger fires once per statement, not per row, so it joins to the inserted table, which holds every inserted row. Each CREATE VIEW/TRIGGER/PROCEDURE must be the first statement in its batch, hence the GO lines.

Big question · Step 8 Join, explain, index, explain again

07_join_explain.sql

Item 8: one query over orders, order_items and products, its plan before and after the indexes.

  • SET SHOWPLAN_TEXT ON – shows how the database will find the rows (the plan) instead of, or as well as, running the query.
  • CREATE INDEX – builds a sorted lookup on a column, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading every row.
  • JOIN … ON – matches rows of two tables on a key; the columns in ON are the first candidates for an index.
Expected: 6 rows, for orders 3, 4 and 5. Table Scan or Clustered Index Scan means a full scan; Index Seek means an index is used. In SSMS you can press Ctrl+L for the graphical plan instead. SQL Server does not index foreign key columns for you, so you add one for each join column and one for the date filter. With only a few rows the optimizer may still choose a full scan, because reading a tiny table is cheaper than using an index; on real volumes the second plan switches to the indexes.

Big question · Step 9 Back up every table, then lose one

08_backup_tables.sql

Item 9 i. Copy each table into a bak_ table, then drop order_items, the table with the two foreign keys.

Expected: bak_order_items holds 10 rows. Dropping a table also drops its indexes and its trigger. The view order_summary stays but fails until the table is back.

Big question · Step 10 Restore the table with its keys

09_restore_table.sql

Item 9 ii. Copy the rows back from bak_order_items, then add back what a copy never carries: the primary key, the foreign keys with their delete rules, the CHECK, the trigger and the indexes.

SELECT * INTO kept the IDENTITY property and the NOT NULL columns, so only the primary key is missing. Expected at the end: 10 rows, a primary key, two foreign keys and the CHECK in the list, and the delete of product 1 fails again, which proves RESTRICT is back.

Big question Task 4, Ajira exam

Done Check your time

Stop the timer. Every file with Good or Excellent is one you can write from memory; practise the others again in the SQL Server tab.

Spring Boot from scratch: a jobs REST API. You will install Java, create a Spring Boot project, connect it to MySQL, and build an API that lists, adds, changes, searches and deletes job adverts. Every file is written by hand, one layer at a time, so you see what each part of Spring Boot does.

curl, Postman or an Angular page
↓ HTTP + JSON
JobController (web layer: URLs)
↓
JobService (business rules)
↓
JobRepository (Spring Data JPA)
↓ Hibernate + JDBC
MySQL: jobs_db.jobs

Words you will meet

WordWhat it means
SpringA Java framework for building server applications. It creates your objects and connects them for you.
Spring BootSpring with sensible defaults: one dependency per feature (a starter), automatic setup, and a built-in web server (Tomcat), so the app runs with one command.
AnnotationA label that starts with @, such as @RestController. It tells Spring what a class or method is for.
BeanAn object that Spring creates and looks after, such as your controller, service and repository.
Dependency injectionSpring hands each bean the other beans it needs, through its constructor. You never write new JobService() yourself.
EntityA Java class that maps to a database table. One object is one row.
RepositoryAn interface that reads and writes entities. Spring Data writes the SQL for you.
REST APIURLs that clients call with GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, sending and receiving JSON.
MavenThe build tool. pom.xml lists the libraries; mvnw (the Maven wrapper) downloads Maven for you.
Never type a real password into this page. The boxes save your text in your browser. Use the demo values shown here.

Core concepts MVC, IoC, DI, beans, scopes, profiles, DTOs

Each concept starts with a tiny example of a few lines. Then it adds one small step at a time, so every step changes only one thing. At the end, answer Check yourself before you open the answer. If you can't answer it, read the steps again. Each concept ends with Where you see it, the practice step that uses it.

1. MVC: Model, View, Controller

Start with this tiny example. Open http://localhost:8080/hello and you see Hello. This class is a Controller: it answers a URL.

@RestController
public class HelloController {
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() { return "Hello"; }
}

Step 1. Add a Model: a class that holds data. A Java record is the shortest way to write one.

public record Job(Long id, String title) {}

Step 2. Let the controller return the model instead of plain text.

@GetMapping("/job")
public Job job() {
    return new Job(1L, "Database Administrator");
}

Step 3. Spring turns the object into JSON before sending it. That JSON is the View: what the client sees.

{"id":1,"title":"Database Administrator"}

Step 4. Now you have all three parts. Here they are in the real project:

PartIts jobIn this project
ModelThe data and the rules about it.Job (the entity), and the service that works on it.
ViewWhat the client receives and sees.The JSON answer. In a website it would be an HTML page (for example a Thymeleaf template).
ControllerTakes the request, calls the model, chooses the answer.JobController and HelloController.

Step 5. What happens inside Spring when a request arrives. Every request goes through one front door, the DispatcherServlet, which finds the right controller method:

curl / browser
   │  GET /api/jobs/1
   ▼
Tomcat (the embedded web server)
   ▼
DispatcherServlet ──► HandlerMapping: "GET /api/jobs/{id}" belongs to JobController.get()
   ▼
JobController.get(1) ──► JobService.findById(1) ──► JobRepository ──► MySQL
   ▼
returns a Job object
   ▼
HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) turns the Job into JSON
   ▼
200 OK  {"id":1,"title":"Database Administrator",...}

Step 6. One last detail. With @Controller the method returns the name of an HTML page. With @RestController it returns the data itself as JSON. A REST API is MVC where the View is JSON.

Check yourself: in the Step 2 example, which part is the Model, which is the View, and which is the Controller?

Model: the Job record. Controller: the job() method in the @RestController class. View: the JSON text Spring sends back.

Where you see it: Step 4 (first controller) and Step 8 (the full controller).

2. Layered architecture

Start with this tiny example. This works, but the controller does everything: it reads the URL and talks to the database.

@GetMapping("/jobs/{id}")
public Job get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return repo.findById(id).orElse(null);
}

Step 1. Problem: if the job does not exist, the client gets an empty answer, and the rule "a missing job is an error" lives inside the web code. Move the rule into a Service:

@Service
public class JobService {
    private final JobRepository repo;
    public JobService(JobRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    public Job findById(Long id) {
        return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new JobNotFoundException(id));
    }
}

Step 2. The controller now only passes the request on. It has no rules and no database code:

@GetMapping("/jobs/{id}")
public Job get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return service.findById(id);
}

Step 3. The Repository is the only layer that touches the database. With Spring Data it is one line:

public interface JobRepository extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> {}

Step 4. Now each layer has one job and talks only to the layer below it:

LayerAnnotationDoesNever does
Controller@RestControllerReads the URL and JSON, picks the status code.SQL or business rules.
Service@ServiceBusiness rules and transactions.Read HTTP headers or write SQL.
Repository@Repository or JpaRepositoryReads and writes the database.Decide business rules.
Entity@EntityHolds one row of data.Call other layers.

Why bother: you can change one layer without breaking the others (for example swap MySQL for PostgreSQL), and test each one alone.

Check yourself: you need the rule "a CLOSED job cannot be edited". Which layer does it go in?

The Service. It is a business rule, so it does not belong in the controller (web) or the repository (database).

Where you see it: Steps 5 to 8, one layer per step.

3. IoC: Inversion of Control

Start with this tiny example. In plain Java you create every object you need. You are in control.

JobService service = new JobService();

Step 1. But JobService needs a repository, the repository needs a database connection, and the controller needs the service. You must build the whole chain yourself, in the right order:

DataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(config);
JobRepository repo = new JobRepositoryImpl(ds);
JobService service = new JobService(repo);
JobController controller = new JobController(service);

Step 2. With Spring you only put a label on each class. You write no new at all:

@Service
public class JobService { ... }

Step 3. When the app starts, Spring finds every labelled class, creates them in the right order and keeps them ready. The control is turned around (inverted): Spring creates your objects, and Spring calls your code. That is Inversion of Control, and the part of Spring that does it is the IoC container.

Check yourself: in this project, who calls JobController.get()?

Spring does (the DispatcherServlet), when a request for GET /api/jobs/{id} arrives. Your code never calls it. That is the "inversion".

Where you see it: you never write new JobService() anywhere in this tab.

4. DI: Dependency Injection

Start with this tiny example. JobService does not create its repository. It asks for one in its constructor. That is all dependency injection means.

public class JobService {
    private final JobRepository repo;
    public JobService(JobRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
}

Step 1. Who hands it over? Spring. Add @Service. Spring sees the constructor needs a JobRepository, finds the bean it already made, and passes it in (injects it).

@Service
public class JobService {
    private final JobRepository repo;
    public JobService(JobRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
}

Step 2. Why it helps: in a test, you pass a fake repository yourself. No database is needed.

JobService service = new JobService(new FakeJobRepository());

Step 3. There are three ways to inject. Use the constructor (the one above). The other two:

// Setter injection: only for optional dependencies
@Autowired
public void setRepo(JobRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

// Field injection: avoid
@Autowired
private JobRepository repo;

Constructor injection is best: the field can be final, the object can never exist without its dependency, and a test can pass a fake one. When a class has only one constructor, Spring uses it without @Autowired.

Step 4. If two beans fit, Spring cannot choose and stops with "expected single matching bean":

public interface Notifier { void send(String msg); }

@Component class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { ... }
@Component class SmsNotifier   implements Notifier { ... }

Step 5. Tell Spring which one: @Primary on a class makes it the default, or @Qualifier picks one by its bean name (the class name with a small first letter).

public AlertService(@Qualifier("smsNotifier") Notifier notifier) { ... }
Check yourself: why is private final JobRepository repo better than an @Autowired field?

A final field set in the constructor can never be null or changed later, and a test can create the class with new and pass a fake. With field injection the object can exist without its repository, and a test cannot set it without Spring.

Where you see it: Step 7 (JobService gets the repository) and Step 8 (JobController gets the service).

5. The ApplicationContext and beans

Start with this tiny example. This line in the main class starts Spring. It creates the ApplicationContext: a box that holds every bean.

SpringApplication.run(JobsApplication.class, args);

Step 1. Put a label on a class and Spring puts one object of it (a bean) in the box:

@Service
public class JobService { ... }

Step 2. You can look inside the box yourself. run returns it:

var ctx = SpringApplication.run(JobsApplication.class, args);
JobService service = ctx.getBean(JobService.class);
System.out.println(ctx.getBeanDefinitionCount() + " beans");

Step 3. A class from a library (such as Java's Clock) cannot get your label. Make it a bean with a @Bean method in a @Configuration class:

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    public Clock clock() { return Clock.systemDefaultZone(); }
}

Step 4. Now any bean can ask for it in its constructor, like any other bean:

public JobService(JobRepository repo, Clock clock) { ... }

Step 5. Spring finds labelled classes by component scanning: it looks in the main class's package and below. Here are both ways to make a bean side by side:

WayWhenExample
A label on your classYour own classes@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController
@Bean method in a @Configuration classClasses from a library, which you cannot changeClock in Step 3
Check yourself: you put a @Service class in the package com.other. What happens?

Spring never finds it, because it only scans com.example.jobs and below. Any class that asks for it fails at start with "No qualifying bean". Move the class under com.example.jobs.

Where you see it: Step 2 (@SpringBootApplication starts the scan) and every labelled class after it.

6. Bean scopes and lifecycle

Start with this tiny example. Call next() from two browsers. Both get 1, 2, 3… from the same counter, because Spring made only one object.

@Service
public class CounterService {
    private int count = 0;
    public int next() { return ++count; }
}

Step 1. One shared object is called a singleton. It is the default scope. The scope says how many objects Spring makes:

ScopeHow manyUse
singleton (default)One, shared by every requestControllers, services, repositories: almost everything
prototypeA new one each time it is injectedObjects that keep their own state
requestOne per HTTP requestData for one request only
sessionOne per logged-in user sessionA shopping cart

Step 2. The danger: a field in a singleton is shared by all users at the same time. Never keep one user's data in a field:

@Service
public class JobService {
    private String currentUser;   // wrong: every request sees and overwrites it
}

Step 3. Pass per-user data as a parameter instead. Parameters and local variables belong to one call only:

public Job create(Job job, String user) { ... }

Step 4. To get a new object each time, change the scope:

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class ReportBuilder { ... }

Step 5. The lifecycle: Spring creates the bean → injects its dependencies → calls @PostConstruct → the bean works → at shutdown calls @PreDestroy.

@PostConstruct
void ready() { System.out.println("CounterService is ready"); }

@PreDestroy
void closing() { System.out.println("CounterService is closing"); }
Check yourself: two users call CounterService.next() at exactly the same moment. Is the count always right?

No. ++count is not one single action, so two threads can read the same value and both write the same number. Use AtomicInteger and incrementAndGet(), or better, keep no changing state in a singleton.

Where you see it: JobService and JobController are singletons: their only fields are final dependencies, never request data.

7. Starters and auto-configuration

Start with this tiny example. This one dependency in pom.xml is enough to run a web server. It is a starter.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

Step 1. A starter brings a whole feature, with versions that work together. spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Tomcat (the web server) and Jackson (for JSON). You write no version numbers.

Step 2. Auto-configuration: when the app starts, Spring Boot looks at what is on the classpath. It finds Tomcat, so it starts a web server on port 8080. You wrote no code for that.

Step 3. Add the JPA starter and the MySQL driver, plus one setting. Spring Boot sees them and creates a database connection pool (HikariCP) for you:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/jobs_db

Step 4. Your own bean always wins. Auto-configuration only creates a bean if you have not made one yourself:

@Bean
public DataSource dataSource() { ... }   // Spring Boot now skips its own

Step 5. To see what was created and why, start the app with --debug and read the CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT:

java -jar target/jobs-api-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --debug
Check yourself: you remove spring-boot-starter-web from pom.xml. What happens when the app starts?

No Tomcat is on the classpath, so no web server starts. The app starts and then stops straight away, and your controllers do not compile, because @RestController comes from that starter.

Where you see it: Step 1 (the four starters) and Step 3 (the database just works once the URL is set).

8. Configuration and profiles

Start with this tiny example. A setting lives in application.properties, outside the code. Change it and restart: there is nothing to recompile.

server.port=8080

Step 1. Add your own setting:

jobs.page-size=20

Step 2. Read it in a bean with @Value:

@Value("${jobs.page-size}")
private int pageSize;

Step 3. Give a default after a colon, in case the setting is missing:

@Value("${jobs.page-size:10}")
private int pageSize;

Step 4. A profile is a set of settings for one environment. Put each set in its own file:

# application-dev.properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# application-prod.properties
server.port=80

Step 5. Choose the profile when you start the app. The profile file is read on top of application.properties, so its values win:

java -jar target/jobs-api-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

Step 6. An environment variable beats both files: SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD replaces spring.datasource.password. That is how real passwords stay out of the code and out of Git.

Check yourself: application.properties says server.port=8080, application-dev.properties says server.port=8081, and you start with the dev profile. Which port?

8081. The profile file is read on top of the main file, so its value wins. A --server.port=9090 on the command line would beat both.

Where you see it: Step 3 (application.properties) and Step 11 (--server.port=9090).

9. DTOs: Data Transfer Objects

Start with this tiny example. A DTO is a small class only for what the API sends or receives. It is separate from the entity.

public record JobResponse(Long id, String title) {}

Step 1. Why? Imagine the entity has a field that must stay private. If the controller returns the entity, that field goes out in the JSON too:

@Entity
public class Job {
    @Id Long id;
    String title;
    String internalNotes;   // goes out in the JSON as well!
}

Step 2. Copy only the safe fields into the DTO:

public record JobResponse(Long id, String title) {

    public static JobResponse from(Job job) {
        return new JobResponse(job.getId(), job.getTitle());
    }
}

Step 3. The controller returns the DTO, not the entity:

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public JobResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return JobResponse.from(service.findById(id));
}

Step 4. Do the same for data coming in. A request DTO holds only the fields a client may send, so a client cannot set id or status:

public record CreateJobRequest(@NotBlank String title, String employer) {}

Step 5. Every problem a DTO solves:

Problem with sending the entityWhat a DTO fixes
Every column goes out, even private ones (a password hash).You choose exactly which fields leave.
Renaming a column changes the API and breaks clients.The API stays the same while the table changes.
Linked entities can loop forever in JSON (Employer → Jobs → Employer …).The DTO holds plain values, not linked entities.
A client could set fields it should not, such as id or status.The request DTO has only the fields a client may send.

This tab sends the Job entity straight out to keep the code short. Real projects usually use DTOs.

Check yourself: a client sends {"id":5,"title":"DBA"} to an endpoint that takes CreateJobRequest. What happens to the id?

It is ignored. CreateJobRequest has no id field, so Jackson has nowhere to put it, and the database chooses the id.

Where you see it: Step 7 has the same idea in a small form: create clears the id, so a client cannot choose it.

10. Annotation cheat sheet

AnnotationMeaning
@SpringBootApplicationMain class: configuration + auto-configuration + component scan
@Component / @Service / @RepositoryMake the class a bean (general / business layer / data layer)
@Controller / @RestControllerWeb controller returning views / returning data (JSON)
@Configuration + @BeanA class whose methods create beans
@Autowired, @Qualifier, @PrimaryInject a bean; choose which one when several fit
@Value("${key}")Read a setting
@Scope, @PostConstruct, @PreDestroyHow many objects; run code after creation / before shutdown
@RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMappingLink a URL and HTTP method to a method
@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBodyRead from the path, the query string, the JSON body
@Valid, @NotBlank, @MinCheck input
@Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValueMap a class to a table
@TransactionalAll-or-nothing method
@RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandlerTurn exceptions into HTTP answers

Why use it: Without a JDK nothing below can build or run. MySQL comes from the DBA tab: install it there first if you have not.

JDK 21 (Eclipse Temurin)adoptium.net. On Windows tick Set JAVA_HOME and Add to PATH in the installer.Compiles and runs Java.

Step 1 Create the project

What it is: Spring Initializr (start.spring.io) generates an empty, ready-to-run Spring Boot project with the libraries you pick.
Why use it: It writes the build file, the folder layout and the main class for you, so you start from a project that already compiles.

You can click through start.spring.io in the browser (Project: Maven, Language: Java, Java: 21, dependencies: Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, MySQL Driver, Validation), or ask for the same zip from the terminal:

terminal

Download the project, unzip it and go into it.

What you got:

jobs-api/
├── pom.xml                          the build file: Java version and libraries

Step 2 Read the build file and the main class

What it is: pom.xml tells Maven which Spring Boot version and which starters to use. JobsApplication.java is the class that starts the app.
Why use it: Knowing these two files lets you add a library or fix a "class not found" error, and explains how one main method starts a whole web server.

pom.xml

The parts of the generated pom.xml that matter. Your version numbers may be newer; keep what Initializr gave you.

spring-boot-starter-parent fixes the versions of every Spring library, so the dependencies need no <version>. Each starter brings a whole feature. runtime means the MySQL driver is needed only when the app runs, not to compile it. You only read this file: there is nothing to type.

JobsApplication.java

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/JobsApplication.java. Initializr wrote it; type it yourself to learn it.

@SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one: it marks a configuration class, switches on auto-configuration (Spring sets up Tomcat, JSON and the database from what is on the classpath), and scans this package and the packages below it for your beans. That is why every class you write must sit in com.example.jobs or below it.

The main class

What it is: A MySQL database and user for the app, and application.properties, the settings file Spring Boot reads at start-up.

create_db.sql

What it is: A controller is a class whose methods answer URLs. @RestController means each method returns data (text or JSON), not a web page.
Why use it: It is the smallest proof that the whole chain works: Java compiles, Tomcat starts, the database connects, and a URL answers.

HelloController.java

Step 5 The entity: a table as a Java class

What it is: An entity is a class marked @Entity. Hibernate (the JPA library inside Spring Data JPA) maps it to a table: each field is a column, each object is a row.
Why use it: You work with Java objects and Hibernate writes the INSERT, SELECT and UPDATE for you. The validation annotations reject bad input before it reaches the database.

Job.java

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/Job.java. After the next run, SHOW TABLES; in jobs_db lists jobs.

jakarta.persistence holds the database annotations and jakarta.validation the input checks. GenerationType.IDENTITY uses MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT for the id. Long and Integer (not long, int) can be null, which a new, unsaved job needs. Hibernate needs the getters and setters, and a no-argument constructor, which Java gives you when you write none.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Package and imports

Write the package line. Import Entity, GeneratedValue, GenerationType, Id and Table from jakarta.persistence, and Min and NotBlank from jakarta.validation.constraints.

Class and id

Mark Job with @Entity and @Table(name = "jobs"). Add private Long id; with @Id and @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY).

The other columns

Add title and employer (both @NotBlank String), location (String), salary (@Min(0) Integer) and status (String, starting as "OPEN").

Getters and setters

Write a getter and a setter for each of the six fields, one per line, and close the class.

Step 6 The repository: database access without SQL

What it is: A repository is an interface that extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> (the entity and the type of its id). Spring Data writes the class behind it while the app starts.
Why use it: You get save, findById, findAll, delete and count for free, and Spring writes the SQL for any method you name the right way.

JobRepository.java

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/JobRepository.java.

Derived queries: Spring reads the method name. findByStatus becomes WHERE status = ?. findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase becomes WHERE UPPER(title) LIKE UPPER('%' || ? || '%'). A spelling mistake in a field name stops the app at start-up.

The interface

Declare public interface JobRepository extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> with two methods: List<Job> findByStatus(String status); and List<Job> findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase(String text);.

Step 7 The service: business rules

What it is: A service (@Service) holds the rules of your app: what happens when a job is not found, what an update may change. The controller calls it; it calls the repository.
Why use it: The controller stays thin and the rules sit in one place you can test. @Transactional makes a method all-or-nothing, like START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT in the DBA tab.

JobNotFoundException.java

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/JobNotFoundException.java. The service throws it when an id does not exist.

It extends RuntimeException, so methods do not have to declare it. In Step 9 it becomes a 404 answer.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

The exception

Write the package line and JobNotFoundException extends RuntimeException with a constructor that takes Long id and calls super("Job " + id + " not found");.

JobService.java

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/JobService.java.

Constructor injection: the service asks for a JobRepository in its constructor and Spring passes one in. The field is final, so it can never be missing. findById returns an Optional: orElseThrow gives the job or throws your exception. create sets the id to null so a client can never overwrite an existing row by sending an id.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Read

Write findAll(String status): all jobs when status is null, otherwise repo.findByStatus(status). Write findById(Long id) with orElseThrow(() -> new JobNotFoundException(id)), and search(String text).

Write

Write create (clear the id, then repo.save), @Transactional update(Long id, Job changes) (load the job, copy the five fields, save) and delete(Long id) (load it, then repo.delete). Close the class.

Step 8 The REST controller: CRUD over HTTP

What it is: The controller maps HTTP methods to service calls: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, DELETE removes. Spring turns your Job objects into JSON and back (with the Jackson library).
Why use it: This is the API that a front end, a mobile app or Postman will call.
RequestMethodAnswer
GET /api/jobs (optional ?status=OPEN)list200 and a JSON list
GET /api/jobs/1get200 and one job, or 404
GET /api/jobs/search?q=datasearch200 and the matching jobs
POST /api/jobscreate201 Created, a Location header and the saved job, or 400
PUT /api/jobs/1update200 and the changed job, 400 or 404
DELETE /api/jobs/1delete204 No Content, or 404

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/JobController.java.

@RequestMapping("/api/jobs") on the class is the start of every URL in it. @PathVariable reads {id} from the path, @RequestBody reads the JSON body, and @Valid runs the checks you put on Job. ResponseEntity lets you choose the status code. /search and /{id} do not clash: Spring prefers the fixed path.

GET endpoints

Step 9 Errors: clear 404 and 400 answers

What it is: A global exception handler (@RestControllerAdvice) catches exceptions from every controller and turns them into a clean JSON answer with the right status code.
Why use it: Without it a missing job gives a 500 error with a long stack trace. With it the client gets 404 {"error": "Job 9 not found"}, and a bad body gets 400 with one message per wrong field.

File: src/main/java/com/example/jobs/GlobalExceptionHandler.java.

@ExceptionHandler(X.class) says which exception the method handles, and @ResponseStatus sets the status code. @Valid throws MethodArgumentNotValidException when a check fails; getFieldErrors() lists each wrong field and its message, such as title: must not be blank.
