Interview questions

What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot?

Spring is the framework: dependency injection, web, data access. Spring Boot sits on top of it and removes the setup: starters bring matching libraries, auto-configuration sets up beans from what is on the classpath, and an embedded Tomcat lets the app run as one jar with java -jar.

What is MVC, and how does Spring MVC handle a request?

Model (the data and rules), View (what the client gets: an HTML page or JSON) and Controller (takes the request and chooses the answer). In Spring every request goes to the DispatcherServlet, which asks the HandlerMapping which controller method fits the URL, calls it, and turns the result into a view or, for @RestController, into JSON with Jackson.

What is the difference between IoC and DI?

IoC (Inversion of Control) is the idea: the framework, not your code, creates and connects the objects. DI (Dependency Injection) is the way Spring does it: it passes each bean the beans it needs, through the constructor, a setter or a field.

Why not use field injection with @Autowired?

The field cannot be final, the class hides what it needs, it can exist half-built, and a plain unit test cannot set the field without Spring or reflection. Constructor injection has none of these problems.

What is the ApplicationContext?

Spring's IoC container: it creates every bean at start-up, injects the dependencies, runs @PostConstruct, and hands beans out when they are needed. SpringApplication.run creates it.

@Component or @Bean?

@Component (and @Service, @Repository ...) goes on your own class, which component scanning finds. @Bean goes on a method in a @Configuration class and returns the object; use it for library classes you cannot annotate, or when building the object needs code.

What is the default bean scope, and what does it mean for thread safety?

Singleton: one object shared by every request at the same time. So a singleton must not keep per-request data in its fields; use local variables. Other scopes are prototype, request and session.

What are Spring profiles?

Named sets of settings for each environment, such as application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties. You pick one with spring.profiles.active. Beans can also be limited to a profile with @Profile("dev").

Why use DTOs instead of returning entities?

A DTO sends only the fields you choose, keeps the API the same when the table changes, avoids endless JSON loops between linked entities, and stops clients from setting fields such as id.

What does @SpringBootApplication do?

It combines @Configuration (the class can define beans), @EnableAutoConfiguration (set things up from the classpath) and @ComponentScan (find beans in this package and below).

What is dependency injection, and why constructor injection?

Spring creates the objects and passes each one the objects it needs, instead of the class calling new. With constructor injection the fields can be final, nothing can be missing, and in a test you simply pass a fake object to the constructor.

@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller and @RestController?

All make a class a bean. @Service and @Repository say which layer it belongs to; @Repository also turns database errors into Spring's own exceptions. @Controller returns web pages; @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody, so it returns data such as JSON.

What are JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA?

JPA is the Java standard for mapping objects to tables (the jakarta.persistence annotations). Hibernate is the library that implements it and writes the SQL. Spring Data JPA adds repositories, so you write an interface and Spring writes the class.

What does spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto do?

It says what Hibernate does to the tables at start-up: none, validate (check they match), update (add what is missing), create (drop and recreate) or create-drop (also drop at shutdown). Use update for learning, validate with Flyway or Liquibase in production.

What does @Transactional do?

Spring starts a transaction before the method and commits it after; if a RuntimeException escapes, it rolls back. It is the Java side of START TRANSACTION / COMMIT / ROLLBACK.

Which status codes should a REST API return?

200 OK for a read or update, 201 Created (with a Location header) for a POST, 204 No Content for a DELETE, 400 for bad input, 404 when the id does not exist, and 500 only for real server errors.

PUT or PATCH?

PUT replaces the whole resource, so the client sends every field. PATCH changes only the fields sent. Both should give the same result when repeated.

Login and security from the smallest example. You start with one HTML form and one Spring Boot controller: 10 lines each. Then each step changes one thing: show a page, use an object, check the input, save to MySQL, hash the password with BCrypt, remember the user, let Spring Security do the login, and add roles. In Part B you build the same login in Angular, with a JWT token, an interceptor and route guards. In Part C the logged-in user gets their own data: notes only they can see, edit and delete, and a page to change their password.

Do the Spring Boot tab first, at least to Step 4. This tab expects Java 21 and MySQL to be installed, and uses the same ideas: controller, service, repository, entity.
HTML form (Part A) or Angular page (Part B)
↓ POST /login
Controller (@PostMapping)
↓
UserService (rules, BCrypt)
↓
UserRepository
↓
MySQL: login_db.users
↓
next page (Part A) or JSON with a token (Part B)

Before you build Spring Boot, MVC and the other tools, one at a time

Read this once before Step 1. You type nothing here: every line below comes back in the steps, where you write it yourself. Each part starts with a few lines, then explains them. If a word is new later, come back to this section.

1. One web request

Start with this tiny example. The browser asks, the server answers. This pair is all a web app does:

GET /login HTTP/1.1            ← browser: "give me the page /login"
Host: localhost:8080

HTTP/1.1 200 OK                ← server: "here it is"
Content-Type: text/html
<html> ...the login form... </html>

The first word is the method, then the path. The answer starts with a status code. You will meet these:

Method or codeMeaningWhere you see it
GETRead something: open a page, fetch data. Nothing changes on the server.Open /login, Step 1
POSTSend something: a form or JSON. The values travel in the body, not in the URL.Send the login form, Step 1
200 OKIt worked, here is the answer.Every page
201 CreatedIt worked and something new was saved.Register from Angular, Step 11
204 No ContentIt worked, and there is nothing to send back.Delete a note, Step 20
302 FoundRedirect: "now open this other URL".redirect:/home, Step 7
400 Bad RequestYour input is wrong, for example an empty username.Validation, Step 11
401 UnauthorizedI do not know who you are: not logged in, or the token is bad.Steps 11 and 13
403 ForbiddenI know who you are, but you are not allowed.A USER opens the admin page, Step 9; someone else's note, Step 20
404 Not FoundNo page or method at this URL.A typo in a mapping
409 ConflictIt clashes with what exists.Username taken, Step 11
500 Internal Server ErrorA bug or crash on the server.Read the console
Check yourself: Why must a login form use POST, not GET?

With GET the values go into the URL: /login?username=john&amp;password=password123. The URL is saved in the browser history, in server logs and in bookmarks. POST puts them in the body.

2. Spring and Spring Boot

Start with this tiny example. This is the whole main class Initializr writes for you:

@SpringBootApplication
public class LoginApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(LoginApplication.class, args);
    }
}

That one run call does three things:

  1. Starts the Spring container (the ApplicationContext): an object that creates your classes and connects them.
  2. Scans the package com.example.login and every package under it for classes marked @Controller, @Service and so on.
  3. Auto-configures what it finds on the classpath. It sees the MySQL driver and spring.datasource.url, so it makes a connection pool. It sees Spring Web, so it starts a Tomcat web server inside your app on port 8080.
What it is: Spring is a Java framework that creates your objects and connects them. Spring Boot is Spring with ready defaults, a built-in web server and starters.
Why use it: Without Boot you would write the setup for Tomcat, the database pool and JSON by hand. Boot does it from the jars you added, and you change only what you need in application.properties.
@SpringBootApplication = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. Because of the scan, a class in another package (say com.example.other) is never found. That is a common reason for a 404 or a "bean not found" error.

A starter is one dependency that brings a whole set of jars. This tab uses these:

DependencyWhat it gives youFrom
spring-boot-starter-webSpring MVC, the Tomcat server, and Jackson (turns Java objects into JSON and back)Step 1
spring-boot-starter-thymeleafTurns the HTML files in templates/ into pagesStep 1
spring-boot-starter-validation@NotBlank, @Size and the other input checksStep 4
spring-boot-starter-data-jpaJPA, Hibernate and Spring Data repositoriesStep 5
mysql-connector-jThe driver that talks to MySQLStep 5
spring-security-cryptoOnly the password encoders, such as BCryptStep 6
spring-boot-starter-securityFull Spring Security: login, sessions, CSRF, rolesStep 8
jjwt-api, jjwt-impl, jjwt-jacksonCreate and check JWT tokensStep 12
Check yourself: What does auto-configuration mean?

Spring Boot looks at the jars on the classpath and your properties, and creates the matching beans for you: a DataSource for MySQL, a Tomcat server for Spring Web, a JSON converter for Jackson. You only override what you want to change.

3. Beans and dependency injection

Start with this tiny example. You never write new UserService(). You ask for it in the constructor:

@Service
public class UserService { ... }

@Controller
public class RegisterController {
    private final UserService userService;

    public RegisterController(UserService userService) {   // Spring passes it in
        this.userService = userService;
    }
}

An object that Spring creates and manages is a bean. Spring sees that the constructor needs a UserService, finds that bean and passes it in. This is dependency injection (DI). Letting Spring, not your code, create the objects is called inversion of control (IoC). By default there is one object of each bean (a singleton), shared by every request.

AnnotationPut it onMeaning
@Componenta classA general bean.
@Controllera classA bean that handles web requests and returns a page name.
@RestControllera class@Controller + @ResponseBody: every method returns data (JSON), not a page.
@Servicea classA bean that holds the business rules.
@Repositorya class or interfaceA bean that talks to the database. With Spring Data you write only the interface.
@Configurationa classA class whose @Bean methods create beans.
@Beana method in a @Configuration classThe object this method returns becomes a bean. You use it for the PasswordEncoder in Step 6 and the SecurityFilterChain in Step 8.
@Controller, @Service and @Repository are all @Component with a clearer name. Constructor injection is the preferred style: the field can be final, a test can call new RegisterController(fakeService), and with one constructor you do not need @Autowired.
Check yourself: Why is it wrong to keep the logged-in username in a field of a controller?

The controller is one shared bean. Every user's request uses the same object, so one user would overwrite the other's name. Per-user data goes in the session (Step 7) or Spring Security (Step 8).

Think of it this wayYou need an engine for your car. Without dependency injection, your class builds its own: new Engine(). With it, your class just says "I need an engine", and Spring, like a parts supplier, delivers one to the constructor. Your class no longer cares where the engine came from, and you can swap it for a test engine easily.

4. MVC: Model, View, Controller

Start with this tiny example. One request, three parts:

@GetMapping("/hello")                     // Controller: receives the request
public String hello(Model model) {
    model.addAttribute("name", "John");   // Model: the data for the page
    return "hello";                       // View: templates/hello.html
}

<!-- templates/hello.html -->
<h1 th:text="${name}">placeholder</h1>   →  the browser gets <h1>John</h1>
PartIn this tabIts job
ModelThe Model object and your data classes such as UserThe data the page shows.
ViewThe Thymeleaf HTML files in src/main/resources/templates/How it looks.
ControllerLoginController, RegisterController and the othersReceives the request, calls the service, chooses the view.

What happens inside Spring for that request:

Browser: GET /hello
↓
DispatcherServlet: Spring's front door; every request enters here
↓ finds the method mapped to /hello
Controller method runs, fills the Model, returns "hello"
↓
View resolver: "hello" → templates/hello.html
↓
Thymeleaf fills ${name}
↓
HTML back to the browser
What it is: Spring MVC is the part of Spring that maps URLs to Java methods and turns what they return into HTML or JSON.
Why use it: Each part changes on its own: you can redesign the HTML without touching Java, and change the rules without touching the HTML. In Part B the View moves to Angular and the controllers return JSON. That is still Spring MVC, in REST style.
Check yourself: What does return "success"; mean in a @Controller, and in a @RestController?

In a @Controller it is a view name: Thymeleaf renders templates/success.html. In a @RestController the text success itself is the response body.

5. The annotations on a controller method

Start with this tiny example. Every word on these two lines has a job:

@PostMapping("/login")
public String login(@RequestParam String username, @RequestParam String password)

@PostMapping("/login")  → run this method for POST /login
@RequestParam           → take the form field with the same name
AnnotationWhat it doesExampleStep
@GetMapping("/x")Runs the method for GET /xOpen the login page1
@PostMapping("/x")Runs the method for POST /xReceive the form1
@RequestMapping("/api")On the class: a prefix for every method in it@RequestMapping("/api/auth")11
@RequestParamOne form field, or one ?key=value in the URL@RequestParam String username1
@ModelAttributeMany form fields into one object (you may leave the word out)User user3
@Valid + BindingResultCheck the object; collect the errors instead of failing@Valid User user, BindingResult result4
@RequestBodyThe JSON body into one object@RequestBody LoginRequest req11
@PathVariableA piece of the URL/users/{id} (not needed in this tab)—
@ResponseStatusSets the status code of the answer@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)11
@ExceptionHandlerTurns an exception into an answerUsername taken → 40911

What the method returns decides what the browser gets:

You returnThe browser gets
"success" in a @ControllerThe page templates/success.html
"redirect:/home"A 302: the browser opens /home itself. Used after a form POST, so refresh does not send the form twice.
An object in a @RestControllerThat object as JSON, written by Jackson
A thrown ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)A 401 with no body you wrote
Check yourself: What is the difference between @RequestParam, @ModelAttribute and @RequestBody?

@RequestParam reads one form field. @ModelAttribute fills a whole object from form fields (an HTML form sends username=john&amp;password=...). @RequestBody fills an object from a JSON body, which is what Angular sends.

6. Layers, JPA and the database

Start with this tiny example. Four small classes, each with one job:

@Entity class User { @Id Long id; String username; String password; }   // one row of the users table
interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> { }        // the SQL, written for you
@Service class UserService { ... repository.save(user) ... }           // the rules
@Controller class RegisterController { ... userService.register(user) ... }  // the web
Controller: knows HTTP and pages
↓
Service: knows the rules (is the name taken? hash the password)
↓
Repository: knows the database
↓
MySQL
WordWhat it is
JPAThe Java standard for saving objects into tables.
HibernateThe library that does the JPA work and writes the SQL. Spring Boot uses it by default.
Spring Data JPAWrites the repository class for you. save, findById and findAll come free, and a method name like findByUsername becomes SELECT ... WHERE username = ?.
@Entity, @Table(name = "users")This class is a table, named users.
@Id, @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)The primary key; MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT fills it.
@Column(unique = true, nullable = false)Column rules that MySQL enforces too.

Why layers? Each class can change alone. Part B proves it: Angular replaces the HTML pages, but UserService and UserRepository stay exactly the same.

Check yourself: Why not call the repository straight from the controller?

Then the rules (name taken, hash the password) would live in the controller. Part B adds a second controller for Angular, and you would have to copy the rules into it. In the service they are written once and used by both.

7. Thymeleaf in one look

Start with this tiny example. Thymeleaf adds th: attributes to normal HTML. The server replaces them before sending the page:

<p th:text="${name}">Name</p>                   → <p>John</p>
<form th:action="@{/register}" th:object="${user}" method="post">
    <input th:field="*{username}">              → <input id="username" name="username" value="">
</form>
AttributeWhat it doesStep
th:text="${name}"Puts the value from the Model in the tag (HTML-escaped, so it is safe)2
th:object="${user}"The form works on this object from the Model3
th:field="*{username}"Sets id, name and value from one field of that object3
th:if, th:errorsShow a tag only when true; show the validation message of a field4
th:action="@{/login}"The form URL. With Spring Security it also adds the hidden CSRF token8
th:each="u : ${users}"Repeat a tag for each item of a list9
Think of it this wayA Thymeleaf page is a form letter with blanks. Plain HTML is the typed text, and every th: attribute marks a blank. The server fills the blanks before posting the letter, so the browser only ever sees the finished page.
${...} means: look on the Model tray.
*{...} means: a field of the th:object.
@{...} means: build the right address for the app.

8. application.properties

Start with this tiny example. Settings are key=value lines that Boot reads when it starts:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/login_db   ← a Spring Boot key
jwt.minutes=60                                               ← your own key, Step 12

@Value("${jwt.minutes}") long minutes                        ← read your own key in Java

Keys that start with spring. are read by Spring Boot itself. Your own keys you read with @Value. A real secret never goes in Git: in production it comes from an environment variable.

<artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>

GET /home   →   302 to /login   (you are not logged in)

↓

Check yourself: Why does Spring Security work as a filter, not inside your controllers?

A filter runs before any controller. A request without a login is stopped before it reaches your code, so you cannot forget the check in one method.

10. Angular in one look

Start with this tiny example. The smallest Angular component:

@Component({
  selector: 'app-hello',

export class Hello {

Angular runs in the browser, served by ng serve on localhost:4200. Spring runs on localhost:8080. They talk only by HTTP with JSON. That is why Part B needs CORS (two addresses) and a token instead of a server page.

PieceWhat it isStep

Part A: the server. Thymeleaf builds each page and the browser only shows it. Part B: Angular in the browser builds the screen, and the server sends only JSON.

   │  ├─ UserService.java
   │  ├─ PasswordConfig.java            BCrypt bean
   │  ├─ SecurityConfig.java            Part A security
   │  ├─ DbUserDetailsService.java
   │  ├─ AuthController.java            Part B: JSON login and register
   │  ├─ ApiController.java
   │  ├─ ApiSecurityConfig.java         Part B security
   │  ├─ JwtService.java
   │  ├─ JwtFilter.java
   │  ├─ Note.java, NoteRepository.java  Part C: each user's notes
   │  ├─ NoteService.java, NoteController.java
   │  └─ AccountController.java         Part C: change password
   └─ resources/
      ├─ application.properties
      └─ templates/                     login, success, register, home, admin .html

login-ui/                               (Angular, port 4200)
└─ src/app/
   ├─ app.config.ts, app.routes.ts, app.ts
   ├─ auth.service.ts, auth.interceptor.ts, auth.guard.ts, notes.service.ts
   └─ login/login.ts, home/home.ts, admin/admin.ts, notes/notes.ts, password/password.ts

You do not create these now. Each step says which file to add or change.

12. Words you will meet

WordWhat it means
AuthenticationWho are you? Checking a username and password (or a token) to prove who is calling.
AuthorizationWhat may you do? Checking whether the logged-in user is allowed to open this page or call this URL, for example only an ADMIN.
HashA one-way scramble of a text. You can check a password against it, but you can never turn it back into the password.
SaltRandom text mixed into each password before hashing, so two users with the same password get different hashes.
BCryptA slow password hash with a built-in salt. The standard choice for passwords in Spring.
SessionMemory on the server for one logged-in browser. The browser keeps only its id, in a cookie called JSESSIONID.
JWTJSON Web Token: a signed text that says who the user is. The client sends it with every request, so the server needs no session.
CSRFCross-Site Request Forgery: another website tricking your browser into sending a form to your app with your cookie. A hidden token in each form stops it.
CORSThe browser rule that blocks a page on one address (localhost:4200) from reading answers from another (localhost:8080) unless that server allows it.
RoleA group of permissions, such as USER or ADMIN.
FilterCode that runs before every request reaches a controller. Spring Security is a chain of filters.
Guard / InterceptorAngular code that runs before opening a page (guard) or before every HTTP call (interceptor).
Never type a real password into this page. The boxes save your text in your browser. Use the demo values shown here: john / password123.

Start here Create the project and the database

What it is: A new Spring Boot project with five starters: Spring Web, Thymeleaf (HTML pages), Spring Data JPA, the MySQL driver and Validation.
Why use it: Every step below adds to this one project, so you always have a working app. The database is set up now because the JPA starter will not start without it, even though you first use it in Step 5.
Think of it this wayThe project is a new house, and the database is its storage room. Spring Initializr is an order form for the house frame: you tick the parts you want (web, thymeleaf, data-jpa...) and it hands you a zip. The database must exist before the first run, because the app knocks on its door the moment it starts. If nobody answers, it stops with an error.

terminal

Concepts in this file

  • curl https://start.spring.io/starter.zip: Downloads a new Spring Boot project as a zip file from the Spring Initializr website. curl is a command-line tool that sends web requests. Receives: the options after -d. Goes to: the file named by -o.Think of it this way: curl is a web browser without a screen: you type an address and it downloads the answer. Here the answer is a zip file with your new project inside.
  • -d type=maven-project -d javaVersion=21: Each -d sends one option to Initializr. This one picks Maven as the build tool and Java 21. Direction: your terminal → start.spring.io.Think of it this way: Each -d is one tick-box on the order form. Maven is the tool that fetches libraries and builds your project, like a shopping assistant for code. Java 21 is the Java version you want.
  • -d dependencies=web,thymeleaf,data-jpa,mysql,validation: The libraries to include: web (web server and controllers), thymeleaf (HTML templates), data-jpa (talk to a database with Java objects), mysql (MySQL driver), validation (check input rules like minimum length). Goes to: the generated pom.xml.Think of it this way: Dependencies are ready-made parts. It is like buying a door instead of carving one. You list the parts you want, and Maven brings them.
  • -d groupId / artifactId / name / packageName: Names for the project: com.example is the company-style prefix, login-app the project id, login the app name, com.example.login the Java package where your classes live.Think of it this way: These are the names on the project's ID card: the company-style prefix, the project id, and the package, which is the folder where your Java files will live.
  • -d baseDir=login-app -o login-app.zip: baseDir is the folder name inside the zip. -o saves the download to a file called login-app.zip. Goes to: login-app.zip in the current folder.Think of it this way: baseDir is the name of the folder inside the zip. -o means "save as": the download gets this file name.
  • tar -xf login-app.zip: Unpacks (extracts) the zip into a folder. Receives: login-app.zip. Goes to: the folder login-app.Think of it this way: This unzips the file, like opening a delivery box.
  • cd login-app: Moves the terminal into the new project folder so later commands run there.Think of it this way: cd means "walk into this folder". Later commands then run from inside it, like working at the desk in that room.

Download the project from start.spring.io, unzip it and go into it.

In Windows PowerShell type curl.exe instead of curl. thymeleaf is the new starter compared with the Spring Boot tab: it turns HTML files in src/main/resources/templates/ into pages.

create_db.sql

Concepts in this file

  • CREATE DATABASE login_db;: SQL command that makes a new empty database called login_db inside MySQL. The app will keep its tables here. Goes to: MySQL server.Think of it this way: A new, empty cupboard where this app will keep its tables.
  • CREATE USER 'login_user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'login_pass';: Makes a database account. 'localhost' means it can only connect from this same computer. IDENTIFIED BY sets its password. Goes to: MySQL. These same values are later used in application.properties.Think of it this way: A key made only for this app. The app logs in with this username and password, not with your own admin account.
  • GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON login_db.* TO 'login_user'@'localhost';: Gives that account permission to do anything (read, write, create tables) on every table (*) of login_db, and nothing outside it.Think of it this way: This tells MySQL: this key may open only the login_db cupboard, and may do anything inside it.

Log in with mysql -u root -p and run these three statements.

The app gets its own user with rights only on login_db. You do not create the users table: Hibernate creates it from the Java class in Step 5.

Database and user

application.properties

Concepts in this file

  • spring.application.name=login: Just a name for the app. Spring Boot shows it in logs.Think of it this way: A name tag for your app. Spring Boot prints it in the logs.
  • spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/login_db: The address of the database. JDBC is Java's standard way to talk to databases. It says: MySQL, on this computer, port 3306, database login_db. Receives: read by Spring Boot at start-up. Goes to: the connection pool that opens connections to MySQL.Think of it this way: The address of the database, like a home address: which city (MySQL), which street number (port 3306), which house (login_db).
  • spring.datasource.username / password: The account Spring uses to log in to MySQL. They must match the user created in create_db.sql. Direction: application.properties → MySQL login.Think of it this way: The key made in create_db.sql. If these do not match what MySQL knows, the app cannot get in.
  • spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update: Lets Hibernate (the JPA tool) create or change tables automatically to match your Java entity classes. update adds missing tables or columns but does not delete data. Direction: entity classes → tables in MySQL.Think of it this way: Hibernate looks at your Java classes and builds or adjusts the tables to match, like a tailor adjusting a suit. update adds what is missing and never throws your data away.
  • spring.jpa.show-sql=true: Prints every SQL statement Hibernate runs into the console, so you can see what happens.Think of it this way: Hibernate narrates every SQL line it sends, so you can watch what happens behind the scenes.
  • spring.thymeleaf.cache=false: Turns off template caching, so edits to HTML files show after a browser refresh without restarting.Think of it this way: Do not memorise the page. Read the HTML file again every time, so your edits show when you refresh.

File: src/main/resources/application.properties. Replace what Initializr wrote with these lines.

Part A · Spring Boot with HTML forms

The server builds every page. The browser only shows HTML and sends forms back.

Step 1 The smallest form and controller

What it is: An HTML form that sends a username and password, and a controller method that receives them.
Why use it: This is the whole idea in its smallest form: the form's action and method choose the URL, and Spring links that URL to your method.
Think of it this wayA form is a letter, and the controller is the person at the address.
action="/login" is the address on the envelope. method="post" means a sealed letter: the data travels inside, not in the URL.
@PostMapping("/login") is the mailbox with that address. Only letters for /login land in it.
@RequestParam String username opens the letter and takes out the line named username.

Start with this tiny example. Two lines of the form decide where the data goes:

<form action="/login" method="post">

action="/login"  → send the data to the URL /login
method="post"    → use HTTP POST, so the values travel in the body, not in the URL

login.html

Concepts in this file

  • <form action="/login" method="post">: A form groups inputs. action is the address the browser sends the data to; method="post" sends it in the request body, not the URL. Goes to: the controller method marked @PostMapping("/login"). Direction: Form → Controller.Think of it this way: The envelope. action is the address the letter goes to, and method="post" means a sealed letter.
  • <input type="text" name="username">: A text box. The name is the label the value travels under. Goes to: the controller parameter called username (matched by name).Think of it this way: A blank line to fill in. The name is the label on that line. Spring matches that label to a variable or field with the same name.
  • <input type="password" name="password">: A text box that hides what you type. Sent under the name password. Goes to: the controller parameter password.Think of it this way: A blank line to fill in. The name is the label on that line. Spring matches that label to a variable or field with the same name.
  • <button type="submit">: Clicking it sends the form to the action address.Think of it this way: The send button. Clicking it posts the letter.
  • placeholder: Grey hint text shown inside an empty box. It is never sent.Think of it this way: Faint hint text inside an empty box, like the word "Name" printed on a form line. It disappears when you type.

File: src/main/resources/templates/login.html.

The name of each input is the key Spring uses. name="username" arrives in the parameter called username.

LoginController.java

Concepts in this file

  • package com.example.login;: Says which folder/group of classes this file belongs to. It must match the project folders.Think of it this way: The address of this file's folder. It must match where the file really sits.
  • import ...: Lets you use a class from another library by its short name. Here: Controller, GetMapping, PostMapping, RequestParam. Without imports Java would not know these names.Think of it this way: Like saying "I will use tools from that toolbox". Without the import, Java does not know the name.
  • @Controller: Marks the class as a web controller: Spring finds it at start-up and sends matching browser requests to its methods. Methods return the name of an HTML template. Receives: browser requests. Goes to: Thymeleaf templates.Think of it this way: A sticker on the class saying "I am a receptionist for web requests". Spring reads the stickers when it starts and sends each request to the right receptionist.
  • @GetMapping("/login"): This method runs when the browser asks for the page /login (a normal visit or link). Browser → GET /login → loginPage()Think of it this way: The mailbox for "show me a page" requests, such as opening a link or typing an address.
  • public String loginPage() { return "login"; }: Returns the text "login". Spring turns it into the template login.html and sends that HTML back. Goes to: login.html → browser.Think of it this way: This method only returns a name, "login". Spring turns that name into the file login.html and sends it to the browser.
  • @PostMapping("/login"): Runs when a form is sent with POST to /login, i.e. when the user clicks Login. Browser → POST /login → login(...)Think of it this way: The mailbox for "here is my form" requests, which happen when the user clicks the button.
  • @RequestParam String username: Takes the form value named username from the request and puts it in this Java variable. Receives: the input with name="username". Direction: Form → Controller.Think of it this way: Open the letter, take out the line of the form with this name, and put it in this variable.
  • @RequestParam String password: Same for the password input. Receives: the input with name="password".Think of it this way: Open the letter, take out the line of the form with this name, and put it in this variable.
  • System.out.println(...): Prints the values to the console (the terminal running the app), just to prove they arrived. Printing a password is only for this demo.Think of it this way: This writes a line in the black terminal window, like a diary entry. It only proves the data arrived. In a real app, never print passwords.
  • return "success";: Shows success.html after the POST.Think of it this way: Do not build the page here. Just say its name, and Spring finds success.html on the templates shelf.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/LoginController.java.

@Controller (not @RestController): the String a method returns is the name of a page. "login" opens templates/login.html. You need the GET method because files in templates/ are never sent directly: a controller must ask for them. @RequestParam String username reads the form field named username. Printing a password is only for this first test: never do it in a real app.

Step 2 Show the data on the next page

What it is: The Model is a box of values the controller fills for the page. Thymeleaf reads them with ${name}.
Why use it: A page that only says "Login received" is not much use. Now the next page can greet the user by name.
Think of it this wayThe Model is a tray. The controller puts labeled items on it, then hands the tray to the page.
model.addAttribute("username", username) puts an item on the tray with the label username.
${username} on the page means: "find the item labeled username on the tray."
The only rule: the label must be spelled the same on both sides. If it is not, the page shows nothing.

Start with this tiny example. One attribute in the controller, one th:text in the page:

model.addAttribute("username", "john");        // in the controller

<span th:text="${username}">user</span>         <!-- in the page: shows john -->

LoginController.java · version 2

Concepts in this file

  • Changed: Version 2 of LoginController: the POST now passes the username to the page. Package, imports and @Controller are as before; one new import: Model.
  • Model model: A box the controller fills with data for the template. Spring creates it and passes it in as a method parameter. Direction: Controller → Template.Think of it this way: Ask Spring: "give me the tray". Spring hands it in, and you only put things on it.
  • model.addAttribute("username", username): Puts the value in the Model under the key "username". Receives: the form value from @RequestParam. Goes to: ${username} in success.html.Think of it this way: Put an item on the tray, with a label. The page finds it again with ${label}. The label must be spelled exactly the same on both sides.
  • return "success";: Still shows success.html, but now it can read username from the Model.Think of it this way: Do not build the page here. Just say its name, and Spring finds success.html on the templates shelf.
  • Flow: Browser → POST /login → login(username, password, model) → success.html shows the name.

Keep working in the same file. The method gets a Model and stops printing.

Step 3 Better: send the form into an object

What it is: Instead of one @RequestParam per field, the method takes one object. Spring creates it and fills each field from the form input with the same name.
Why use it: A register form can have many fields. One object keeps the method short, and the same class can later be checked, saved to the database and hashed.
Think of it this wayth:object="${user}" means:
"For everything inside this form, use the user object as the reference object."
Thymeleaf sees ${user} and looks in the Model for something named user. It finds:
model.addAttribute("user", new User());
So ${user} points to that Java object.

After that, *{username} is a short way to say "the username field of that object". It is like a page headed John: below it you just write "first name", not "John's first name" every time.

Start with this tiny example. The method takes a User, and Spring fills it:

@PostMapping("/register")
public String register(User user) {          // username=john&password=123
    System.out.println(user.getUsername());  //   → user.setUsername("john")
    return "success";                        //   → user.setPassword("123")
}

User.java

Concepts in this file

  • public class User: A plain Java class that holds one user's data. It is a model: it carries data between the form and the controller.Think of it this way: A blank form card with slots (username, password). One object is one filled-in card.
  • private String username; private String password;: Fields (variables) that store the data. private means only this class can touch them directly.Think of it this way: The slots on the card. private is a locked box: other code uses the getter and setter "windows" to look in or put things in.
  • getUsername() / getPassword(): Getters: methods that return the field value. Goes to: whoever reads it, e.g. the controller or Thymeleaf.Think of it this way: A window to look in. It gives you the value stored in the box.
  • setUsername(String) / setPassword(String): Setters: methods that store a new value. this.username = username copies the parameter into the field. Receives: a value from Spring when it fills the object from a form.Think of it this way: A window to put something in. Spring uses it to fill the card from the form.
  • Why getters and setters: Spring and Thymeleaf use them to fill and read the object by field name.Think of it this way: Spring and Thymeleaf cannot open the locked boxes. They use the windows, found by name.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/User.java.

Spring needs the setters to fill the object: input username calls setUsername. A form field with no matching setter is ignored.

@RequestParamOne form field or ?key=value in the URL@RequestParam String username

Step 4 Check the input: validation

What it is: Annotations such as @NotBlank and @Size on the fields, and @Valid in the controller, which checks them before your code runs.
Why use it: Right now an empty username or a 1-letter password is accepted. Validation rejects it and shows the message next to the field.
Think of it this wayValidation is a bouncer at the door. Before the method runs, @Valid asks the bouncer to check each guest against the rules: @NotBlank means "you must give a name", @Size means "it must be long enough".
BindingResult is the bouncer's notebook: who failed, and why.
Returning "register" again means: send the guest back to the form, with the notebook, so the page can show the messages.

Start with this tiny example. One annotation on a field is a rule:

@NotBlank                 // must not be empty or only spaces
private String username;

Goes to: BindingResult as an error if it fails.Think of it this way: A rule: it may not be empty or only spaces, like a form that refuses a blank name.
  • @Size(min = 3, max = 50): Username must be 3 to 50 characters long.Think of it this way: A rule: the length must be between 3 and 50 characters, like holding a ruler against the text.
  • @Size(min = 8, message = "..."): Password must be at least 8 characters. message is the error text shown to the user. Goes to: the page via th:errors.Think of it this way: The same ruler for passwords. The message is what the user sees when the rule fails.
  • Where it runs: Browser → form → Spring binds a User → @Valid checks these annotations → errors go to BindingResult.Think of it this way: The rule is only stuck on the field. It is checked when the controller asks for it with @Valid.

Step 5 Save users in MySQL

What it is: The User class becomes an entity (a table), a repository saves it, and a service holds the rule "a username can be used only once".
Why use it: Until now nothing was kept: restart the app and every user is gone. Now registering really creates an account.
Think of it this wayAn entity is a table described in Java. The class is the table, each field is a column, and each object is one row.
The repository is a librarian: you say save(user) and it files the row. You never write the SQL.
The service is the manager between the controller and the librarian. It applies the rules first, for example "is this username already taken?".

Start with this tiny example. Once User is an entity, one line saves it:

userRepository.save(user);      // INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES (?, ?)

User.java · version 3

Concepts in this file

  • Changed: User becomes a database entity: each User object is one row in a table. New JPA imports (Column, Entity, GeneratedValue, GenerationType, Id, Table) come from jakarta.persistence. A new id field is added; the setId setter is not needed.
  • @Entity: Tells JPA (Hibernate) that this class maps to a database table. Direction: Java class ↔ MySQL table.Think of it this way: A sticker: "this class is a table". One object is one row.
  • @Table(name = "users"): The table is called users. Created automatically thanks to ddl-auto=update.Think of it this way: The table's name tag. Without it, Spring picks a name by itself.
  • @Id: Marks id as the primary key: the unique number of each row.Think of it this way: The ID column: a unique number for each row, like a student number. The database counts for you (1, 2, 3...), so you never set it.
  • @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY): The database makes the id itself (auto-increment: 1, 2, 3...). You never set it. Receives: the id from MySQL after save. Goes to: getId().Think of it this way: The database counts for you: 1, 2, 3... You never set the id yourself.
  • @Column(unique = true, nullable = false): On username: no two rows may share it, and it cannot be empty (NULL) in the table.Think of it this way: Two rules. No two rows may have the same username (unique), and it may not be empty (nullable = false).
  • @Column(nullable = false): On password: the column must always have a value.Think of it this way: A rule for this column: it may not be empty, and it has a maximum length if one is given.
  • Validation annotations: @NotBlank and @Size stay as before: they check form input, while @Column shapes the table.Think of it this way: The rules from Step 4 are still on the fields. Now the same class is also the table.

Keep working in the same file. It becomes a table.

@Column(unique = true) makes MySQL refuse a second john, even if a bug skips the check in the service. There is a getter for id but no setter, so a form can never set the id.

Step 6 Never store a password: hash it with BCrypt

What it is: BCrypt turns a password into a 60-character hash. You store the hash. To log in, BCrypt hashes the typed password the same way and compares.
Why use it: A hash cannot be turned back into the password, so a stolen table does not reveal passwords. BCrypt is also slow on purpose, which makes guessing millions of passwords too slow.
Think of it this wayHashing is a meat grinder. It is easy to turn steak into mince, and impossible to turn mince back into steak. BCrypt grinds the password, and you store only the mince.
At login you grind what the user typed and compare. BCrypt also adds a pinch of random salt, so two users with the same password get different stored text. That is why you use matches(...) and never equals(...).

Start with this tiny example. Three lines show everything BCrypt does:

PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
String hash = encoder.encode("password123");
System.out.println(encoder.matches("password123", hash));   // true
System.out.println(encoder.matches("password124", hash));   // false

Run encode twice on the same password and you get two different hashes, because each one has its own random salt. matches still works, because the salt is stored inside the hash:

$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy
 │  │  └──── salt: 22 characters ────┘└──── hash: 31 characters ────┘
 │  └─ cost 10: 2^10 = 1,024 rounds. Cost 11 is twice as slow, cost 12 four times.
 └──── BCrypt version

  • <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>: The publisher of the library (Spring Security).Think of it this way: Who made it. The groupId is the maker of the library.
  • <artifactId>spring-security-crypto</artifactId>: The library name: password hashing tools only, without the full security system. Goes to: provides PasswordEncoder and BCryptPasswordEncoder.Think of it this way: Which product from that maker. This one is only the password-hashing part, not the whole security guard.
  • No <version>: Spring Boot already knows a matching version, so none is written.Think of it this way: Spring Boot already knows which version fits, so it picks it for you.

Add one dependency inside <dependencies> in pom.xml.

Only the hashing part of Spring Security, without the login screens. Spring Boot picks the version. In Step 8 you add the full security starter, which includes it.

Check yourself: why not use SHA-256 or MD5 for passwords?

They are built to be fast: a graphics card can try billions of guesses per second. BCrypt is slow on purpose (and the cost can be raised as computers get faster), and it adds a salt to every hash, so one precomputed list of hashes cannot crack every user at once.

Step 7 Remember who is logged in: the session

What it is: An HttpSession is a small store on the server for one browser. Spring gives the browser a cookie, JSESSIONID, and finds the same session on its next request.
Why use it: Right now the app forgets you as soon as the Welcome page is shown. With a session, other pages can know who you are.
Think of it this wayA session is a cloakroom ticket. At login the server keeps your details in the back room and gives the browser a numbered ticket (a cookie). On every later request the browser shows the ticket, and the server finds your things. Logout means tearing the ticket up.

Start with this tiny example. Write a value at login, and read it on any later request:

session.setAttribute("username", "john");          // at login
Object who = session.getAttribute("username");     // on any later page: "john"

  • session.setAttribute("username", username): Stores the name in the session after a good login. Goes to: server memory. Read later by HomeController.Think of it this way: Hang something on the visitor's hook: "username = john".
  • return "redirect:/home";: Tells the browser to make a new GET request to /home instead of showing a page now. This avoids re-sending the form on refresh. It is like telling a visitor, "not this desk, go to desk 4".

"redirect:/home" tells the browser to load /home with a new GET. This is Post/Redirect/Get: pressing refresh on the home page no longer sends the password again.

Step 8 Let Spring Security do the login

What it is: Spring Security is a chain of filters in front of every controller. It checks the session, shows the login page, checks the password with your PasswordEncoder, and handles logout.
Why use it: It replaces your hand-written checks with one set of rules, and adds protections you would likely forget: CSRF tokens, a new session id after login, and secure headers.
Think of it this waySpring Security is a guard standing in front of the whole building. Before this step you checked the door by hand inside each controller. Now the guard checks every visitor before any controller runs.
SecurityConfig is the guard's rule book: which doors are open to everyone, and which need a login.
DbUserDetailsService is the guard's phone call to your database: "does this username exist, and what is the hashed password?"

Start with this tiny example. Add one dependency and restart, with no other change:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

Now every URL asks you to log in. The log prints Using generated security password: ... for a user called user. That is Spring Security's default: lock everything. Next you tell it which pages are open and where your users are.

pom.xml

Concepts in this file

  • spring-boot-starter-security: A starter bundle: adds Spring Security. It puts a filter in front of every request that checks who the user is and what they may open. Spring Boot manages the version. Direction: Browser request → security filters → controllers.Think of it this way: One shopping-list line that brings the whole security guard.
  • groupId org.springframework.boot: The publisher. artifactId is the library name.Think of it this way: Who made it. The groupId is the maker of the library.
  • Default effect: By default every page is locked and a generated login page appears until you write your own rules (see SecurityConfig).Think of it this way: Just adding it locks every page. The guard starts working at once.

Add the starter inside <dependencies>. You can remove spring-security-crypto: the starter includes it.

SecurityConfig.java

Concepts in this file

  • @Configuration: This class holds security settings for Spring. New imports are about HttpSecurity and SecurityFilterChain.Think of it this way: A sticker: "this class sets things up when the app starts".
  • @Bean SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http): Defines the security rules as a bean. Spring passes in HttpSecurity, a builder to describe the rules. throws Exception is needed because building can fail.Think of it this way: The result of this method is kept by Spring, ready to hand out whenever someone asks for it. It is like a tool in a shared tool cupboard.
  • authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> ...): Starts the list of who may open which URL. The -> part is a lambda (a short inline function).Think of it this way: The part of the rule book about who may open which door.
  • requestMatchers("/register", "/login", "/error").permitAll(): These three addresses are open to everyone, even not logged in.Think of it this way: These doors are open to everyone, with no login needed.
  • anyRequest().authenticated(): Every other URL needs a logged-in user. Otherwise the browser is sent to the login page.Think of it this way: Every other door: show your ID first.
  • formLogin(form -> form.loginPage("/login"): Use our own login.html at /login instead of Spring's default page. Spring itself handles the POST to /login. Receives: username and password fields. Direction: Form → Spring Security (not our controller).Think of it this way: Use my own login page, not Spring's default one.
  • defaultSuccessUrl("/home", true): After a good login always go to /home. true forces it.Think of it this way: After a good login, always go to /home.
  • permitAll(): Lets everybody see the login form pages.Think of it this way: Everyone may see the login page, even if not logged in. Otherwise nobody could log in.
  • logout(logout -> logout.logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout")): Enables Spring's logout (POST /logout) and then sends the user to /login with ?logout so the page can show a message.Think of it this way: Where to go after logout.
  • return http.build();: Builds and hands the finished rules to Spring.Think of it this way: Hand the finished rule book to Spring.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/SecurityConfig.java. The rules, in one place.

Rules are read top to bottom and the first match wins, so anyRequest() goes last. /error is open so error pages work for everyone. formLogin uses your page for GET /login, and Spring Security itself handles POST /login: it reads the fields named username and password, exactly the names your form already uses.

DbUserDetailsService.java

Concepts in this file

  • implements UserDetailsService: Spring Security asks this interface: 'find me this user'. Our class answers using the database. New imports: UserDetails, UserDetailsService, UsernameNotFoundException.Think of it this way: A promise: "I can look up a user by name for the guard".
  • @Service: Spring registers it, and Spring Security finds it automatically.Think of it this way: A sticker: "I am the manager, the rules live here". Spring creates one and keeps it ready.
  • loadUserByUsername(String username): Called by Spring Security during login with the typed name. Receives: username from the login form. Goes to: Spring Security as a UserDetails.Think of it this way: The guard's question: "tell me about this username".
  • @Override: Says this method replaces the one defined in the interface.Think of it this way: A marker: "I am replacing a method that the interface requires". The compiler then checks you spelled it right.
  • repo.findByUsername(username).orElseThrow(...): Gets the User from MySQL, or throws UsernameNotFoundException if none, which Spring Security treats as a failed login.Think of it this way: Take the card out of the box. If the box is empty, ring the alarm "user not found".
  • User.withUsername(...).password(...).roles("USER").build(): Builds Spring Security's own User (full name written because our class is also called User). It carries name, the stored hash and a role. Spring compares the typed password with this hash using the PasswordEncoder bean. Goes to: Spring Security. Direction: MySQL → Security.Think of it this way: Convert your card into Spring's own ID card: username, hashed password and badge.
  • roles("USER"): Gives every user the role USER (stored internally as ROLE_USER).Think of it this way: Stick the USER badge on the ID card.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/DbUserDetailsService.java. Tells Spring Security where your users are.

At login Spring Security calls loadUserByUsername, then checks the typed password against the hash with your PasswordEncoder bean. You never compare passwords yourself any more. Spring Security also has a class called User, so it is written with its full package name to avoid a clash with yours.

Restart. The generated password is gone from the log, because Spring Security now uses your DbUserDetailsService. Open /home: you go to your login page. Log in as john / password123, then log out.

Spring Security filter chain (simplified), in front of every controller:

request ─► CsrfFilter ─► UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter ─► ... ─► AuthorizationFilter ─► your controller
             │              │ POST /login only:                          │ checks your rules:
             │              │ loadUserByUsername → BCrypt matches        │ permitAll / authenticated
             │              │ → store the user in the session            │ → redirect to /login if not logged in
             └ refuses a POST without the right _csrf token
Check yourself: what is the difference between authentication and authorization in this step?

Authentication: the UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter checks john's password and remembers him. Authorization: the rules in authorizeHttpRequests decide that a logged-in user may open /home. So far the only authorization rule is "logged in or not". Step 9 adds roles.

Step 9 Authorization: roles

What it is: Each user gets a role, USER or ADMIN. Rules say which roles may open which URLs.
Why use it: Being logged in is not enough for every page. An admin page that lists all users must be closed to normal users.
Think of it this wayAuthentication asks "who are you?" (your ID card). Authorization asks "what may you do?" (the colour of your badge).
A role is a badge. The USER badge opens the normal rooms, and the ADMIN badge also opens the admin room. Spring looks at the badge at each door.

Start with this tiny example. One rule closes a whole set of URLs to everyone except admins:

.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")

StatusMeansExample here
401 UnauthorizedNot authenticated: we do not know who you are.Not logged in. In Part A you are redirected to the login page instead; the API in Part B answers 401.
403 ForbiddenAuthenticated, but not allowed.mary opens /admin.
Check yourself: you make mary an ADMIN in SQL while she is logged in. Can she open /admin straight away?

No. Her roles were loaded into her session when she logged in. She must log out and log in again, which calls loadUserByUsername again and reads the new role.

Part B · Angular with a token

Now the page is an Angular app on http://localhost:4200, and Spring Boot only answers JSON under /api. The same users and BCrypt hashes are used, so john and mary work here too. Install Node.js and the Angular CLI first (see the Developer · PSRS tab, Step 6, or run npm install -g @angular/cli).

Part A: sessionPart B: JWT token
Who keeps the loginThe server, in a sessionThe client, in a signed token
What the browser sendsA JSESSIONID cookie, automaticallyA header Authorization: Bearer <token>, added by your code
LogoutDelete the session on the serverForget the token on the client. It still works until it expires.
CSRF protectionNeeded: cookies are sent automaticallyNot needed: another site cannot add your header
Good forServer-rendered pagesAngular, mobile apps, several servers

Step 10 The smallest Angular login

What it is: An Angular component with two boxes and a button. [(ngModel)] links each box to a field in the class.
Why use it: This is Step 1 again in Angular: the same form, but the values land in a TypeScript class instead of being sent by the browser.
Think of it this wayIn Part A the server built each page. Now Angular is a waiter in the browser: it takes the order (the form), carries it to the kitchen (Spring Boot), and brings back the food (JSON). The page never reloads. An input linked to a field works like two cups joined by a string: type in one and the other changes too.

Start with this tiny example. One input, linked to one field:

<input [(ngModel)]="username" />      // typing "john" sets this.username = "john"

Step 11 Spring Boot answers JSON; Angular calls it

What it is: A @RestController under /api that reads JSON with @RequestBody, a second security chain for /api/**, and an Angular service that sends the POST.
Why use it: Angular cannot use Thymeleaf pages. It needs plain data, and the API needs rules that fit a token, not a session.
Think of it this wayJSON is a plain-text packing slip, for example {"username":"john","password":"123"}.
@RequestBody tells Spring: "unpack the slip and fill this Java object."
A REST controller sends back data (the parcel), not a finished page.
If Angular and Spring run on different ports, the server must also say "yes, that other address may call me" (CORS). Otherwise the browser blocks the call, even though the server is fine.

Start with this tiny example. A record for the JSON coming in, and @RequestBody to read it:

public record LoginRequest(String username, String password) {}

@PostMapping("/login")
public String login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) {    // {"username":"john","password":"..."}
    return "Hello " + req.username();
}

AuthController.java

Concepts in this file

  • @RestController: Like @Controller, but methods return data (JSON) instead of template names. For Angular, not HTML pages. Direction: Controller → JSON in the HTTP response.Think of it this way: Like @Controller, but it returns data (JSON), not pages.
  • @RequestMapping("/api/auth"): Prefix for all addresses in this class. So /login here means /api/auth/login.Think of it this way: Every address in this class begins with this text.
  • public record LoginRequest(String username, String password): A short class for the incoming login JSON. A record makes fields and getters like username() automatically. Receives: JSON {username, password} from Angular.Think of it this way: A small data holder for the packing slip that comes in. Each field is one item on the slip.
  • public record LoginResponse(String username, String role): The shape of the answer sent back as JSON. Goes to: Angular.Think of it this way: A small data holder for the packing slip that goes out. It contains only what is safe to show (never the password hash).
  • @PostMapping("/login") login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req): @RequestBody reads the JSON body of the request and converts it into the record. Angular → POST /api/auth/login → login() → UserService.login → MySQL.Think of it this way: The mailbox for "here is my form" requests, which happen when the user clicks the button.
  • orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)): If the login is wrong, answers with HTTP status 401 Unauthorized. New imports: HttpStatus, ResponseStatusException.Think of it this way: No match means answer 401: "not allowed".
  • return new LoginResponse(...): On success, returns the username and role, converted to JSON. Goes to: Angular.Think of it this way: Fill the outgoing slip. Spring turns it into JSON by itself.
  • @PostMapping("/register") @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED): Registers a new user. On success the reply has status 201 Created and no body (void).Think of it this way: The mailbox for "here is my data". @ResponseStatus(CREATED) answers with 201, meaning "created", instead of the default 200.
  • @Valid @RequestBody User user: Reads the JSON as a User and checks its validation rules. If invalid, Spring replies 400. Angular → POST /api/auth/register → UserService.register.Think of it this way: Unpack the JSON slip into the object and check its rules, in one go.
  • @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class): Catches that error if thrown in this controller (username taken) and runs taken.Think of it this way: A safety net. If this kind of alarm rings anywhere in this class, run this method instead of crashing.
  • @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CONFLICT) Map.of("error", e.getMessage()): Replies 409 Conflict with JSON like {"error": "Username already taken"}. Goes to: Angular.Think of it this way: Answer with 409, "conflict" (the username is taken), and a small JSON message with the reason.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/AuthController.java. Login and register for Angular.

It reuses UserService.login from Step 6, so the BCrypt check is the same. A wrong password gives 401, a bad input (@Valid) gives 400, and a taken username gives 409 Conflict through the @ExceptionHandler. The two records are the JSON shapes: Spring turns JSON into LoginRequest and LoginResponse into JSON.

Class and JSON shapes

A @RestController at @RequestMapping("/api/auth") with two records: LoginRequest(String username, String password) and LoginResponse(String username, String role). Then the UserService from the constructor.

Login

ApiSecurityConfig.java

Concepts in this file

  • Why: A second security chain only for /api/** so the Angular app gets status codes, not login pages. The first chain (SecurityConfig) stays for the Thymeleaf pages. New imports are for Order, Customizer, SessionCreationPolicy, HttpStatusEntryPoint, HttpStatus and the CORS classes.
  • @Order(1): Chains are tried in order. This one is checked first.Think of it this way: There can be several rule books. This one is read first.
  • securityMatcher("/api/**"): This chain applies only to URLs starting with /api/.Think of it this way: This rule book applies only to addresses that start with /api.
  • csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()): Turns off CSRF protection (the hidden-token check used by forms). A JSON API has no such forms. Be careful: only for APIs that do not use cookies for login.Think of it this way: CSRF protection is for pages that use cookies. This API will use a token, not a cookie, so it is switched off here.
  • cors(Customizer.withDefaults()): Turns on CORS and uses the CorsConfigurationSource bean below.Think of it this way: Use the list of allowed visitors that is defined below (CORS).
  • sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS): The server keeps no session. Each request must carry its own proof of identity.Think of it this way: Do not keep a cloakroom. Every request must prove who it is on its own.
  • requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll(); anyRequest().authenticated(): Login and register are open. Any other /api URL needs authentication.Think of it this way: These doors are open to everyone, with no login needed.
  • authenticationEntryPoint(new HttpStatusEntryPoint(UNAUTHORIZED)): When not authenticated, reply 401 instead of redirecting to the login page. Goes to: Angular as an HTTP status.Think of it this way: When someone is not logged in, answer with a plain 401. Do not redirect to a login page, because Angular is not a page the server can redirect.
  • corsConfigurationSource(): Defines CORS: which other websites may call the API. The browser blocks calls between different addresses unless the server allows them.Think of it this way: The guest list of who may call this server from another address.
  • setAllowedOrigins(List.of("http://localhost:4200")): Only the Angular dev server may call the API.Think of it this way: Only the Angular app at this address is on the guest list.
  • setAllowedMethods / setAllowedHeaders: Allowed HTTP methods and request headers (Authorization, Content-Type).Think of it this way: Which kinds of calls (GET, POST...) and which headers are allowed.
  • registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", config): Applies these rules to all /api URLs. Direction: Angular (port 4200) → Spring (port 8080) is allowed.Think of it this way: Apply the guest list to every address under /api.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/ApiSecurityConfig.java. A second set of rules, only for /api/**.

@Order(1) makes Spring Security try this chain first; securityMatcher limits it to /api/**. Every other URL falls through to SecurityConfig from Part A. STATELESS: no session, every request must prove itself (with a token from Step 12). CSRF off: it protects cookies, and this API uses no cookies. 401 instead of a redirect: Angular cannot show a redirect to an HTML login page.

Package and imports

Package line and the 13 imports shown in the full code.

The API chain

A @Configuration class with an @Order(1) @Bean api(HttpSecurity http): securityMatcher("/api/**"), CSRF off, CORS on, no session, /api/auth/** open and everything else authenticated, and a 401 entry point.

Allow Angular's address

A CorsConfigurationSource bean that allows the origin http://localhost:4200, the methods GET POST PUT DELETE OPTIONS and the headers Authorization and Content-Type, for /api/**.

Why CORS is needed:

Angular page at http://localhost:4200  ──POST──►  API at http://localhost:8080
             (one origin)                              (another origin: the port differs)

1. The browser first sends OPTIONS /api/auth/login  ("may 4200 send a POST with Content-Type?")
2. Spring answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:4200
3. Only then does the browser send the real POST and let Angular read the answer.

curl and Postman ignore CORS: it is a rule inside browsers.

Step 12 JWT: the server gives Angular a token

What it is: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is three Base64 parts joined by dots: a header, the payload (who you are, until when) and a signature made with a secret only the server knows.
Why use it: With no session (STATELESS), the next request must prove who it is. The client sends the token, and the server checks the signature: if one character of the payload was changed, the check fails.
Think of it this wayA JWT is a festival wristband. You show your ticket (the password) once at the gate and get a wristband. After that you only show the wristband.
It has three parts separated by dots: the header, the payload (who you are and when it expires), and the signature (a stamp only the server can make).
Anyone can read a wristband, but nobody can fake the stamp. So never put secrets inside it.

Start with this tiny example. This is a whole JWT. Only the colors are added here:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJqb2huIiwicm9sZSI6IkFETUlOIiwiaWF0IjoxNzkzNzUwNDAwLCJleHAiOjE3OTM3NTQwMDB9.kVgLDQ2AVXBAcuhCf5kY8mPYgt3U4OjwrkzeVFZphCM

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9   header:  {"alg":"HS256"}
eyJzdWIiOiJqb2huIiwicm9sZSI6IkFETUlOIiwiaWF0IjoxNzkzNzUwNDAwLCJleHAiOjE3OTM3NTQwMDB9   payload: {"sub":"john","role":"ADMIN","iat":1793750400,"exp":1793754000}
kVgLDQ2AVXBAcuhCf5kY8mPYgt3U4OjwrkzeVFZphCM   signature: HMAC-SHA256 of the first two parts, with the server's secret

Anyone can read the payload: it is only Base64, not encryption. So never put a password or private data in it. Nobody can change it without the secret, because the signature would no longer match.

pom.xml

Concepts in this file

  • <dependency>: One library Maven downloads and adds to the project. Identified by groupId (owner) + artifactId (name) + version.Think of it this way: One line on the shopping list (pom.xml): "please bring me this library".
  • jjwt-api: JJWT is a library to create and read JWTs (JSON Web Tokens: signed text that proves who you are). The api jar holds the classes you write code against, such as Jwts.builder(). Used by: JwtService.java.Think of it this way: The public part: the names you call in your code.
  • jjwt-impl: The real working code behind the api. Not needed to compile, so it has <scope>runtime</scope>: only present when the app runs.Think of it this way: The engine behind it. It is only needed when the app runs.
  • jjwt-jackson: Lets JJWT turn token contents to and from JSON, using Jackson (the JSON library Spring already uses). Also runtime scope.Think of it this way: Lets JWT read and write its JSON parts.
  • <version>0.12.6</version>: The version. All three jars must use the same one so they fit together.Think of it this way: The version of the library. The three jjwt lines should use the same version.

Add the JJWT library (three parts) inside <dependencies>.

Spring Boot does not manage JJWT's version, so you write it. jjwt-api is what your code uses; the other two are only needed at run time.

Goes to: this.key and this.minutes.Think of it this way: Read the value from application.properties and put it in this variable.
  • Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes(UTF_8)): Turns the secret text into bytes, then into a SecretKey object for HMAC signing. The same key signs and checks tokens. Receives: secret string. Goes to: field key.Think of it this way: Turn the secret text into a real stamp key.
  • create(username, role): Builds a signed token string for one user. Receives: username and role from AuthController after a good login. Returns: the token String.Think of it this way: Make a wristband for this user.
  • Jwts.builder().subject(...).claim("role", role): Starts a token. subject is who the token is about (the username). claim adds your own named value into the token body.Think of it this way: Write on the wristband: who it is for (subject) and extra facts (claims) such as the role.
  • .issuedAt(...).expiration(...): Writes the creation time and the end time (now + minutes) into the token. After that time, checking fails.Think of it this way: Print the issue time and the expiry time on the wristband.
  • .signWith(key).compact(): Signs the token with the secret key so it cannot be changed unnoticed, then builds the final text header.payload.signature. Goes to: returned to the controller, then to Angular.Think of it this way: Press the secret stamp, then squeeze the three parts into one string.
  • username(token): Reads a token back. Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key)...parseSignedClaims(token) checks the signature and the expiry, and throws JwtException if either is bad. getPayload().getSubject() returns the username inside. Receives: token text from JwtFilter. Returns: the username.Think of it this way: Read who the wristband belongs to. It also checks the stamp, and a fake or expired one raises an alarm.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/JwtService.java. Makes a token and reads one back.

create writes the payload (sub = username, role, issued-at, expiry) and signs it. username checks the signature and the expiry first: a changed or expired token throws a JwtException instead of returning a name.

Step 13 A filter reads the token on every request

What it is: A filter that runs before every /api request: it reads the Authorization: Bearer ... header, checks the token and tells Spring Security who the user is.
Why use it: Spring Security does not read JWTs from JJWT by itself. Your filter is the bridge: after it runs, hasRole and authenticated() work exactly as in Part A.
Think of it this wayA filter is a checkpoint on the road to the controller. Every request drives through it.
It reads the header Authorization: Bearer ..., checks the stamp, and if it is good it tells Spring "this is john, let him through". No wristband, or a fake one, and the request is turned back.

Start with this tiny example. The token arrives in one header. The first 7 characters are the word Bearer and a space:

String header = request.getHeader("Authorization");   // "Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..."
String token = header.substring(7);                   // "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..."

JwtFilter.java

Concepts in this file

  • extends OncePerRequestFilter: A filter is code that runs on each request before the controller. This base class guarantees it runs once per request. Receives: every request that matches /api/**.Think of it this way: A checkpoint that runs exactly once for each request.
  • JwtFilter(JwtService jwt, UserDetailsService users): Constructor with the two helpers it needs. It has no @Component, so ApiSecurityConfig creates it with new and passes them in. Receives: JwtService and DbUserDetailsService from ApiSecurityConfig.Think of it this way: Spring delivers the tool through the constructor. Your class says what it needs, and Spring brings it.
  • request.getHeader("Authorization"): Reads the Authorization header. A token arrives as Bearer <token>. Receives: header sent by the Angular interceptor or curl.Think of it this way: Read the Authorization line on the envelope.
  • header.substring(7): Cuts off the first 7 characters ("Bearer ") to leave only the token. Goes to: jwt.username(token).Think of it this way: Cut off the first 7 characters (the word Bearer and a space), so only the wristband is left.
  • users.loadUserByUsername(username): Loads the user (with roles) from the database by the name found in the token. Receives: username from the token. Returns: a UserDetails.Think of it this way: Look the person up in the database, to get their current badges.
  • new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(user, null, user.getAuthorities()): Builds a "this person is logged in" object. No password (null) because the token already proved it.Think of it this way: Make the name tag: the user, no password needed any more, and the badges.
  • SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth): Stores the logged-in person for this request. Later rules (authenticated(), hasRole) and controllers (Authentication auth) read it from here. Goes to: Spring Security rules and ApiController.Think of it this way: Pin the name tag on for the rest of this request. Controllers can now see who it is.
  • catch (JwtException | ...): A bad, expired or unknown-user token is ignored, so the request stays anonymous and the rules answer 401.Think of it this way: A fake or expired wristband: pin nothing. The guard will answer 401 later.
  • chain.doFilter(request, response): Passes the request on to the next filter and finally the controller. Always runs, with or without login.Think of it this way: Wave the request on to the next checkpoint. If you forget this line, every request stops here.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/JwtFilter.java. No @Component: the API chain creates it, so it runs only for /api/**.

OncePerRequestFilter runs once per request. Putting an Authentication in the SecurityContextHolder means "this request is john, with these roles". The roles come from the database through your DbUserDetailsService, so a role change counts on the next request. chain.doFilter always runs, or the request would stop here.

Class and helpers

A class JwtFilter that extends OncePerRequestFilter, with a JwtService and a UserDetailsService from the constructor.

Read the header

Override doFilterInternal(request, response, chain). Read the Authorization header, and continue only if it starts with "Bearer ".

Log the user in for this request

In a try: get the username from the token, load the user, make a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(user, null, user.getAuthorities()) and put it in the SecurityContextHolder. Catch JwtException | IllegalArgumentException | UsernameNotFoundException (a bad token, an empty one, or a deleted user) and do nothing.

Pass the request on

After the if, always call chain.doFilter(request, response);.

Step 14 Angular keeps the token and sends it

What it is: The service stores the token after login, and an HTTP interceptor adds the Authorization header to every request.
Why use it: Without the interceptor you would add the header by hand in every call, and one forgotten header gives a 401.
Think of it this wayAn interceptor is a mail clerk who stamps every outgoing letter. You do not add the token to each request yourself. The interceptor adds the Authorization header to every call Angular sends. The token itself is kept like a wristband in your pocket, so it is ready when the clerk needs it.

Start with this tiny example. An interceptor is a function that can change every request on its way out:

export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  return next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: 'Bearer abc' } }));
};
