What you already wrote

tap runs code on the answer without changing it: here it saves the token. sessionStorage is cleared when the tab is closed. localStorage would survive a restart, but both can be read by any script on the page, so a cross-site scripting (XSS) bug could steal the token. The safest place is an HttpOnly cookie, which scripts cannot read.

Step 15 Pages, routes and guards

What it is: A route guard (CanActivateFn) runs before Angular opens a page and can send the user elsewhere. You add a home page, an admin page and the routes.
Why use it: A user who is not logged in should land on the login page, not on an empty home page full of 401 errors.
Think of it this wayA guard is a doorman for a page. Before Angular opens /home it asks the guard: "is this person logged in?" Yes: open the page. No: send them to /login.
Important: the guard protects the screen only. The server must still check the token on every request, because anyone can change what is in their own browser.

Start with this tiny example. A guard is a function that returns true (open the page) or another address:

export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = () =>
  inject(AuthService).isLoggedIn() ? true : inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login']);

auth.guard.ts

Concepts in this file

  • CanActivateFn: A guard: a function Angular asks before opening a route. It returns true (open) or a redirect (go elsewhere). Used by: canActivate in app.routes.ts.Think of it this way: A type of function that answers "may this person open this page?" with yes or no.
  • authGuard: Lets the user in only if logged in. Otherwise sends them to the login page. Receives: AuthService.isLoggedIn(). Goes to: true, or redirect to /login.Think of it this way: The doorman: is this person logged in?
  • inject(AuthService).isLoggedIn() ? true : ...: A guard has no constructor, so inject() is used inside the function to get services.Think of it this way: Ask Angular for the helper (AuthService). Angular delivers the same shared one everywhere.
  • inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login']): Builds a redirect address. Returning it tells Angular to go there instead.Think of it this way: Ask Angular for the tool that moves between pages.
  • adminGuard: Lets only admins in; others go back to /home. It protects the screen only; the real protection is hasRole("ADMIN") on the server. Receives: AuthService.isAdmin().Think of it this way: A second doorman: does this person have the ADMIN badge?

createUrlTree is a redirect. A guard only decides what the screen shows: anyone can type sessionStorage.setItem('role','ADMIN') in the console and open the admin page. The real protection is on the server, which still answers 403, so the page stays empty.

Step 16 When the token runs out

What it is: The interceptor also watches the answers. On a 401 it forgets the token and goes back to the login page.
Why use it: A token expires (here after 60 minutes). Without this, the user stays on a page where every call silently fails.
Think of it this wayA token is a day pass at a theme park. When it runs out, the server answers 401, "not allowed". catchError is the attendant who notices the 401 and sends you back to the ticket office (the login page).

Start with this tiny example. pipe(catchError(...)) runs only when a request fails:

return next(req).pipe(
  catchError((err) => { console.log(err.status); return throwError(() => err); }),
);

Concepts in this file

  • next(req).pipe(catchError(...)): Sends the request, then watches the answer. catchError runs only if the answer is an error. Receives: the error from the server.Think of it this way: Pass the request on, but listen for trouble in the reply.
  • err: HttpErrorResponse: The error object. err.status is the HTTP code, such as 401.Think of it this way: The trouble report. It has the status number, such as 401.
  • if (err.status === 401) { sessionStorage.clear(); router.navigate(['/login']); }: The token is useless, so delete it and show the login page. Goes to: browser storage cleared, route /login.Think of it this way: 401 means the wristband is missing, wrong or expired. Clear the pocket and go to the login page.
  • return throwError(() => err): Passes the error on, so the component's own error handler still runs. Goes to: the subscriber's error callback.Think of it this way: Pass the trouble on, so the screen can still show its own message.
  • Unchanged: The token-adding part (clone with Authorization header) is as before.

Test it quickly: set jwt.minutes=1 in application.properties, restart Spring Boot, log in, wait one minute and reload /home: you are back on the login page. Set it back to 60.

Way to end a JWT loginHowCost
Short expiryTokens live 15 to 60 minutesThe user logs in again often
Refresh tokenA long-lived second token, kept in an HttpOnly cookie, gets a new short tokenMore code: one more endpoint and a table
Deny listStore the ids of logged-out tokens until they expire, and refuse themA database or Redis check on every request
Check yourself: a user logs out in Angular, but someone copied their token earlier. Does the token still work?

Yes, until it expires: the server keeps no list of tokens. That is why tokens are short-lived. A deny list or refresh tokens can end them sooner.

Interview questions

What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication proves who you are (username and password, or a token). Authorization decides what you may do once known (roles such as ADMIN). Failing the first gives 401, failing the second gives 403.

Why hash passwords instead of encrypting them?

Encryption can be reversed with the key, so a stolen key reveals every password. A hash is one-way: the app never needs the password back, it only checks that a typed password gives the same hash.

Why BCrypt and not MD5 or SHA-256?

MD5 and SHA-256 are fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second. BCrypt is slow on purpose, its cost factor can be raised over time, and it salts every hash.

What is a salt, and where does BCrypt keep it?

Random data mixed into each password before hashing, so equal passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. BCrypt stores it inside the 60-character hash itself, after the cost, so no extra column is needed.

How does Spring fill an object from a form?

Data binding: for each request parameter it calls the setter with the same name (username → setUsername). That is @ModelAttribute, which is the default for an object parameter.

@RequestParam, @ModelAttribute or @RequestBody?

@RequestParam: one form field or query value. @ModelAttribute: many form fields into one object. @RequestBody: a JSON body, read by Jackson.

What is mass assignment, and how do you stop it?

A client sends a field it should not set (role=ADMIN) and binding copies it into the object. Bind into a DTO that only has the allowed fields, or set sensitive fields in the service, as Step 9 does.

What does Spring Security's filter chain do?

It is a list of servlet filters in front of every request: CSRF checks, reading the login form or a token, storing the user in the SecurityContext, and finally checking the authorization rules before the controller runs.

What is UserDetailsService for?

It tells Spring Security how to load a user by username (here from MySQL). Spring Security then compares the password with the PasswordEncoder bean and reads the roles from the returned UserDetails.

Session or JWT?

A session keeps the login on the server and the browser sends a cookie: simple, easy to revoke, good for server-rendered pages. A JWT keeps it in a signed token the client sends: no server memory, works across several servers and for mobile or Angular clients, but hard to revoke before it expires.

Is a JWT encrypted?

No, a normal JWT (JWS) is only signed. Anyone can decode the payload, so it must not hold secrets. The signature only proves nobody changed it.

Where should Angular keep the token?

In memory or sessionStorage is simple, but any script on the page can read it, so an XSS bug can steal it. An HttpOnly, Secure cookie cannot be read by scripts, but then CSRF protection is needed again.

What is CSRF, and why is it off for the JWT API?

Another site makes your browser send a request with your cookie. A hidden token in each form stops it. The JWT API uses no cookies, and another site cannot add your Authorization header, so CSRF cannot happen there.

What is CORS, and who enforces it?

The browser rule that stops a page on one origin (scheme, host, port) from reading answers from another, unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Only browsers enforce it; curl and Postman ignore it. It is not a server security feature.

401 or 403?

401 Unauthorized: not authenticated (no or bad token). 403 Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed (mary on an admin URL).

hasRole or hasAuthority?

hasRole("ADMIN") checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN: Spring adds the ROLE_ prefix. hasAuthority checks the exact string, which suits fine-grained permissions such as jobs:delete.

Is an Angular route guard security?

No. It runs in the user's browser and can be bypassed. It only improves the user experience. Every rule must also be checked on the server.

What does an HTTP interceptor do?

It runs for every HttpClient request and response: here it adds the Bearer header and handles 401 in one place, instead of in every call.

How do you log out with a JWT?

The client forgets the token, and the server keeps tokens short-lived. To end a token sooner you need a deny list of logged-out token ids, or short access tokens with refresh tokens you can revoke.

Why show the same message for a wrong username and a wrong password?

Different messages would let anyone find out which usernames exist (user enumeration), which helps password-guessing attacks.

Part C · After login: the user's own data

Login only answers "who are you?". Now the app uses that answer: every user gets their own notes, can edit and delete only their own, and can change their password. Part C builds on the Part B code (the JWT API and Angular). One rule runs through all of it: the owner always comes from the token, never from the request.

Step 18 My notes: data that belongs to a user

What it is: A notes table where each row has an owner, and an API that returns only the notes of the user who is calling.
Why use it: Almost every real app works like this: my orders, my messages, my files. If the owner came from the request, anyone could ask for anyone's data.
Think of it this wayEvery note has an owner, like a name written on each locker. The server never trusts the browser to say who you are. It reads your name from the token (Principal), and asks the database only for the lockers with your name on them.

Start with this tiny example. The owner comes from the token, through Principal:

@GetMapping("/api/notes")
public List<NoteView> mine(Principal principal) {
    return notes.mine(principal.getName());          // "john", from the token
}

// WRONG: the caller chooses whose notes to read
public List<NoteView> mine(@RequestParam String owner) { ... }   // ?owner=john

Spring Security fills Principal from the Authentication your JwtFilter stored. The client cannot change it without breaking the token's signature.

Note.java

Concepts in this file

  • @Entity: Marks the class as a database table. Hibernate manages it.Think of it this way: A sticker: "this class is a table". One object is one row.
  • @Table(name = "notes"): The table is called notes.Think of it this way: The table's name tag. Without it, Spring picks a name by itself.
  • @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY): id is the primary key. IDENTITY lets MySQL fill it with 1, 2, 3 on insert. Receives: the number from MySQL after save().Think of it this way: The ID column: a unique number for each row, like a student number. The database counts for you (1, 2, 3...), so you never set it.
  • @Column(nullable = false, length = 100): On title: column cannot be empty and holds up to 100 characters. text uses length 2000.Think of it this way: A rule for this column: it may not be empty, and it has a maximum length if one is given.
  • @ManyToOne(optional = false): Many notes belong to one user. optional = false means a note must always have an owner. Receives: a User object. Goes to: the owner_id column.Think of it this way: Many notes belong to one user, like many lockers with one owner. optional = false means no locker without an owner.
  • @JoinColumn(name = "owner_id"): The notes table gets a column owner_id holding the id of the user, a foreign key to the users table.Think of it this way: The column in the notes table that holds the owner's id. It is like a name written on each locker.
  • getters and setters: Hibernate and Spring use them to read and fill the fields. There is no setId because the database makes the id.Think of it this way: The windows to look in and put things in, like for the User card.

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/Note.java. One row of the new notes table.

@ManyToOne means many notes belong to one user. Hibernate makes a column owner_id with a foreign key to users.id, so MySQL refuses a note whose owner does not exist. optional = false makes the column NOT NULL.

NoteRepository.java

Concepts in this file

  • public interface NoteRepository extends JpaRepository<Note, Long>: an interface with no body. Spring Data builds the real class at startup. Note is the entity (table) it manages, Long is the type of its id. It gives free methods such as save, findById, findAll, delete. Receives: Note objects from the service. Goes to: the MySQL table notes (and back).Think of it this way: You only write the outline of a librarian, and Spring builds the real one. You get ready-made methods such as save, findAll and deleteById. The two types in the brackets are: the card type, and the type of its id.
  • findByOwnerUsernameOrderByIdDesc(String username): a query written only by its name. Spring reads it as: find Notes where owner.username equals the argument, sorted by id from newest to oldest. Roughly SQL: SELECT ... FROM notes JOIN users ... WHERE username = ? ORDER BY id DESC. Receives: a username text from NoteService. Goes to: MySQL as a query; returns a List<Note> back to the service.Think of it this way: Spring reads the long name as a sentence: find the notes whose owner's username is X, newest first. The method name is the query.
  • List<Note>: the return type, a list of Note objects (empty list if none found).Think of it this way: A list of many notes, not just one.
  • Flow: NoteService → NoteRepository → MySQL (notes JOIN users).

File: src/main/java/com/example/login/NoteRepository.java.

Spring Data reads the method name: findBy + OwnerUsername (the username of the owner) + OrderByIdDesc (newest first). It writes SELECT ... FROM notes n JOIN users u ON u.id = n.owner_id WHERE u.username = ? ORDER BY n.id DESC for you.

Check yourself: why does the API return NoteView and not Note?

Jackson writes every getter of the object. Note.getOwner() is a User, and User.getPassword() is the BCrypt hash, so every note would leak its owner's hash and role. A DTO sends only the fields you choose.

Step 20 Edit and delete: only your own notes

What it is: PUT /api/notes/{id} and DELETE /api/notes/{id}, each checking that the note belongs to the caller before changing it.
Why use it: This is the most common security bug in real APIs: IDOR, Insecure Direct Object Reference. The URL holds an id, and the server forgets to check whose it is.
Think of it this wayThe bug: the URL says /notes/5, and the server only checks that note 5 exists. Then anyone can delete anyone's note just by changing the number.
The fix: also check that note 5 belongs to you. It is like a hotel: the key opens room 5 only if your name is on the booking.

Start with this tiny example. The bug in two lines, and the fix:

// mary sends DELETE /api/notes/1, and note 1 is john's
notes.deleteById(id);                                    // WRONG: john's note is gone

Note note = notes.findById(id).orElseThrow(...);         // 404 if it does not exist
if (!note.getOwner().getUsername().equals(username))     // 403 if it is not yours
    throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);

Being logged in is not enough. The rule anyRequest().authenticated() lets mary in; only the owner check in the service stops her.

NoteService.java · version 2

Concepts in this file

  • Changed from the earlier NoteService: three methods added (mineById, update, delete) with an ownership check. Reason: without it, any logged-in user could edit or delete another user's note by guessing its id (this bug is called IDOR). mine and create are unchanged.
  • mineById(Long id, String username): loads a note and checks it belongs to the user. Receives: note id and the username from the token. Returns: the Note, or throws an error.Think of it this way: Fetch the note, but only if it is mine.
  • notes.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)): look up by id; if no such note, throw an error that becomes HTTP 404.Think of it this way: Find the note. If it does not exist, answer 404, "not found".
  • if (!note.getOwner().getUsername().equals(username)): if the note's owner is not the caller, throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN) gives HTTP 403.Think of it this way: If the owner is not this person, refuse. The number in the address is never trusted on its own.
  • update(id, username, title, text): calls mineById first (so the check always runs), changes title and text, then notes.save(note) runs an UPDATE. Goes to: MySQL notes table; the updated Note returns to the controller.Think of it this way: Both start by checking that the note is really yours.
  • delete(id, username): notes.delete(mineById(id, username)) removes the row only after the check passes. Goes to: MySQL DELETE.Think of it this way: Both start by checking that the note is really yours.
  • import ...ResponseStatusException / HttpStatus: lets service code choose the HTTP status of the error answer.Think of it this way: Like saying "I will use tools from that toolbox". Without the import, Java does not know the name.

Step 21 Change your password

What it is: POST /api/me/password with the current and the new password. The server checks the current one with BCrypt, then saves the new hash.
Why use it: Asking for the current password means a stolen token, or a laptop left unlocked, is not enough to take over the account.
Think of it this wayChanging a password is login and register stuck together. First prove you know the old password (the matches check). Then grind the new one (the hash) and save it. Never skip the first part, or anyone who borrows your open laptop can lock you out.

Start with this tiny example. It is the login check from Step 6, then the register hash:

if (!encoder.matches(oldPassword, user.getPassword()))   // same check as login
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Current password is wrong");
user.setPassword(encoder.encode(newPassword));            // same hash as register

Concepts in this file

  • @Service: marks this class as the business-logic layer. Spring creates one object of it and keeps it ready to hand to other classes.Think of it this way: A sticker: "I am the manager, the rules live here". Spring creates one and keeps it ready.
  • PasswordEncoder encoder: the tool that hashes passwords (one-way scrambling) and checks them. It is the bean defined earlier in PasswordConfig. Spring passes it in through the constructor. Receives: UserRepository and PasswordEncoder from Spring (constructor injection). Goes to: the two private final fields.Think of it this way: The meat grinder, delivered by Spring.
  • register(User user): version with hashing: refuses a taken name, forces the role to USER, hashes the password, then saves. Setting the role here means a visitor cannot make themselves admin. Receives: a User from the controller. Goes to: MySQL via repo.save, returns the saved User.Think of it this way: The manager's job: check the rules, then file the card.
  • encoder.encode(...): turns the plain password into a hash. The plain text is never stored. Receives: plain password. Goes to: user.setPassword, then the database.Think of it this way: Grind the password. You save the mince, never the original.
  • login(...): finds the user by name and keeps it only if the password matches. Returns an Optional: empty means login failed. encoder.matches(plain, hash) hashes the typed password and compares it with the stored hash. Receives: username and typed password. Goes to: the caller as Optional<User>.Think of it this way: The login method from before. It now also keeps the token in the browser pocket.
  • changePassword(...) (NEW): loads the user, checks the old password, and if it is wrong throws IllegalArgumentException. Otherwise it hashes the new password and saves. orElseThrow() throws if the user does not exist. Receives: username, oldPassword, newPassword from AccountController. Goes to: MySQL (UPDATE of the password hash). The exception goes back up to the controller.Think of it this way: Check the old password, grind the new one, and save it.

Check yourself: mary changes her password. Does the token she had before still work?

Yes, until it expires: the server only checks the signature and the expiry. If the password was changed because the token was stolen, that is a problem. A fix: store a passwordChangedAt time on the user, and in JwtFilter refuse tokens whose iat (issued at) is older.

Check Part C works

  • check_notes.sql shows each note with its owner's username.

Interview questions for Part C

What is IDOR?

Insecure Direct Object Reference: the URL or body has an id (/api/notes/1), and the server acts on it without checking that the caller may use that object. The fix is an ownership check on the server for every id.

Why take the owner from the token and not from the request?

Anything in the request (body, URL, header the client writes) the client controls. The token is signed by the server, so the username in it cannot be changed.

Why return a DTO instead of the entity?

The entity can carry fields the client must not see (the password hash, the role) or must not set. A DTO lists exactly what goes out, and a request record lists exactly what may come in, which also stops mass assignment.

403 or 404 for someone else's object?

403 says "it exists, but not for you". 404 hides that it exists, so ids cannot be probed. Both are correct; 404 is safer for private data.

What does @ManyToOne create in the database?

A foreign key column (here owner_id) in the "many" table pointing to the primary key of the "one" table, with a foreign key constraint.

Why ask for the current password when changing it?

So a stolen token or an open session alone cannot lock the real owner out. Many sites also ask again before changing the e-mail address.

Where should the ownership check live: controller or service?

In the service, in one method that every id-based operation calls, so a new controller or endpoint cannot skip it.

MySQL interview revision: simple examples for every topic. A beginner-friendly study guide covering queries, subqueries, ranking, triggers, stored procedures, transactions, control flow, window functions, indexes and backups. Every example uses one simple company database with employees and departments.

Jump to: Basic queries · Subqueries · Ranking functions · Triggers · Stored procedures · Transactions · Control flow · Window functions · Indexes · Backup and restore · Quick revision table

1. Basic queries SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

A query retrieves, adds, updates or deletes data in a database.

-- Read all employees
SELECT * FROM employees;

-- Find employees earning more than 500000
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 500000;

-- Add an employee
INSERT INTO employees (name, salary, department_id)
VALUES ('Richard', 800000, 1);

-- Update salary
UPDATE employees
SET salary = 900000
WHERE name = 'Richard';

-- Delete an employee
DELETE FROM employees
WHERE name = 'Richard';
Remember the four common operations: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

2. Subqueries a query inside a query

A subquery is a query inside another query. Example: find employees earning more than the average salary.

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary)
    FROM employees
);

How it works:

  1. The inner query calculates the average salary.
  2. The outer query finds employees earning more than that average.

Another example: employees who belong to the IT department, assuming departments has the columns shown.

SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE department_id IN (
    SELECT id
    FROM departments
    WHERE department_name = 'IT'
);

3. Ranking functions RANK, DENSE_RANK, ROW_NUMBER

Ranking functions give each row a position based on its value.

SELECT
    name,
    salary,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS employee_rank
FROM employees;
FunctionPurpose
RANK()Ties share a rank; the next rank is skipped
DENSE_RANK()Ties share a rank; no rank is skipped
ROW_NUMBER()Gives each row a unique row number

Scores of 90, 90 and 80 give:

ScoreRANKDENSE_RANKROW_NUMBER*
90111
90112
80323
* For ROW_NUMBER(), add a tie-breaker such as the employee ID if you need a predictable order.

4. Triggers run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE

A trigger runs automatically when a chosen event happens on a table. Example: record every new employee in an audit table.

First, create the audit table:

CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    message VARCHAR(255),
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

Create the trigger:

DELIMITER //

CREATE TRIGGER after_employee_insert
AFTER INSERT ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO audit_log (message)
    VALUES (CONCAT('New employee: ', NEW.name));
END //

DELIMITER ;

Test it:

INSERT INTO employees (name, salary, department_id)
VALUES ('Anna', 600000, 2);

SELECT * FROM audit_log;

The trigger records the new employee by itself.

  • NEW is the new row (on INSERT and UPDATE).
  • OLD is the row as it was before (on UPDATE and DELETE).
  • MySQL triggers fire on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, BEFORE or AFTER the change.

5. Stored procedures saved SQL you run with CALL

A stored procedure is a group of SQL statements saved in the database and run with CALL. Example: get employees earning at least a given salary.

DELIMITER //

CREATE PROCEDURE GetEmployeesBySalary(
    IN min_salary DECIMAL(10,2)
)
BEGIN
    SELECT name, salary
    FROM employees
    WHERE salary >= min_salary;
END //

DELIMITER ;

Run it:

CALL GetEmployeesBySalary(500000);

Important keywords:

  • CREATE PROCEDURE creates the procedure.
  • IN takes an input value.
  • BEGIN and END wrap the procedure body.
  • CALL runs the procedure.

6. Transactions all together or not at all

A transaction groups changes so they are saved together, or undone together if something goes wrong. Example: move money between two accounts. Suppose accounts has account_id and balance.

START TRANSACTION;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 10000
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 10000
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT;

This takes 10000 from account 1 and adds 10000 to account 2. If you find an error before committing, undo it with:

ROLLBACK;
Important: COMMIT saves the changes; ROLLBACK undoes the changes not yet committed. For a real transfer, also check that the sender has enough money and that both accounts exist before you commit.

7. Control flow in stored procedures IF, CASE, WHILE

Control flow lets a procedure make decisions or repeat work.

A. IF ... ELSE

Check whether a salary is high or low.

DELIMITER //

CREATE PROCEDURE CheckSalary(IN emp_salary DECIMAL(10,2))
BEGIN
    IF emp_salary >= 1000000 THEN
        SELECT 'High Salary' AS result;
    ELSE
        SELECT 'Low Salary' AS result;
    END IF;
END //

DELIMITER ;

Run it: CALL CheckSalary(1200000); Result: High Salary

B. CASE

Use CASE when there are several conditions. It also works in a normal SELECT.

SELECT
    name,
    salary,
    CASE
        WHEN salary >= 1000000 THEN 'High'
        WHEN salary >= 500000 THEN 'Medium'
        ELSE 'Low'
    END AS salary_level
FROM employees;

C. Loops

A loop repeats statements. This procedure counts from 1 to 5.

DELIMITER //

CREATE PROCEDURE CountNumbers()
BEGIN
    DECLARE counter INT DEFAULT 1;

    WHILE counter <= 5 DO
        SELECT counter;
        SET counter = counter + 1;
    END WHILE;
END //

DELIMITER ;

Run it: CALL CountNumbers(); It repeats until counter is greater than 5.

8. Window functions OVER()

A window function works out a value across related rows without merging them into one row, unlike GROUP BY. Example: each employee's salary next to the average salary of everyone.

SELECT
    name,
    salary,
    AVG(salary) OVER () AS average_salary
FROM employees;

Every employee stays visible, and the average appears on each row. A running total of salaries:

SELECT
    name,
    salary,
    SUM(salary) OVER (
        ORDER BY id
    ) AS running_total
FROM employees;

Common window functions:

  • RANK(): ranking with gaps after ties
  • ROW_NUMBER(): unique row numbers
  • DENSE_RANK(): ranking without gaps
  • SUM() OVER(): windowed sum
  • AVG() OVER(): windowed average
  • LAG() and LEAD(): read the previous and the next row
Ranking functions are a type of window function.

9. Indexes find rows faster

An index helps MySQL find rows faster, like the index at the back of a book. Suppose you often search employees by name:

CREATE INDEX idx_employee_name
ON employees(name);

Now this search can use the index to find Richard faster:

SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE name = 'Richard';

Other useful examples:

-- Index salary
CREATE INDEX idx_salary
ON employees(salary);

-- Create a unique index
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_email
ON employees(email);

The unique index needs an email column and stops two rows having the same (non-NULL) email.

See the indexes: SHOW INDEX FROM employees; Remove one: DROP INDEX idx_employee_name ON employees;

Remember: indexes speed up searches and joins, but they use storage and slow down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, because MySQL must keep them up to date.

10. Backup and restore mysqldump

A backup is a copy of your database that you can use to recover the data if it is lost or damaged.

A. Create a backup

Run this in Command Prompt or PowerShell, not inside the mysql> prompt:

mysqldump -u root -p company_db > company_backup.sql
  • mysqldump exports the database.
  • -u root is the MySQL user.
  • -p asks for the password.
  • company_db is the database to back up.
  • > writes the output to company_backup.sql.

The file holds the SQL statements that recreate the tables and their data.

B. Restore a backup

First create the target database, inside MySQL:

CREATE DATABASE company_restore;

Then, in Command Prompt or PowerShell:

mysql -u root -p company_restore < company_backup.sql

This loads the backup into company_restore.

C. Check the restore

USE company_restore;

SHOW TABLES;

SELECT * FROM employees;

You should see the restored tables and their data.

Important: keep backups in a safe place and test restoring them now and then. A backup is only useful if you can restore it.

Oral interview

Speak about yourself
with confidence

First learn how to introduce yourself in the past, present and future. Then practise 24 common software developer and AI interview questions, each with a model answer you can make your own.

Oral interview preparation. An oral interview tests how clearly you speak, not how much you can type. Read each answer aloud, then say it again in your own words. Answers are written in simple English so that you can remember them.

Jump to: Tenses guide · Build your introduction · Explain an organization · About yourself · Software development · AI and ML · Final year project · Best vocabulary · Delivery tips

Start here explain yourself in every tense

Every good introduction moves through time: who you are now, what you did, and what you will do. Use this table to build sentences.

TenseUse it forExample about yourself
Past simpleFinished actions, education, historyI completed my Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science. I built a speed control system for my final year project.
Past perfectSomething that happened before another past momentBefore I started my internship, I had learned Python and Java.
Present simpleWho you are, facts, routineI am a Computer Science graduate. I work at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.
Present continuousWhat is happening now, this periodI am working on [your current task] and I am preparing for a developer role.
Present perfectExperience that counts now, no exact dateI have worked as an intern for two years and I have used Git every day.
Present perfect continuousSomething started in the past and still going onI have been working at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT for two years.
Future (will / going to)Plans, goals, promisesI will move into a full developer role. I am going to learn cloud tools.
Future continuousWhat you will be doing at a future timeIn five years I will be leading a small team.
Future perfectSomething finished by a future timeBy 2030 I will have become a senior developer.
Conditional (would)What you would do if hired, polite goalsIf you hire me, I would learn your systems quickly and deliver on time.
The 3-step formula: Education (past simple: what I studied and built) → Experience (present perfect: what I have done up to now) → Future (what I want next). Say it in about 60 seconds. Finish with a short reason why you are a good fit.

Build your introduction type your facts, get your speech

Fill in the boxes with your own facts. The page writes a short introduction in the past, present and future. It stays in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere. Then read it aloud and change the words so it sounds like you.

Explain an organization your school, your company, or the one you want to join

Use the same order: what it is, its history, what it does now, what it is planning. Fill in the boxes and press the button.

Example: your organization in all tenses

PAST     "Before, breeders and researchers used traditional methods.
          They were slow and mostly manual."
PRESENT  "Today the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT is a research
          organisation that works for food security. It develops digital tools
          that help researchers and breeders work faster."
PERFECT  "These tools have helped breeders save time, and the organisation
          has been improving them step by step."
FUTURE   "In the future it will keep building tools that make research
          faster, and I will help to build them."

1. About yourself the questions that open every interview

1. Tell us about yourself.

Model answer

Use Education, Experience, Future: start with your Bachelor’s degree, then your work experience, then your goal. Keep it to about 60 seconds.

“My name is [Name]. First, my education: I completed my Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science at [University] in [year], and for my final year project I built Vehicle’s Automatic Speed Control Using AI, where a camera and a YOLO model read traffic signs and the vehicle slows down by itself. Then, my experience: for the last two years I have worked as an intern at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, a research organisation that works for food security by developing digital tools that help researchers and plant breeders work faster than with traditional methods. My work is to [what you do, e.g. support the software and data side of these tools]. In this time I have worked with Java, Spring Boot, MySQL and Git. Looking ahead, I want to work as a software developer who uses AI to solve real problems, and I am looking for a team where I can keep learning and add value.”

Do not read out your CV. Give two facts about your degree, two or three about your experience, and one clear goal.

2. What did you study at university?

Model answer

“I completed a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science at [University] in [year]. The courses I enjoyed most were programming (Java and Python), database systems, software engineering and artificial intelligence. I also did practical work: building web applications with Spring Boot and a MySQL database, and for my final year project I trained an object detection model. Since then I have spent two years as an intern at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, applying what I learned in a real organization. The degree taught me to break a big problem into small steps and to test each step.”

3. Why do you want this position?

Model answer

“There are three reasons. First, the role matches what I have been practising for two years: backend development, data and AI. Second, [Company] works on [what the company does], and I want to take the experience I gained as an intern at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and use it on your products as a full team member. Third, I learn best in a team with experienced developers, and I am ready to move from intern to a full developer role.”

Before the interview, read the company website and replace the bracket with one true sentence about what they do.

4. What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Model answer

Strengths: “I learn new tools fast, I finish what I start, and I like to test my work. For example, I learned YOLO and OpenCV for my final year project in a few weeks and got it working on a real camera, and I have kept learning new tools during my two years at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.”

Weakness (honest, with a fix): “I used to spend too long trying to make my code perfect. Now I build a working version first, then improve it, and I set a time limit for each task.”

A weakness must be real but not fatal for the job, and you must say what you are doing about it.

Bonus. What does your organization do? (Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT)

Model answer

“The Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT is a research organisation. Its work supports food security. One way it does this is by developing digital tools that help researchers and plant breeders work faster than they could with the traditional methods they used before, which were slow and mostly manual. With these tools, researchers can collect, manage and analyse their data more quickly, so they can make decisions sooner. My role is to [what you do] for these tools.”

Short version (15 seconds): “It is a research organisation that works for food security by building digital tools that help breeders work faster than with traditional methods.”

Only say specific numbers, crops or tool names that you know are true. If asked for more detail, describe the tool you personally worked on.

5. Where do you see yourself in 5 years?

Model answer

“In five years I will have grown from an intern with two years of experience into a strong, trusted developer. I hope to be leading small features or a small team, and to have experience in both backend systems and AI. I also want to keep learning, for example cloud and MLOps, so that I can take products from an idea to production.”

Stay close to the job. Do not say “I want your job” or “I want to open my own company”.

2. Software development OOP, Spring Boot, REST, SQL, Git

6. What is Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)?

Model answer

OOP is a way of writing programs as objects that hold data (fields) and behaviour (methods). It has four pillars:

Encapsulation: keep data private and expose it through methods. Inheritance: a class reuses another class (Car extends Vehicle). Polymorphism: the same method call behaves differently for different objects. Abstraction: show what something does and hide how.

Example: a Vehicle class with speed and brake(); Car and Truck extend it and brake differently.

7. Explain the difference between an interface and a class.

Model answer

A class is a blueprint that can hold fields, constructors and full method code, and you can create objects from it. An interface is a contract: it lists the methods a class must have, and says nothing about how they work. You cannot create an object of an interface directly.

A class can extend only one class but implement many interfaces. In Spring we often code to an interface, such as UserService, so the implementation can change without breaking the callers.

8. What is dependency injection in Spring Boot?

Model answer

Dependency injection means a class does not create the objects it needs; Spring creates them and hands them in. The objects Spring manages are called beans (marked with @Service, @Repository, @Component).

Best practice is constructor injection: public UserController(UserService service) { this.service = service; }. Benefits: less coupling, easier testing (you can pass a fake service), and cleaner code.

9. What is a REST API?

Model answer

REST is a style for web services where each thing (a resource, such as a user) has a URL, and you use standard HTTP methods on it: GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove. It is stateless, meaning each request carries everything the server needs, and data usually travels as JSON.

Example: GET /api/users/5 returns user 5 with status 200; a missing user returns 404.

10. What is the difference between GET and POST requests?

Model answer

GET reads data. Parameters are in the URL, it should not change anything on the server, it can be cached and bookmarked, and repeating it is safe. POST sends data in the request body to create or process something, it is not cached, and repeating it may create duplicates. Never send passwords with GET because the URL is logged and visible.

11. What is Git and why do we use it?

Model answer

Git is a version control system. It records every change to the code, lets many people work on the same project through branches, and lets you go back if something breaks. Daily flow: git add, git commit, git push, and a pull request for review. GitHub is the website that hosts the repository.

Items 11 to 15 were missing from your list, so they were added here as likely follow-up questions.

12. What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?

Model answer

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in its own table (users.id); it cannot be null or repeated. A foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table (orders.user_id), which links the tables and keeps the data consistent.

13. What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?

Model answer

INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, and fills the right-side columns with NULL when there is no match. Example: LEFT JOIN customers to orders shows customers who have never ordered.

14. What is Spring Boot and why use it?

Model answer

Spring Boot is a framework that makes it fast to build Java applications. It gives auto-configuration, an embedded server (Tomcat), starter dependencies, and easy support for REST, databases (Spring Data JPA) and security. You can run a service with one command and very little setup.

15. What is authentication versus authorization, and what is a JWT?

Model answer

Authentication proves who you are (login). Authorization decides what you may do (roles such as ADMIN or USER). A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token the server gives after login; the client sends it with each request, and the server checks the signature, so it does not need to keep a session.

3. AI and machine learning ML, YOLO, precision, recall, mAP

16. What is machine learning?

Model answer

Machine learning is when a computer learns patterns from data instead of being given fixed rules. We give it examples, it adjusts its internal numbers to make fewer mistakes, and then it can predict on new data. Example: show thousands of labelled sign photos and it learns to recognise a stop sign.

17. What is the difference between AI, Machine Learning and Deep Learning?

Model answer

They are nested. AI is the big idea: machines doing tasks that need intelligence. Machine learning is a part of AI that learns from data. Deep learning is a part of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, and it is what makes image, speech and language models work well.

Picture three circles, one inside the other: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning.

18. What is YOLO used for?

Model answer

YOLO (“You Only Look Once”) is a deep learning model for real-time object detection. It looks at the whole image once and returns, in one pass, a box around each object, its class (for example “speed limit 50”) and a confidence score. Because it is fast, it works on live camera video, which is why I used it for traffic signs.

19. What do precision and recall mean?

Model answer

Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP): of everything the model said was a sign, how much really was. Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN): of all the real signs, how many the model found.

For my project, low precision means false signs that slow the car for no reason; low recall means missed signs, which is more dangerous. I want both high, and the F1 score combines them.

20. What is mAP in object detection?

Model answer

mAP is mean Average Precision, the main score for detection. For each class we plot precision against recall and take the area under the curve (the Average Precision); mAP is the average over all classes. A box counts as correct when its overlap with the real box (IoU) is above a threshold: mAP@0.5 uses 0.5, and mAP@0.5:0.95 averages over stricter thresholds. Higher is better, with 1.0 the maximum.

4. Final year project Vehicle’s Automatic Speed Control Using AI

21. Explain your “Vehicle’s Automatic Speed Control Using AI” project.

Model answer

“This was my final year project at university. It is a system that adjusts a vehicle’s speed automatically by reading road signs. The problem: drivers miss or ignore speed limit signs, which causes accidents and fines. My solution: a camera watches the road, a YOLO model detects the traffic sign and tells me which one it is, the program reads the speed limit, compares it to the current speed, and sends a command to the speed controller to slow down or hold the speed. The result: [add your real result, for example ‘it detected signs with mAP of 0.__ and reduced speed within __ seconds’].”

Replace every [bracket] with your real numbers. If you do not know a number, say how you tested instead of inventing one.

22. What technologies did you use?

Model answer

“AI: Python, YOLO (Ultralytics), OpenCV for camera and image handling. Data: a labelled traffic sign dataset [name it], with augmentation. Hardware: a camera, a [Raspberry Pi / laptop] and a [microcontroller such as Arduino] with a motor driver to control speed. Software: [Java Spring Boot or Python] for the control logic, Git and GitHub for version control.”

List only what you really used. An interviewer will ask a follow-up about every item you name.

23. What challenges did you face?

Model answer

Use the STAR shape: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Example:

“The model worked well on my dataset but missed signs in strong sunlight and at night (situation). I needed it to work in real conditions (task). I added augmented images with different brightness and blur, collected extra photos myself, and tuned the confidence threshold (action). Detection became far more reliable, and I learned that data quality matters more than the model (result).”

Other true challenges you can use: slow frame rate on small hardware, similar-looking signs, and making the vehicle slow down smoothly instead of suddenly.

24. How did the AI detect traffic signs?

Model answer

1. The camera captures a frame. 2. OpenCV resizes it and prepares it for the model. 3. The YOLO network, trained on labelled sign images, scans the frame once and outputs boxes, class names and confidence scores. 4. I keep detections above a confidence threshold (for example 0.5) and remove duplicate boxes with non-max suppression. 5. The detected class, such as “Speed limit 50”, becomes a target speed. 6. The controller compares it to the current speed and lowers or holds the speed.

Training: I labelled signs with boxes, trained for [N] epochs, and checked precision, recall and mAP on a test set the model had not seen.

Best vocabulary the words and phrases to use most

Use simple, strong words. These are the most useful ones in interviews. Pick five or six that fit you and use them naturally; do not try to use them all.

Strong action verbs (instead of "I did")

Instead ofSayExample
madebuilt, developed, designed, createdI developed a REST API with Spring Boot.
fixedresolved, debugged, solvedI resolved a slow query by adding an index.
helpedsupported, assisted, contributed toI supported researchers with their data.
usedapplied, implemented, worked withI implemented object detection with YOLO.
made betterimproved, optimized, streamlinedI optimized the report so it ran faster.
looked atanalyzed, investigated, reviewedI analyzed the data and found the cause.

startedlaunched, initiated, introducedI introduced Git to the team.
learnedmastered, picked up, adapted toI picked up Docker in two weeks.
handledmanaged, maintained, deliveredI delivered the feature on time.

Words that describe you (strengths)

WordUse it in a sentence
reliableI am reliable: when I promise a task, I finish it.
analyticalI am analytical, so I look at the data before I decide.

Connecting phrases (to sound organized)

PurposePhrases
Start an answer“That’s a good question.” · “Let me explain.” · “In simple terms…” · “There are three main points.”
OrderFirst… · Then… · After that… · Finally…

Finish“To sum up…” · “In short…” · “That is how I would do it.”

Time words: "Since then", "since", "for"

"Since then" means "from that time until now" or "after that point in time". Use it to connect something in the past (your degree) to the present (your experience). Use it with the present perfect (have/has + verb).
PhraseMeaningExample
Since thenfrom that time until now; after that pointI completed my degree in [year]. Since then, I have worked as an intern for two years.
since + point in timefrom a specific start until nowI have worked at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT since [year].
for + length of timehow long it has lastedI have used Java and Spring Boot for two years.
agohow long before now (past simple)I finished my final year project [two years] ago.
up to now / so faruntil the present momentSo far, I have built three projects.
After that / Afterwardsthe next step in the storyI graduated. After that, I joined the Alliance as an intern.
Currently / At the momentnowI am currently improving my skills in AI and cloud tools.
In the future / Looking aheadwhat comes nextLooking ahead, I want to become a software developer who uses AI.
Remember: after since then use the present perfect (I have learned), not the past simple. Say "Since then, I have learned Spring Boot", not "Since then, I learned Spring Boot".

Practice: choose five verbs and three describing words from above, then write two sentences about your work at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT using them. Say the sentences aloud until they feel natural.

Delivery tips how to sound confident

TipHow
Be shortAnswer in 30 to 90 seconds. Stop, then let the interviewer ask more.
Use STARFor “challenge” or “experience” questions: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Be honestSay “I have not used that, but I would learn it by…”. Never invent numbers.
Think aloudFor a technical question, say what you know first, then build the answer step by step.
Practise out loudRecord yourself on your phone. Listen for filler words (“umm”, “like”) and speak more slowly.
Ask a questionAt the end ask: “What does a good first three months look like in this role?”
Know your projectBe ready to explain every tool and every number you put on your CV.
Important: the model answers contain [brackets] and example numbers. Replace them with your real facts before the interview. Your own true answer always sounds better than a memorised one.
